Grokking Beyond the Euclidean Norm of Model Parameters

Pascal Jr Tikeng Notsawo    Guillaume Dumas    Guillaume Rabusseau
Abstract

Grokking refers to a delayed generalization following overfitting when optimizing artificial neural networks with gradient-based methods. In this work, we demonstrate that grokking can be induced by regularization, either explicit or implicit. More precisely, we show that when there exists a model with a property PP (e.g., sparse or low-rank weights) that generalizes on the problem of interest, gradient descent with a small but non-zero regularization of PP (e.g., ℓ1\ell_{1} or nuclear norm regularization) results in grokking. This extends previous work showing that small non-zero weight decay induces grokking. Moreover, our analysis shows that over-parameterization by adding depth makes it possible to grok or ungrok without explicitly using regularization, which is impossible in shallow cases. We further show that the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm is not a reliable proxy for generalization when the model is regularized toward a different property PP, as the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm grows in many cases where no weight decay is used, but the model generalizes anyway. We also show that grokking can be amplified solely through data selection, with any other hyperparameter fixed.

Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

The optimization of machine learning models today relies entirely on gradient descent (GD). The reasons behind the ability of such a procedure to converge towards generalizing solutions are still not fully understood, particularly in over-parameterized regimes.  Power et al. (2022) recently observed an even more surprising feature of this optimization procedure, grokking: optimization first converges to a solution that memorizes the training data, but after a sufficiently long training time, it suddenly converges on a solution that generalizes.

Previous work has shown that grokking can be observed by using a large-scale initialization and a small (but non-zero) weight decay  (Liu et al., 2023a; Lyu et al., 2023). Moreover, some works have shown that the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the model weights can be used during optimization as a progression measure for generalization since it generally decreases during the transition from memorization to generalization  (Liu et al., 2023a; Thilak et al., 2022; Varma et al., 2023). All these theories have left open the question of whether we always need an ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization to observe delayed generalization or whether the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the parameter is always a good predictor of grokking. This paper attempts to answer these questions. We show that the dynamic of grokking goes beyond the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm, that is: If there exists a model with a property PP (e.g., sparse or low-rank weights) that fits the data, then GD with a small non-zero regularization of PP (e.g., ℓ1\ell_{1} or nuclear norm regularization) will also result in grokking, provided the number of training samples is large enough. Moreover, the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the parameters is no longer guaranteed to decrease with generalization when it is not the property sought.

We first establish our main theorem (Theorem 2.1), which theoretically characterizes the relation between grokking and regularization. This theorem is a cornerstone of our argument, demonstrating that the generalization delay scales like 1/(α​β)1/(\alpha\beta), where α\alpha is the learning rate and β\beta is the regularization strength of an arbitrary appropriate regularizer. This theoretical characterization extends previous observations, which have been mainly focused on ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization, providing a more general framework for understanding grokking dynamics.

Building upon this theoretical foundation, we validate its implications both theoretically and empirically across various settings: sparsity (Theorem 3.1) and low-rankness (Theorem 3.4). For sparsity, we focus on a linear teacher-student setup and show that recovery of sparse vectors using gradient descent and Lasso exhibits a grokking phenomenon, which is impossible using only ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization, regardless of the initialization scale, as advocated by previous art (Lyu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b). Moreover, with a deeper over-parameterized model, there is no need for explicit ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization, as gradient descent is implicitly biased toward such sparse solutions. Similarly, we focus on matrix factorization for the low-rank structure and demonstrate that nuclear norm regularization (denoted ℓ∗\ell_{*}) is necessary for generalization in the shallow case. This complements prior work demonstrating that deeper linear networks can factorize low-rank matrices without explicit regularization (Arora et al., 2018, 2019).

These findings hold beyond shallow and/or linear networks. We show that ℓ1\ell_{1} or ℓ∗\ell_{*} can replace ℓ2\ell_{2} in a more general setting and induce grokking. We demonstrate this on a nonlinear teacher-student setup, on the algorithmic data setup where grokking was first observed (Power et al., 2022), and on image classification tasks. In settings where ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization is not used, the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the model parameters tends to grow during training and after generalization, yet optimization still produces a generalizable solution. This directly challenges the previously held belief that the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of parameters is always a good indicator of grokking.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows111Code to reproduce our experiments: https://github.com/Tikquuss/grokking_beyong_l2_norm.:

  1. (i)

    We show that grokking can be induced by the interplay between the sparse/low-rank structure of the solution and the ℓ1\ell_{1}/ℓ∗\ell_{*} regularization used during training, extending previous results on ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization (Lyu et al., 2023). Our theoretical results extend beyond these specific regularizations, as we characterize the relationship between grokking time, regularization strength, and learning rate in a general setting.

  2. (ii)

    We show that regularization is necessary to observe grokking on sparse or low-rank solutions. Moreover, we empirically show that in deep linear networks, the sparse/low-rank structure of the data is enough to have generalization without explicit regularization. Adding depth makes it possible to grok or ungrok simply from the implicit regularization of gradient descent.

  3. (iii)

    Leveraging the notion of coherence, we show that grokking can be amplified solely through data selection.

  4. (iv)

    We show that ℓ1\ell_{1}/ℓ∗\ell_{*} can replace ℓ2\ell_{2} in a more general setting and induce grokking. Moreover, in such a scenario, and in the shallow sparse/low-rank scenario mentioned above, the grokking phenomenon can not be explained by the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm.

  5. (v)

    We also show that other forms of domain-specific regularizers strongly affect the delay between memorization and generalization.

This paper is organized as follows. We begin by presenting our main theoretical result on grokking time and regularization in Section 2. Sections 3 extend our theoretical framework to concrete sparse recovery and matrix factorization settings, establishing additional theoretical results and providing empirical validation of the two-phase dynamics predicted by our main theorem. Our findings are extended to general non-linear models and other domain-specific regularizations in Section 4. Finally, we discuss and conclude our work in Section 5.

Throughout this paper, Ω​(⋅)\Omega(\cdot), 𝒪​(⋅)\mathcal{O}(\cdot) and Θ​(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) follow their standard asymptotic definitions.

2 Learning Dynamics: Early and Later Bias

In this section, we will illustrate our hypothesis concerning the induction of grokking by regularization.  Lyu et al. (2023) proved that enlarging the initialization scale and/or reducing the weight decay delays the transition from memorization to generalization, a conclusion already drawn experimentally by Liu et al. (2023a). As we will see below, replacing the weight decay with various other regularizations similarly impacts the generalization delay.

2.2 Theoretical Insights

We now provide high-level theoretical insights on how the dynamics of regularized gradient descent can induce grokking. Let g:ℝp→[0,∞)g:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to[0,\infty) be a differentiable function, h:ℝp→[0,∞)h:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to[0,\infty) be a subdifferentiable function and β>0\beta>0. Typically, gg is the loss function of an overparameterized neural network on the training data, while hh serves as the regularizer. Our goal is to minimize the composite objective f:=g+β​hf:=g+\beta h using subgradient descent with a learning rate α>0\alpha>0. The update rule for this problem is given by

𝐱(t+1)=𝐱(t)−α​(G​(𝐱(t))+β​H​(𝐱(t)))​∀t≥0\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)}=\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\alpha\left(G(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\right)\ \forall t\geq 0 (1)

where G​(𝐱)=∇g​(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x})=\nabla g(\mathbf{x}) is the gradient of gg at 𝐱\mathbf{x} and H​(𝐱)∈∂h​(𝐱)H(\mathbf{x})\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}) is any subgradient of hh at 𝐱\mathbf{x}. We let f∗:=inf𝐱∈ℝpf​(𝐱)f^{*}:=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}f(\mathbf{x}) and Θf:=arg​min𝐱∈ℝp⁡f​(𝐱)⊂ℝp\Theta_{f}:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}f(\mathbf{x})\subset\mathbb{R}^{p}. Similarly, we define g∗g^{*} and Θg\Theta_{g}, and assume g∗=0g^{*}=0 without loss of generality. Lastly, we let hg∗:=inf𝐱∈Θgh​(𝐱)h_{g}^{*}:=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{g}}h(\mathbf{x}) and dist⁡(𝐱,Θf):=inf𝐲∈Θf‖𝐱−𝐲‖2\operatorname{dist}(\mathbf{x},\Theta_{f}):=\inf_{\mathbf{y}\in\Theta_{f}}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}. Intuitively, the training dynamics can be decomposed into two phases under certain conditions on α\alpha and β\beta. The iterates 𝐱(t)\mathbf{x}^{(t)} initially move toward a solution close to the initialization 𝐱(0)\mathbf{x}^{(0)} that minimizes gg (for instance, the kernel solution associated with gg). Later in training, the influence of H​(𝐱)H(\mathbf{x}) dominates the update, driving h​(𝐱(t))≈hg∗h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\approx h_{g}^{*} and f​(𝐱(t))≈f∗f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\approx f^{*} within an additional Θ​(1/α​β)\Theta(1/\alpha\beta) training steps.

We define the Chatterjee–Łojasiewicz (CL) constant for gg at 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} with radius r>0r>0 as (Chatterjee, 2022):

χ​(g,𝐱,r):=inf𝐲∈B​(𝐱,r),g​(𝐲)≠0‖∇g​(𝐲)‖22/g​(𝐲)\chi(g,\mathbf{x},r):=\inf_{\mathbf{y}\in B(\mathbf{x},r),g(\mathbf{y})\neq 0}\|\nabla g(\mathbf{y})\|_{2}^{2}/g(\mathbf{y}) (2)

where B​(𝐱,r):={𝐲∈ℝp∣‖𝐱−𝐲‖2≤r}B(\mathbf{x},r):=\left\{\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\mid\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}\leq r\right\}. The function gg is said to satisfy the rr-CL inequality at 𝐱\mathbf{x} or to be rr-CL at 𝐱\mathbf{x} if and only if 4​g​(𝐱)<r2​χ​(g,𝐱,r)4g(\mathbf{x})<r^{2}\chi(g,\mathbf{x},r). The CL inequality is a strengthening of the classical Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality (Chatterjee, 2022), which has been shown to hold for wide overparameterized neural networks in a neighborhood of their initialization (Liu et al., 2021). The advantage here is that we will require the CL inequality to be satisfied only at initialization for the theorem to hold, unlike the result under PL, which requires the function to satisfy the PL inequality over its entire domain (Karimi et al., 2020).

Theorem 2.1 highlights a dichotomy between memorization and regularization and formalizes a two-phase dynamic in the training process, under the CL assumption on the loss function gg at initialization. The first phase, described in the first bullet point of the theorem, shows that for a sufficiently small regularization strength β\beta, the iterates 𝐱(t)\mathbf{x}^{(t)} remain close to initialization and quickly minimize gg, with g​(𝐱(t1))≤ϵgg(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})})\leq\epsilon_{g}. This corresponds to memorization of the training data, as the model fits the loss gg while staying in a local region where regularization does not dominate. By choosing β\beta too large, we may never minimize gg, hence the lower bound βC\beta^{C} on ϵg\epsilon_{g}, which vanishes as β→0\beta\rightarrow 0.

In the second phase, captured in the second bullet point, when gg and its gradient are already small, the regularization term β​h​(𝐱)\beta h(\mathbf{x}) gradually drives the iterates toward low values of hh, until reaching h​(𝐱(t))≈hg∗h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\approx h_{g}^{*} and f​(𝐱(t))≈f∗f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\approx f^{*} within Θ​(1/α​β)\Theta(1/\alpha\beta) additional steps. If this late-phase bias induced by hh is aligned with generalization, then the grokking time is proportional to 1/α​β1/\alpha\beta (see Figure 2). This observation is consistent with previous findings for h​(𝐱)=‖𝐱‖22h(\mathbf{x})=\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}, where grokking time scales as 1/β1/\beta (Lyu et al., 2023). The learning rate α\alpha does not appear in that result because Lyu et al. (2023) analyze the continuous-time gradient flow setting.

3 Beyond Weight Decay

In this section, we will illustrate examples in which late phase bias associated with generalization is not driven by ℓ2\ell_{2}, namely, sparse recovery and low rank matrix factorization. Indeed, we will see that the use of weight decay alone causes an abrupt transition in the generalization error, as predicted by previous works, but that this transition does not correspond to generalization. We will also show that for a fixed training data size, the depth of the model used or an appropriate choice of training samples can significantly reduce the grokking delay.

We consider the operator ℱ𝐚​(𝐌)=𝐌𝐚∈ℝN\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{M})=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} that take NN measurement vectors {𝐌i∈ℝn}i\{\mathbf{M}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\}_{i} and return the measures {𝐌i⊤​𝐚}i\{\mathbf{M}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{a}\}_{i} of 𝐚∈ℝn\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. For a matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the operator vec⁡(𝐀)∈ℝm​n\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A})\in\mathbb{R}^{mn} stacks the column of 𝐀\mathbf{A} in a vector; σmax/min/i​(𝐀)\sigma_{\max/\min/i}(\mathbf{A}) is the maximum/minimum/ithi^{\text{th}} singular values of 𝐀\mathbf{A}; ‖𝐀‖∗:=∑iσi​(𝐀)\|\mathbf{A}\|_{*}:=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}(\mathbf{A}) and ‖𝐀‖2→2:=σmax​(𝐀)\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2\rightarrow 2}:=\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}).

3.1 Sparse Recovery

Consider a sparse vector 𝐚∗∈ℝn\mathbf{a}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, i.e. s=‖𝐚∗‖0≪ns=\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{0}\ll n, where ‖𝐚∗‖0\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{0} is the number of non-zero components of 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}. Given 𝐲∗=𝐗𝐚∗+𝝃\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}^{*}+\boldsymbol{\xi} with 𝐗∈ℝN×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n} a design matrix and 𝝃∈ℝN\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} a noise vector, we want to minimize f​(𝐚)=g​(𝐚)+β​h​(𝐚)f(\mathbf{a})=g(\mathbf{a})+\beta h(\mathbf{a}) using gradient descent with a learning rate α>0\alpha>0, where 𝐠​(𝐚)=12​‖𝐗𝐚−𝐲∗‖22\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a})=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2} and h​(𝐚)=‖𝐚‖1h(\mathbf{a})=\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1}. Like in Theorem 2.1, the update 𝐚(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)} first moves near the least square solution 𝐚^:=(𝐗⊤​𝐗)†​𝐗⊤​𝐲∗\hat{\mathbf{a}}:=\left(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\right)^{{\dagger}}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}^{*} leading to memorization, with g​(𝐚^)≤12​‖𝝃‖22g(\hat{\mathbf{a}})\leq\frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}. Later in training, ∂h​(𝐚)\partial h(\mathbf{a}) dominates the update, leading to ‖𝐚(t)‖1−‖𝐚∗‖1=𝒪​(α​β)\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}=\mathcal{O}(\alpha\beta) in the order of 1/(α​β)1/(\alpha\beta) more training steps. When α​β\alpha\beta is small, this causes a non-trivial delay between memorization and generalization, i.e., grokking.

Theorem 3.1.

Assume the learning rate, regularization coefficient and the noise term satisfy 0<α​σmax​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)<20<\alpha\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})<2, 0<β​n<σmax​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)0<\beta\sqrt{n}<\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}) and ‖𝐗⊤​𝛏‖2≤C​α​β\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{C\alpha}\beta, C>0C>0. Let ρ2:=σmax​(𝕀n−α​𝐗⊤​𝐗)\rho_{2}:=\sigma_{\max}\left(\mathbb{I}_{n}-\alpha\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\right). There exist t1<∞t_{1}<\infty and C′>0C^{\prime}>0 such that ‖𝐚(t)−^​𝐚‖2≤2​α​β​n1/21−ρ2​∀t≥t1\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{a}\|_{2}\leq\frac{2\alpha\beta n^{1/2}}{1-\rho_{2}}\ \forall t\geq t_{1}, and mint1≤t≤t2⁡(‖𝐚(t)‖1−‖𝐚∗‖1)≤η+(C+C′)​α​β2⟺t2≥t1+Δ​t​(η,t1)\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\right)\leq\frac{\eta+(C+C^{\prime})\alpha\beta}{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\Delta t(\eta,t_{1}), Δ​t​(η,t1):=‖𝐚(t1)−𝐚∗‖22α​β​η\Delta t(\eta,t_{1}):=\frac{\|\mathbf{a}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}}{\alpha\beta\eta}, for any η>0\eta>0.

Proof.

See the proof in section C.4 of the Appendix. ∎

Now let illustrate why 𝐗𝐚(t)=𝐲∗\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}^{(t)}=\mathbf{y}^{*} (memorization) and ‖𝐚(t)‖1=‖𝐚∗‖1\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}=\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1} are enough to conclude 𝐚(t)=𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{(t)}=\mathbf{a}^{*} (generalization) when NN is large enough with a specific class of design matrices 𝐗\mathbf{X} commonly used in practice (Foucart & Rauhut, 2013). For that, let us consider the problem in a more general context, where we have a measurement matrix 𝐌∈ℝN×n\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n} and a list of noisy measurements 𝐲∗=ℱ𝐛∗​(𝐌)+𝝃∈ℝN\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{b}^{*}}(\mathbf{M})+\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} of an unknown signal 𝐛∗∈ℝn\mathbf{b}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} assumed sparse in a know basis Φ∈ℝn×n\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, i.e. 𝐛∗=∑i=1n𝐚i∗​Φ:,i=Φ​𝐚∗\mathbf{b}^{*}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{a}^{*}_{i}\Phi_{:,i}=\Phi\mathbf{a}^{*} with ‖𝐚∗‖0≪n\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{0}\ll n. The aim is to find 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} by minimizing ‖𝐚‖0\|\mathbf{a}\|_{0} subject to ‖ℱΦ​𝐚​(𝐌)−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ\|\mathcal{F}_{\Phi\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{M})-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon, where ϵ\epsilon an upper bound on the size of the error term 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi}, ‖𝝃‖2≤ϵ\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon. Since this is NP-hard (Natarajan, 1995; Donoho, 2006a), ‖𝐚‖0\|\mathbf{a}\|_{0} is often relaxed to its tightest convex relaxation, ‖𝐚‖1\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1} (Foucart & Rauhut, 2013; Chandrasekaran et al., 2012), leading to the convex problem of minimizing ‖𝐚‖1​ subject to ​‖𝐗𝐚−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1}\text{ subject to }\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon, with 𝐗=𝐌​Φ\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{M}\Phi. This is equivalent to the problem of minimizing f​(𝐚)f(\mathbf{a}) presented above, for a suitable choice of β\beta (Rockafellar, 1970; Boyd & Vandenberghe, 2004; Candes et al., 2006).

While classical sparse recovery assumes that the true signal is exactly sparse and the measurements are noise-free, in practice, it is common to design the measurement matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M} for stable and robust recovery. Stability refers to the ability of a reconstruction method to recover an approximation 𝐚\mathbf{a} of a signal 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} whose energy is concentrated on a few components (i.e., approximately sparse), with reconstruction error controlled by the sparsity defect inf‖𝐚‖0≤s‖𝐚∗−𝐚‖\inf_{\|\mathbf{a}\|_{0}\leq s}\|\mathbf{a}^{*}-\mathbf{a}\|, the distance from 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} to the set of exactly ss-sparse vectors. Robustness, on the other hand, means that the reconstruction is resilient to measurement noise, i.e., small perturbations in the observed measurements 𝐲∗=ℱ𝐛∗​(𝐌)+𝝃\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{b}^{*}}(\mathbf{M})+\boldsymbol{\xi} lead to small deviations in the reconstructed signal 𝐚\mathbf{a}, with the error scaling with the noise level ϵ≥‖𝝃‖2\epsilon\geq\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}.

Definition 3.2 (Robust Null Space Property).

A matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is said to satisfy the robust null space property with constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and τ>0\tau>0 relative to a set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] if ‖𝐮S‖1​<ρ∥​𝐮[n]\S∥1+τ​‖𝐀𝐮‖2\|\mathbf{u}_{S}\|_{1}<\rho\|\mathbf{u}_{[n]\backslash S}\|_{1}+\tau\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}\|_{2} for all 𝐮∈ℝn\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}; where 𝐮S=[𝐮i]i∈S∈ℝ|S|\mathbf{u}_{S}=[\mathbf{u}_{i}]_{i\in S}\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|}. It is said to satisfy the robust null space property of order s∈ℕ∗s\in\mathbb{N}^{*} if it satisfies the robust null space property relative to any set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] with |S|≤s|S|\leq s.

Theorem 3.3.

Assume the matrix 𝐗∈ℝN×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n} satisfies the robust null space property with constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and τ>0\tau>0 relative to the support of 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}. Then, under the same condition as in Theorem 3.1 on α\alpha, β\beta and 𝛏\boldsymbol{\xi}, there exist C1,C2,C3>0C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}>0 such that mint1≤t≤t2⁡‖𝐚(t)−𝐚∗‖1≤C1​η+C2​α​β+C3​‖𝛏‖2\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\leq C_{1}\eta+C_{2}\alpha\beta+C_{3}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2} if and only if t2≥t1+Δ​t​(η,t1)​∀η>0t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\Delta t(\eta,t_{1})\ \forall\eta>0.

Proof.

Proof in Section C.5 of the appendix. ∎

It is worth noting that we should instead quantify the training error 12​∑i=1N(y​(𝐗i)−y∗​(𝐗i))2=g​(𝐚)\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(y(\mathbf{X}_{i})-y^{*}(\mathbf{X}_{i})\right)^{2}=g(\mathbf{a}) and the generalization error ℰ​(𝐚)=𝔼𝐱,ε​(y​(𝐱)−yε∗​(𝐱))2\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{a})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\varepsilon}\left(y(\mathbf{x})-y_{\varepsilon}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\right)^{2}, as is common in the context of grokking, with y​(𝐱)=𝐱⊤​𝐚y(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{a} and yε∗​(𝐱)=𝐱⊤​𝐚∗+εy_{\varepsilon}^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{a}^{*}+\varepsilon in our case. Assuming 𝔼​ε=0\mathbb{E}\varepsilon=0, and using Σ=𝔼​[𝐱𝐱⊤]\Sigma=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}], we get ℰ​(𝐚)=(𝐚−𝐚∗)⊤​Σ​(𝐚−𝐚∗)+𝔼​ε2\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{a})=\left(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\right)^{\top}\Sigma\left(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\right)+\mathbb{E}\varepsilon^{2}. Random matrices with independent entries, notably Gaussian and Bernoulli matrices, allow for the lowest restricted isometry constant and, thus, better recovery of sparse vectors (Rauhut, 2010). Under this independent and identically distributed (iid) assumption, we have Σ=σ2​𝐈n\Sigma=\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}_{n} for a certain σ>0\sigma>0, which implies ℰ​(𝐚)=σ2​‖𝐚−𝐚∗‖22+𝔼​ε2\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{a})=\sigma^{2}\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\varepsilon^{2}. So ‖𝐚−𝐚∗‖22\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2} captures well the notion of test (or validation) error commonly used in the context of grokking, while 𝔼​ε2\mathbb{E}\varepsilon^{2} captures the irreducible part of that error.

Memorization

When the initialization 𝐚(1)\mathbf{a}^{(1)} is close to 𝐚^\hat{\mathbf{a}}, it takes less time to memorize since t1t_{1} decreases with ‖𝐚(1)−𝐚^‖∞\|\mathbf{a}^{(1)}-\hat{\mathbf{a}}\|_{\infty}. Another alternative for reducing the term α​β1−ρ2\frac{\alpha\beta}{1-\rho_{2}} and guaranteeing perfect memorization earlier is to reduce β\beta. But this increases the generalization delay Δ​t\Delta t. Low signal-to-noise ratio ‖𝐚∗‖22/𝔼​‖𝝃‖22\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}/\mathbb{E}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2} and over-regularization (large β\beta) also make perfect memorization difficult.

Generalization

After memorization, when ‖𝐚(t)‖1−‖𝐚∗‖1\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1} becomes too small, we have ‖𝐚(t)−𝐚∗‖1≈0\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\approx 0 (Figure 3) since for the problem of interest, the sparse solution 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} is the minimum ℓ1\ell_{1} solution to ‖𝐗𝐚−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon under the sparsity constraint s=‖𝐚∗‖0≪ns=\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{0}\ll n and certain assumptions on 𝐗\mathbf{X} (as illustrated above). The additional number of steps it takes to reach this minimum ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm solution is inversely proportional to α​β\alpha\beta, so that the smaller α​β\alpha\beta is, the longer it takes to recover 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} (grokking), and the smaller is the error ‖𝐚(t)−𝐚∗‖1\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1} when t→∞t\rightarrow\infty (Figure 4).

Validation Experiments

Using (n,s,N,α,β)=(102,5,30,10−1,10−5)(n,s,N,\alpha,\beta)=(10^{2},5,30,10^{-1},10^{-5}), we observe a grokking-like pattern, where the training error ‖𝐗𝐚(t)−𝐲∗‖2\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2} first decreases to 10−610^{-6}, then after a long training time, the recovery error ‖𝐚(t)−𝐚∗‖2\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2} decreases and matches the training error (Figure 3). The generalization results from the interplay between the sparsity level s=‖𝐚∗‖0s=\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{0}, the number of measures NN, the ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization β\beta and the learning rate α\alpha. Small ss requires small NN for generalization. Generalization occurs mainly for small (but non-zero) β\beta (Figure 4). Large β\beta pushes the recovery error to plateau at a suboptimal value early in training (causing complete memorization) or oscillations (causing no memorization). However, small values require longer training time to plateau and generally do so at a lower value of recovery error (grokking). We provided more experiments in Section H.1 of the Appendix.

Other Iterative Method for ℓ1\ell_{1} Minimization

The above results hold for the projected subgradient method, for which the update writes 𝐚(t+1)=Π​(𝐚(t)−α​β​H​(𝐚(t)))\mathbf{a}^{(t+1)}=\Pi\left(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\alpha\beta H(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})\right) with Π\Pi the projection on the set {𝐚∣𝐗𝐚=𝐲∗}\{\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{y}^{*}\}; and for the proximal gradient descent method; for which the update writes 𝐚(t+1)=Sα​β​(𝐚(t)−α​G​(𝐚(t)))\mathbf{a}^{(t+1)}=S_{\alpha\beta}\left(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\alpha G(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})\right) with Sγ​(𝐚)=sign⁡(𝐚)⊙max⁡(|𝐚|−γ,0)S_{\gamma}(\mathbf{a})=\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{a})\odot\max(|\mathbf{a}|-\gamma,0) the soft-thresholding operator. Note the dichotomy between these two methods. Each uses one of the terms of f​(𝐚)f(\mathbf{a}) as the objective to be minimized and the other as a constraint. After every gradient descent update with the gradient of the objective, the iterate is projected onto the feasible set of the constraint. Still, they all exhibit a grokking behavior (more details in Section D.1 of the Appendix). One training step is enough for the projected subgradient to get zero training error. This further shows that generalization here is primarily driven by hh.

3.2 Matrix Factorization

In this section, we study grokking for matrix factorization and extend the results of the previous section on sparse recovery. Given a low rank matrix 𝐀∗∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} of rank rr and a measurement matrix 𝐗∈ℝN×n1​n2\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n_{1}n_{2}}; we aim to minimize rank(𝐀)⁡ s.t. ​‖ℱ𝐚​(𝐗)−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ\operatorname*{rank}(\mathbf{A})\text{ s.t. }\|\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}}\left(\mathbf{X}\right)-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon for 𝐀∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} and 𝐚=vec⁡(𝐀)∈ℝn1​n2\mathbf{a}=\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}n_{2}}; where 𝐲∗=ℱvec⁡(𝐀∗)​(𝐗)+𝝃\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathcal{F}_{\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})}\left(\mathbf{X}\right)+\boldsymbol{\xi} are the measures and 𝝃∈ℝN\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} the error term with ‖𝝃‖2≤ϵ\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon. This is NP-hard (Vandenberghe & Boyd, 1996; Fazel et al., 2004). The usual convex approach for matrix factorization is to  minimize ​‖𝐀‖∗​ s.t. ​‖ℱ𝐚​(𝐗)−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ\text{ minimize }\|\mathbf{A}\|_{*}\text{ s.t. }\|\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}}\left(\mathbf{X}\right)-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon since the trace norm is the tightest convex relaxation of the rank (Fazel et al., 2001; Recht et al., 2010; Candes & Recht, 2012).

Let n=n1​n2n=n_{1}n_{2} and 𝐀∗=𝐔∗​Σ∗​𝐕∗⊤\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{U}^{*}\Sigma^{*}\mathbf{V}^{*\top} be the full SVD of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*}. We are dealing with a compressed sensing problem with the signal vector 𝐚∗=vec⁡(𝐀∗)=Φ​vec⁡(Σ∗)\mathbf{a}^{*}=\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})=\Phi\operatorname{vec}(\Sigma^{*}); where vec⁡(Σ∗)∈ℝn\operatorname{vec}(\Sigma^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is sparse since ‖Σ∗‖0=r≤min⁡(n1,n2)≪n\|\Sigma^{*}\|_{0}=r\leq\min(n_{1},n_{2})\ll n; and Φ=𝐕∗⊗𝐔∗∈ℝn×n\Phi=\mathbf{V}^{*}\otimes\mathbf{U}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} (Kronecker product) has orthonormal column since Φ⊤​Φ=(𝐕∗⊤​𝐕∗)⊗(𝐔∗⊤​𝐔∗)=𝕀n\Phi^{\top}\Phi=\left(\mathbf{V}^{*\top}\mathbf{V}^{*}\right)\otimes\left(\mathbf{U}^{*\top}\mathbf{U}^{*}\right)=\mathbb{I}_{n}. This framework encompasses several matrix factorization problems. Matrix sensing seeks the matrix 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} from NN measurement matrices {𝐗i∈ℝn1×n2}i∈[N]\{\mathbf{X}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}\}_{i\in[N]} and measures 𝐲∗=(tr⁡(𝐗i⊤​𝐀∗))i∈[N]\mathbf{y}^{*}=\left(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{X}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{*})\right)_{i\in[N]}. In this case 𝐗=[vec⁡(𝐗i)]i∈[N]∈ℝN×n\mathbf{X}=[\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X}_{i})]_{i\in[N]}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n} since 𝐲i∗=ℱ𝐚∗​(vec⁡(𝐗i))\mathbf{y}^{*}_{i}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}^{*}}(\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X}_{i})). For a matrix completion task, we have NN measurement vectors222 For standard matrix completion, each 𝐗i(1)\mathbf{X}^{(1)}_{i} (resp. 𝐗i(2)\mathbf{X}^{(2)}_{i}) represents a row ℓ∈[n1]\ell\in[n_{1}] (resp. a column c∈[n2]c\in[n_{2}]) of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} (one-hot encoded in dimensions n1n_{1} and n2n_{2} respectively), giving 𝐲i∗=𝐀ℓ​c∗\mathbf{y}^{*}_{i}=\mathbf{A}^{*}_{\ell c}. (𝐗i(1),𝐗i(2))∈ℝn1×ℝn2\left(\mathbf{X}^{(1)}_{i},\mathbf{X}^{(2)}_{i}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\times\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}} and measures 𝐲i∗=𝐗i(1)⊤​𝐀∗​𝐗i(2)=ℱ𝐚∗​(𝐗i(2)⊗𝐗i(1))\mathbf{y}_{i}^{*}=\mathbf{X}^{(1)\top}_{i}\mathbf{A}^{*}\mathbf{X}^{(2)}_{i}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}^{*}}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(2)}_{i}\otimes\mathbf{X}^{(1)}_{i}\right), that is 𝐲∗=ℱ𝐚∗​(𝐗)\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}^{*}}\left(\mathbf{X}\right) with 𝐗=𝐗(2)∙𝐗(1)∈ℝN×n\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}^{(2)}\bullet\mathbf{X}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n} (face-splitting product).

We now analyze grokking when minimizing f​(𝐀)=12​‖𝐗​vec⁡(𝐀)−𝐲∗‖22+β​‖𝐀‖∗f(\mathbf{A})=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A})-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta\|\mathbf{A}\|_{*} via subgradient descent with learning rate α\alpha. Like in sparse recovery, under some condition on α\alpha and β\beta, the training dynamics can be decomposed in two phases; the memorization phase where update 𝐀(t)\mathbf{A}^{(t)} first moves near the least square solution vec⁡(𝐀^):=(𝐗⊤​𝐗)†​𝐗⊤​𝐲∗\operatorname{vec}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}):=\left(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\right)^{{\dagger}}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}^{*}, and a generalization phase where 𝐀(t)\mathbf{A}^{(t)} converge to the minimum ℓ∗\ell_{*} solution.

Theorem 3.4.

Assume the learning rate, the regularization coefficient and the noise satisfy 0<α​σmax​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)<20<\alpha\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})<2, 0<β​min⁡(n1,n2)<σmax​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)0<\beta\sqrt{\min(n_{1},n_{2})}<\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}) and ‖𝐗⊤​𝛏‖2≤C​α​β\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{C\alpha}\beta, C>0C>0. Let ρ2:=σmax​(𝕀n−α​𝐗⊤​𝐗)\rho_{2}:=\sigma_{\max}\left(\mathbb{I}_{n}-\alpha\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\right). There exist t1<∞t_{1}<\infty and C′>0C^{\prime}>0 such that ‖vec⁡(𝐀(t)−^​𝐀)‖2≤2​α​β​n1/21−ρ2​∀t≥t1\|\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{A})\|_{2}\leq\frac{2\alpha\beta n^{1/2}}{1-\rho_{2}}\ \forall t\geq t_{1}, and mint1≤t≤t2⁡(‖𝐀(t)‖∗−‖𝐀∗‖∗)=η+(C+C′)​α​β2⟺t2≥t1+Δ​t​(η,t1)\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(\|\mathbf{A}^{(t)}\|_{*}-\|\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{*}\right)=\frac{\eta+(C+C^{\prime})\alpha\beta}{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\Delta t(\eta,t_{1}), Δ​t​(η,t1):=‖𝐀(t1)−𝐀∗‖F2α​β​η\Delta t(\eta,t_{1}):=\frac{\|\mathbf{A}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{\text{F}}^{2}}{\alpha\beta\eta}, for any η>0\eta>0.

Proof.

See proof in Section C.6 of the Appendix. ∎

For a suitable 𝐗\mathbf{X}, 𝐗​vec⁡(𝐀(t))=𝐲∗\mathbf{X}\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})=\mathbf{y}^{*} (memorization) and ‖𝐀(t)‖∗=‖𝐀∗‖∗\|\mathbf{A}^{(t)}\|_{*}=\|\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{*} are enough to conclude 𝐀(t)=𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{(t)}=\mathbf{A}^{*}.

Theorem 3.5.

Assume the linear measurement map ℱ⋅​(𝐗)\mathcal{F}_{\cdot}(\mathbf{X}) satisfies the robust rank null space property of order rr with constants ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and τ>0\tau>0, i.e for all 𝐀∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}, ∑ℓ=1rσℓ​(𝐀)≤ρ​∑ℓ=r+1min⁡{n1,n2}σℓ​(𝐀)+τ​‖ℱvec⁡(𝐀)​(𝐗)‖2\sum_{\ell=1}^{r}\sigma_{\ell}(\mathbf{A})\leq\rho\sum_{\ell=r+1}^{\min\{n_{1},n_{2}\}}\sigma_{\ell}(\mathbf{A})+\tau\|\mathcal{F}_{\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A})}(\mathbf{X})\|_{2}. Then, under the same condition as in Theorem 3.4 on α\alpha, β\beta and 𝛏\boldsymbol{\xi}, there exist C1,C2,C3>0C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}>0 such that mint1≤t≤t2⁡‖𝐀(t)−𝐀∗‖∗≤C1​η+C2​α​β+C3​‖𝛏‖2\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{*}\leq C_{1}\eta+C_{2}\alpha\beta+C_{3}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2} if and only if t2≥t1+Δ​t​(η,t1)t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\Delta t(\eta,t_{1}), for any η>0\eta>0.

Proof.

Section C.7 of the appendix. ∎

Despite the similarity between this result and the one obtained on sparse recovery, this similarity is trivial only in the early phases of training. In fact, in sparse recovery problems, we take into account only the iterate 𝐚(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)}, whereas, in matrix factorization, we take into account not only the singular value matrix Σ(t)\Sigma^{(t)} of the iterate 𝐀(t)\mathbf{A}^{(t)}, but also its matrix of singular vectors 𝐔(t)\mathbf{U}^{(t)} (left) and 𝐕(t)\mathbf{V}^{(t)} (right). We used the Wedin’s sin⁡Θ\sin\Theta bound  (Wedin, 1972) to quantify the variations of singular vectors after the memorization phase, and the result shows that they change by at most 𝒪​(α​β/(γ−1))\mathcal{O}\left(\alpha\beta/(\gamma-1)\right) at each iteration, with γ=σmin​(𝐀(t1))/σmax​(𝐀∗)\gamma=\sigma_{\min}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t_{1})}\right)/\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^{*}). Also, if we take a matrix factorization problem and optimize it with only ℓ1\ell_{1}, there is no grokking unless the matrix is extremely sparse so that the notion of sparsity prevails over the notion of rank, which shows the point of studying ℓ∗\ell_{*} separately. Finally, neural networks trained with ℓ1\ell_{1}, ℓ2\ell_{2}, and ℓ∗\ell_{*} have very different properties.

Generalization

When G​(𝐀)G(\mathbf{A}) become negligible compare to β​H​(𝐀)\beta H(\mathbf{A}), the singular values start involving approximately as σi​(𝐀(t+1)−𝐀∗)=|σi​(𝐀(t)−𝐀∗)−α​β|\sigma_{i}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}-\mathbf{A}^{*}\right)=|\sigma_{i}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\mathbf{A}^{*}\right)-\alpha\beta| up to and error of order α​β/(γ−1)\alpha\beta/(\gamma-1). This leads to a generalization through a multiscale singular value decay phenomenon (Figure 5). The small singular value after memorization converges to 0, followed by the next smaller one until ‖𝐀(t)‖∗≈‖𝐀∗‖∗\|\mathbf{A}^{(t)}\|_{*}\approx\|\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{*}. This process requires Θ​(1/α​β)\Theta\left(1/\alpha\beta\right) steps.

Validation Experiments

We set (n1,n2,r,N,α,β)=(10,10,2,70,10−1,10−4)(n_{1},n_{2},r,N,\alpha,\beta)=(10,10,2,70,10^{-1},10^{-4}), and optimize the noiseless matrix completion problem using subgradient descent. We observe a grokking-like pattern, where the training error ‖𝐗​vec⁡𝐀(t)−𝐲∗‖2\|\mathbf{X}\operatorname{vec}\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2} first decreases to 10−410^{-4}, then after a long training time, the recovery error ‖𝐀(t)−𝐀∗‖F\|\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{\text{F}} decreases and matches the training error (Figures 5 and 6).

Other Iterative Method for ℓ∗\ell_{*} Minimization

The above results hold for the projected subgradient method, for which the update writes 𝐀(t+1)=Π​(𝐀(t)−α​β​H​(𝐀(t)))\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}=\Pi\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\alpha\beta H(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})\right) with Π\Pi the projection on the set {𝐀,𝐗​vec⁡𝐀=𝐲∗}\{\mathbf{A},\mathbf{X}\operatorname{vec}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{y}^{*}\}; and for the proximal gradient descent method; for which the update writes 𝐀(t+1)=Sα​β​(𝐀(t)−α​G​(𝐀(t)))\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}=S_{\alpha\beta}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\alpha G(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})\right) with Sγ​(𝐀)=𝐔​max⁡(Σ−γ,0)​𝐕⊤S_{\gamma}(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{U}\max(\Sigma-\gamma,0)\mathbf{V}^{\top} the soft-thresholding operator for 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top} under SVD, where max(Σ−γ,0)i​j=δi​jmax(Σi​j−γ,0)\max(\Sigma-\gamma,0)_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\max(\Sigma_{ij}-\gamma,0). More details in Section D.2.

3.3 Grokking Without Understanding

Contrary to prior studies (Lyu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a), we find that in the over-parameterized regime (N<nN<n), large-scale initialization and non-zero weight decay do not necessarily lead to grokking (Figure 7). In fact, by using only the ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization under large-scale initialization, there is an abrupt transition in the generalization error during training, driven by changes in the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm of the model parameters. This transition, however, does not result in convergence to an optimal solution and can arise even in cases where the problem has no optimal solution due to insufficient training samples (such as sparse recovery or matrix completion using a number of samples far below the theoretical limit required for optimal recovery). We call this phenomenon “grokking without understanding” like Levi et al. (2024) who illustrated it in the case of linear classification, and we attribute it to the fact that the assumptions underlying prior theoretical predictions, particularly Assumption 3.2 of Lyu et al. (2023), are violated in our setting (more details in the Section E of the Appendix).

For the problems above (sparse recovery and matrix factorization), by replacing h​(𝐚)h(\mathbf{a}) in f​(𝐚)=g​(𝐚)+β​h​(𝐚)f(\mathbf{a})=g(\mathbf{a})+\beta h(\mathbf{a}) by h​(𝐚)=12​‖𝐚‖22h(\mathbf{a})=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{a}\|_{2}^{2}, the model converge to the least square solution 𝐚^:=(𝐗⊤​𝐗+β​𝕀n)†​𝐗⊤​𝐲∗\hat{\mathbf{a}}:=\left(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}+\beta\mathbb{I}_{n}\right)^{{\dagger}}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}^{*}, but this solution can not give rise to generalization when N<nN<n.

Theorem 3.6.

Define ρ2:=‖𝕀n−α​(𝐗⊤​𝐗+β​𝕀n)‖2→2\rho_{2}:=\left\|\mathbb{I}_{n}-\alpha\left(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}+\beta\mathbb{I}_{n}\right)\right\|_{2\rightarrow 2}. Assume the learning rate satisfies 0<α<2σmax​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)+β0<\alpha<\frac{2}{\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})+\beta}. Then ‖𝐚(t)−𝐚^‖2≤ρ2t−1​‖𝐚(1)−𝐚^‖2​∀t≥1\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{\mathbf{a}}\|_{2}\leq\rho_{2}^{t-1}\|\mathbf{a}^{(1)}-\hat{\mathbf{a}}\|_{2}\ \forall t\geq 1. On the other hand, for N<nN<n, ‖𝐚^−𝐚∗‖22≥‖(𝕀n−𝐗⊤​(𝐗𝐗⊤)†​𝐗)​𝐚∗‖22\|\hat{\mathbf{a}}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}\geq\|\left(\mathbb{I}_{n}-\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^{\top})^{\dagger}\mathbf{X}\right)\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}. In particular, if 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} has a nonzero component orthogonal to the column space of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, then 𝐚^\hat{\mathbf{a}} cannot perfectly generalize to 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}.

Proof.

Section  C.8 of the Appendix. ∎

Even when ℓ1\ell_{1} is present, if the weight decay β\beta is choose such that ‖𝐚^‖∞≪α​β\|\hat{\mathbf{a}}\|_{\infty}\ll\alpha\beta, then 𝐚(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)} will get stuck near 𝐚^\hat{\mathbf{a}}, and there will be no generalization. So, a bad choice of β\beta can be detrimental to generalization (it is better not to use ℓ2\ell_{2} on that problem unless the initialization scale is nontrivial). Since the minimum ℓ2\ell_{2} norm solution only gives memorization, the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm cannot be used as an indicator of grokking.

3.4 Amplifying Grokking through Data Selection

The analysis of recovery guarantees for matrix factorization hinges on local coherence of the target matrix 𝐀∗=𝐔∗​Σ∗​𝐕∗⊤\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{U}^{*}\Sigma^{*}\mathbf{V}^{*\top} (compact SVD). The local coherence measures μi=n1r​‖𝐔∗⊤​𝐞i(n1)‖2\mu_{i}=\frac{n_{1}}{r}\|\mathbf{U}^{*\top}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(n_{1})}\|^{2} and νj=n2r​‖𝐕∗⊤​𝐞j(n2)‖2\nu_{j}=\frac{n_{2}}{r}\|\mathbf{V}^{*\top}\mathbf{e}_{j}^{(n_{2})}\|^{2} (for (i,j)∈[n1]×[n2](i,j)\in[n_{1}]\times[n_{2}]) quantify how strongly individual rows and columns align with the top singular vectors, where 𝐞i(ni)\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(n_{i})} be the it​hi^{th} vector of the canonical basis of ℝni\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}}. These quantities, also known as leverage scores, indicate the “influence” of each row ii or column jj on the low-rank structure. A row/column with a high leverage score projects strongly onto the span of the singular vectors, meaning that a relatively small number of its entries capture much of the matrix’s structure. Uniformly low coherence (μi\mu_{i} and νi\nu_{i} close to 11) implies that the matrix’s information is well-distributed across rows and columns, thereby reducing the number of samples needed for exact recovery. The significance of local coherence extends to sampling strategies and recovery bounds. For matrix completion, given N≤n1​n2N\leq n_{1}n_{2} and τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], we select the first τ​N\tau N entries (i,j)(i,j) with the highest values of μi+νj\mu_{i}+\nu_{j}, and the remaining (1−τ)​N(1-\tau)N entries uniformly among the rest. As τ→1\tau\rightarrow 1, performance improves, and the number of examples required to generalize decreases exponentially, as does the time it takes the models to do so (Figure 8).

Unlike matrix factorization, large values of coherence are detrimental to generalization for compressed sensing. The incoherence between the measurement vectors (rows of 𝐌\mathbf{M}) and the sparse basis (columns of Φ\Phi) is crucial for successfully recovering 𝐛∗=Φ​𝐚∗\mathbf{b}^{*}=\Phi\mathbf{a}^{*} from the measures 𝐲∗=𝐌𝐛∗+𝝃\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{b}^{*}+\boldsymbol{\xi}. If 𝐌\mathbf{M} is incoherent with Φ\Phi, each measurement captures a distinct “view” of 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*}, reducing redundancy. This diversity of information allows for the successful reconstruction of 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} even with fewer measurements (e.g., below the Nyquist rate for signals). We also observed that higher coherence increases the number of samples required for recovery and delays generalization, while lower coherence results in faster generalization and better recovery. While grokking has been studied extensively, the impact of data selection on grokking remains largely unexplored, making this one of the first works to address this critical aspect. We provide more details in Section G.

3.5 Implicit Bias of the Depth

We explore the role of overparameterization in sparse recovery using a linear network parameterized as 𝐚=⊙k=1L𝐀k\mathbf{a}=\odot_{k=1}^{L}\mathbf{A}_{k}, where the depth L≥2L\geq 2 introduces overparameterization without altering the linearity of the function class. Our findings reveal that depth can replace ℓ1\ell_{1}-regularization for generalization when initialization is small, as the gradient updates introduce a preconditioning effect that promotes sparsity and enables signal recovery. Unlike the shallow case (L=1L=1), where sparsity cannot be enforced without ℓ1\ell_{1}-regularization, depth provides an implicit mechanism that biases updates toward sparsity, resulting in better generalization with fewer measurements (Figure 9). Additionally, depth reduces the generalization delay, with abrupt phase transitions and a staircase-like loss curve during training. The generalization error decreases with increasing depth LL, showing that depth effectively compensates for fewer measurements and facilitates recovery, albeit at the cost of longer training times. For L≥2L\geq 2, large-scale initialization combined with small non-zero ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularization results in grokking, unlike the shallow case where the phenomenon of “grokking without understanding” is observed. More details in Section  F.1 of the Appendix.

We discuss deep matrix factorization in Section F.2 of the Appendix, as it is already well-known that overparametrization by adding depth makes it possible to recover low-rank matrices without any explicit regularization (Gunasekar et al., 2017; Arora et al., 2019; Gidel et al., 2019; Gissin et al., 2019; Razin & Cohen, 2020; Li et al., 2020).

4 General Setting

In this section, we show that ℓ1\ell_{1}, ℓ∗\ell_{*}, and other domain-specific regularizers can replace ℓ2\ell_{2} in a more general setting and induce or control grokking.

Non linear Teacher-Student

We consider a teacher 𝐲∗​(𝐱)=𝐁∗​ϕ​(𝐀∗​𝐱)\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{B}^{*}\phi(\mathbf{A}^{*}\mathbf{x}) from ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} to ℝc\mathbb{R}^{c} with rr hidden neurons; where ϕ​(z)=max⁡(z,0)\phi(z)=\max(z,0). We independently sample NN inputs output pair 𝒟train={(𝐱i,𝐲∗​(𝐱i))}i=1N\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{i}))\}_{i=1}^{N} and optimize the parameters θ=(𝐀,𝐁)\theta=(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}) of a student 𝐲θ​(𝐱)=𝐁​ϕ​(𝐀𝐱)\mathbf{y}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{B}\phi(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}) on them with the square loss function g​(θ)=12​N​∑i=1N‖𝐲θ​(𝐱i)−𝐲∗​(𝐱i)‖22g(\theta)=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|\mathbf{y}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\|_{2}^{2} and different regularizer h​(θ)h(\theta), ℓp\ell_{p} for p∈{1,2,∗}p\in\{1,2,*\}. For all of these regularizer, the smaller is α​β\alpha\beta, the longer is the delay between memorization and generalization (see Figures 10 for the training curve with ℓ1\ell_{1}, and 31, 32,  33 for more results with ℓ∗⁣/2\ell_{*/2}).

Domain Specific Regularization

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (Raissi et al., 2019) leverage prior knowledge from differential equations by incorporating their residuals into the loss function, ensuring that solutions remain consistent with physical laws. Sobolev training (Czarnecki et al., 2017) generalizes this idea by incorporating not only input-output pairs but also derivatives of the target function. We optimizer the student from the previous paragraph by adding on the objective function the first order Sobolev penalty βN​∑i=1N‖∂𝐲θ∂𝐱​(𝐱i)−∂𝐲∗∂𝐱​(𝐱i)‖F2\frac{\beta}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\|\frac{\partial\mathbf{y}_{\theta}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-\frac{\partial\mathbf{y}^{*}}{\partial\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\|_{\text{F}}^{2}, where the hyperparameter β\beta ensures that the model not only fits the data but also respects known smoothness constraints or differential structure, which is crucial in physics-based applications. Large α​β\alpha\beta values lead to faster grokking ( Figures 11 and 34).

Classification

On the algorithmic dataset (Power et al., 2022), ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ∗\ell_{*} have the same effect on grokking as ℓ2\ell_{2}, i.e., smaller regularization coefficient (and learning rate) delay generalization (see Figure 2 for ℓ∗\ell_{*}, and 30 for ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ2\ell_{2}). We observe a similar phenomenon on a two-layer ReLU MLP trained on MNIST (Section H.3.4).

5 Discussion and Conclusion

This work extends the understanding of grokking, showing that the transition from memorization to generalization can be induced not just by ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization but also by sparsity or low-rank structure regularization (e.g., ℓ1\ell_{1} and nuclear norm regularization) or domain-specific regularization. These findings are particularly relevant in practice, where large-scale initialization is not always feasible, yet grokking still occurs. Sparse and low-rank-based models with good generalization performance are very useful in machine learning today, not only because they consume less memory during training and inference but also because they are more interpretable than their dense and full-rank counterparts. The sparsity and low-rank assumptions are also central to techniques such as Low-Rank Adaptation of larger deep learning models (Hu et al., 2021) and model pruning (Han et al., 2015) in resource-efficient deep learning; sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023) for AI safety (Bereska & Gavves, 2024); to name a few.

Our results highlight that in deep models, gradient descent implicitly drives the model towards solutions with sparse or low-rank properties, effectively mitigating overfitting (Arora et al., 2018). We also study the impact of data selection on grokking and demonstrate that it can be mitigated solely through data selection.

Appendix A Related Works

A.1 Grokking

Universality

Liu et al. (2023a) took the first step in demonstrating the universality of grokking by inducing it on non-algorithmic data, notably on image classification, sentiment analysis, and molecule property prediction. On the same line, Gromov (2023); 𝐯\mathbf{v}Zunkovi𝐯\mathbf{v}c & Ilievski (2024); Levi et al. (2024) show that grokking can occur for (analytically solvable toy) models. Barak et al. (2022) observed grokking on the binary sparse parity problem, Charton (2024) on greatest common divisor (with Transformer), Doshi et al. (2024b) on modular polynomials, Lyu et al. (2023) on matrix completion and sparse linear predictors, Beck et al. (2024) and Levi et al. (2024) on binary logistic classification, Xu et al. (2023) on XOR-cluster training data. Miller et al. (2024b) show that grokking occurs beyond neural networks—in models like Gaussian process (regression and classification), linear regression, and Bayesian neural networks—driven by a trade-off between model complexity and error, not just feature learning or weight decay. Wang et al. (2024) and Abramov et al. (2025) show that grokking enables Transformers to develop reasoning abilities, emerging only after extended training, whether on synthetic comparison/composition tasks or real-world multi-hop reasoning augmented with inferred facts. Li (2024) observe that both binary and ternary Transformer exhibit grokking on modular addition under weight decay regularization, and do not do so without weight decay. Mallinar et al. (2024) show that grokking occurs beyond neural networks and gradient descent, as kernel-based Recursive Feature Machines trained with Average Gradient Outer Product also exhibit delayed generalization through emergent structured features. Kumar et al. (2024) find that mice show grokking-like behavior, i.e., even after behavioral performance plateaus, neural representations in sensory cortex continue evolving, improving generalization through margin maximization. Mustafa & Burkholz (2024) investigate grokking-like phenomena in Graph Neural Networks, particularly focusing on tasks involving heterophilic and homophilic graphs.

Interpretability and Explainability

Since the concept of “grokking” emerged, numerous theories have been proposed to explain the phenomenon. Liu et al. (2023b) present representation learning as the main underlying factor of the existence of generalizing solutions, supporting Power et al. (2022)’s preliminary observations. Exploring the direction that separates generalization from memorization solutions (i.e., progressions measures for generalization), recent studies shed light on various factors, such as neuron activity (Nanda et al., 2023), weight norm of the model parameters (Liu et al., 2023a), sparsity (Merrill et al., 2023), time scales of pattern formation (Davies et al., 2023), Fourier gap (Barak et al., 2022), last layer norm (Thilak et al., 2022), fast vs low-frequency components (Zhou et al., 2024), mutual information ratio of neural representation (Song et al., 2024), phase transition (Clauw et al., 2024; Rubin et al., 2024), rank minimization (Yunis et al., 2024), rise and fall in model complexity (DeMoss et al., 2024; Humayun et al., 2024), etc. Also, weight decay and weight norm decrease (Liu et al., 2023a; Varma et al., 2023), a gradual process facilitated by optimization (Nanda et al., 2023; Merrill et al., 2023; Barak et al., 2022; Davies et al., 2023; Notsawo et al., 2023), the instability induced by the Adam optimizer (Thilak et al., 2022), are among the factors that has been use to explain why the transition from memorization to generalization. According to Varma et al. (2023), grokking arises from a generalizing circuit being favored over a memorizing circuit. Miller et al. (2024a) introduce a method to quantify the sharpness of the grokking transition in neural networks. Doshi et al. (2024a) show that in the presence of label corruption, grokking can still occur, with networks first generalizing before later unlearning memorized noise, highlighting a separation between generalization and memorization phases. Zhu et al. (2024) show that grokking in language models emerges when training data exceeds a critical size, with larger models requiring more data to generalize beyond memorization. Huang et al. (2024) propose a unified framework explaining grokking, double descent, and emergent abilities through the lens of competition between memorization and generalization circuits. Chughtai et al. (2023) and Stander et al. (2024) reverse engineer (small) neural networks learning finite group composition via mathematical representation theory. Golechha (2024) show that ℓ2\ell_{2} norm alone can not explain grokking, as it occurs even outside the typical “goldilocks zone”(Liu et al., 2023a), and propose alternative measures like activation sparsity and weight entropy that better track generalization dynamics. Prieto et al. (2025) explain grokking as a result of Softmax Collapse—numerical instability from floating-point errors that halts learning after memorization.

Predictability

To the question of whether grokking can be predicted, Notsawo et al. (2023) answered in the affirmative, proposing as a predictable measure the spectral signature of the training loss in the early optimization phases of the model training. Hu et al. (2024) models neural network training as a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) over weight statistics to uncover discrete training phases. Applied to grokking tasks, this reveals distinct latent states corresponding to memorization and generalization, with “detour” states explaining delayed generalization. The approach offers a structured way to analyze and predict grokking by linking it to transitions between these latent training states. Murty et al. (2023) explore how vanilla Transformers eventually grok hierarchical rules after extended training, and find that weight norm and attention sparsity are inconsistent and often unreliable for forecasting generalization. They introduce a “tree-structuredness” (Murty et al., 2022) metric that significantly outperforms weight norm in predicting whether and when a model will grok. Miller et al. (2024b) argue that grokking may be possible in any model where the solution search is guided by complexity and error. This notion of complexity is related to what we refer to as regularization in our work. Fan et al. (2024) show that deeper MLPs on MNIST grok more often and in stages, and that weight norm poorly predicts generalization compared to internal feature rank dynamics.

Stochasticity

Our work also contradicts the hypothesis put forward when grokking was first observed, namely that grokking may be due to stochasticity or an anomaly in the optimization (Power et al., 2022; Thilak et al., 2022). For sparse recovery and matrix factorization, the optimization algorithms we use are all deterministic (up to initialization).

Feature Learning

Kumar et al. (2023) show that grokking can emerge without weight decay, as a result of a delayed transition from lazy (fixed-feature) to rich (feature-learning) dynamics during training. In contrast, Lyu et al. (2023) explain grokking through implicit bias, showing that large initialization and small weight decay induce a shift from kernel-like to margin-maximizing behavior, highlighting different but complementary mechanisms behind grokking. Xu et al. (2023) provide a theoretical example of grokking in ReLU networks by analyzing the feature learning process under GD, and show that test generalization can emerge well after perfect (and initially non-generalizing) memorization of noisy XOR-cluster training data. Morwani et al. (2024) demonstrate that neural networks trained on tasks like modular addition and sparse parity naturally converge to solutions based on Fourier features and group-theoretic representations (Nanda et al., 2023; Chughtai et al., 2023). This behavior arises from the principle of margin maximization, even without explicit regularization, providing a theoretical explanation for grokking as a delayed transition from memorization to structured feature learning.

Large Initialization and ℓ2\ell_{2} Regularization

A direct work related to ours on grokking is Lyu et al. (2023), which analyzes the emergence of grokking under ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization and large-scale initialization in homogeneous models. Their results show that under such conditions, grokking can occur as a delayed generalization phenomenon. However, their analysis is limited to ℓ2\ell_{2} weight decay and does not generalize to other regularization schemes. In contrast, our work extends beyond ℓ2\ell_{2}, demonstrating that grokking also arises under ℓ1\ell_{1} and nuclear norm (ℓ∗\ell_{*}) regularization, even without large-scale initialization. In the theoretical settings we study—such as sparse recovery and low-rank matrix factorization—ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization alone fails to induce grokking. Instead, it produces a sharp drop in generalization error during training that does not correspond to true generalization. We refer to this failure mode as grokking without understanding, which we attribute to the violation of key assumptions in Lyu et al. (2023) (notably Assumption 3.2). Our results further show that grokking may even be necessary in practice: for instance, when targeting low-rank solutions via ℓ∗\ell_{*} regularization, it is preferable to use the smallest feasible regularization strength and train well beyond the point of overfitting to achieve generalization. Levi et al. (2024) work on classification settings and show that the sharp increase in generalization accuracy may not imply a transition from “memorization” to “understanding” but can be an artifact of the accuracy measure. This aligns with the “grokking without understanding” problem we observe in sparse recovery and low-rank matrix factorization.

Accelerating Grokking

Park et al. (2024) accelerate grokking by using data augmentation for commutative operations and transfer learning across model components aligned with the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation. Lee et al. (2024) accelerate grokking by amplifying slow gradient components, reducing training time across tasks. Xu et al. (2025) accelerate grokking by initializing larger models with embeddings from smaller trained models, eliminating delayed generalization. Minegishi et al. (2025) show that grokking can be accelerated by identifying “grokking tickets”—sparse subnetworks that emerge after generalization—and retraining them, which leads to much faster generalization than the original dense model. (Prieto et al., 2025) accelerate grokking using a stable softmax variant and a gradient projection method to prevent collapse and enable faster generalization without regularization.

Sparsity and Low-Rankness

Barak et al. (2022) observed grokking on the binary sparse parity problem, and Merrill et al. (2023) shows that two subnetworks compete during training on such a task: a dense (memorization) subnetwork and a sparse (generalization) subnetwork. Since a very sparse network that generalizes the sparse parity data can be built (Merrill et al., 2023), we conjecture that it is this sparsity that gives the models trained on this task their grokking nature, as well as the algorithmic dataset (Power et al., 2022), but leave further investigation for future work. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to formally study grokking in the context of sparse recovery and low-rank matrix factorization (the shallow case). Lyu et al. (2023) show that low-rank matrix completion problems exhibit grokking with large initialization. But we prove that even on such a simple model, we do not need way decay and large initialization to observe grokking, but just ℓ1⁣/∗\ell_{1/*} regularization.

A.2 Model Distillation, Sparse Dictionary Learning, Sparse Auto-Encoder, and Coreset Selection

Note that the parameterization 𝐛=Φ​𝐚\mathbf{b}=\Phi\mathbf{a} gives ℱ𝐚​(𝐱)=𝐚⊤​Φ⊤​𝐱\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{a}^{\top}\Phi^{\top}\mathbf{x}, i.e. ℱ𝐚​(𝐗)=𝐗​Φ​𝐚\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{X}\Phi\mathbf{a}; which is a two-layer linear neural network with the weights of the first layer given by Φ⊤∈ℝm×n\Phi^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} (fixed) and those of the second layer given by 𝐚∈ℝm\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, to be optimized. Compressed sensing thus corresponds somehow to a model distillation (teacher-student), where we aimed to find a sparse version of model parameters using fewer data points. This could be strengthened by assuming that we have only the measures 𝐲∗\mathbf{y}^{*} of the sparse representation 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} of the signal and the measurement matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M}, but not the basis in which it is sparse, and the problem is to find both Φ\Phi and 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}, i.e.  minimize ​‖𝐚‖1​ subject to ​‖ℱΦ​𝐚​(𝐌)−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ​ and ​Φ∈𝒞\text{ minimize }\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1}\text{ subject to }\|\mathcal{F}_{\Phi\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{M})-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon\text{ and }\Phi\in\mathcal{C}. This is the case for matrix factorization, where the sparse basis (singular vector space) is jointly optimized along with the sought sparse coordinates 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} (singular values). Here, 𝒞\mathcal{C} can be the set of orthonormal matrix (Φ⊤​Φ=𝕀n\Phi^{\top}\Phi=\mathbb{I}_{n}), unit column norm matrix ( Φ:,i⊤​Φ:,i=1\Phi_{:,i}^{\top}\Phi_{:,i}=1), etc. It can be interesting to see if ℓ1\ell_{1} allows us to recover the parameters with fewer samples than the most used ℓ2\ell_{2} in deep learning. Looking for a sparse 𝐚\mathbf{a} mean, we assume that only a few components of the representation 𝐡​(𝐱)=Φ⊤​𝐱∈ℝn\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})=\Phi^{\top}\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} contribute to the output 𝐲​(𝐱)=𝐚⊤​𝐡​(𝐱)\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x}). This kind of method (sparse auto-encoder) is used a lot in mechanistic interpretability today to separate and interpret the features a pre-trained model has learned (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023), a promising direction for AI safety (Bereska & Gavves, 2024). Compressed sensing theory gives us an idea of how to select data to extract important features with the fewest possible examples: we need to select the samples that are most “incoherent” with the feature extractor (assumed fixed).

This formulation is also related to:

  • •

    The coreset selection problem (Tsang et al., 2005; Huggins et al., 2017; Lucic et al., 2018), which consists of selecting a small subset comprised of most informative training samples such that training on this subset can achieve comparable or even better performance with that on the full dataset (Zhou et al., 2022).

  • •

    The sparse dictionary learning problem (Olshausen & Field, 1996; Aharon et al., 2006; Mairal et al., 2010, 2014), where we have a collection 𝐁∈ℝd×N\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} of NN point in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and aim to write each of them as a combination of a few numbers of atoms of a dictionary Φ∈ℝd×n\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}, that is 𝐁:,i=Φ​𝐀:,i​∀i∈[N]\mathbf{B}_{:,i}=\Phi\mathbf{A}_{:,i}\forall i\in[N], with ‖𝐀:,i‖0\|\mathbf{A}_{:,i}\|_{0} small. Let 𝒞={𝐂∈ℝd×n,‖𝐂:,i‖2≤1​∀i∈[n]}\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n},\|\mathbf{C}_{:,i}\|_{2}\leq 1\ \forall i\in[n]\}. We want Φ^=arg⁡minΦ∈𝒞⁡1N​∑i=1Nl​(𝐁:,i,Φ)\hat{\Phi}=\arg\min_{\Phi\in\mathcal{C}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}l(\mathbf{B}_{:,i},\Phi) with l​(𝐛,Φ)=min𝐚∈ℝn⁡‖𝐛−Φ​𝐚‖22+λ​‖𝐚‖1l(\mathbf{b},\Phi)=\min_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\|\mathbf{b}-\Phi\mathbf{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1}. That is

    Φ^,𝐀^=arg​minΦ∈𝒞,𝐀∈ℝn×N⁡1N​‖𝐁−Φ​𝐀‖F2+λ​∑i=1N‖𝐀:,i‖1\hat{\Phi},\hat{\mathbf{A}}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\Phi\in\mathcal{C},\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times N}}\frac{1}{N}\|\mathbf{B}-\Phi\mathbf{A}\|_{\text{F}}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|\mathbf{A}_{:,i}\|_{1}

    The generalization error is ℰ​(Φ)=𝔼𝐛​l​(𝐛,Φ)\mathcal{E}(\Phi)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}}l(\mathbf{b},\Phi). The sparse coding problem l​(𝐛,Φ)=min𝐚∈ℝn⁡‖𝐛−Φ​𝐚‖22+λ​‖𝐚‖1l(\mathbf{b},\Phi)=\min_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\|\mathbf{b}-\Phi\mathbf{a}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1} is just the problem we study above.

We leave these points as a future direction for this work.

A.3 Finite Field

Compressed Sensing

In compressed sensing and sparse recovery in 𝔽p=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}_{p}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} (for a prime integer pp), incoherence between the measurement matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M} and the sparse basis Φ\Phi remains important but requires modular arithmetic. Recovery of a sparse signal 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*} from the measurements 𝐲∗=𝐌​Φ​𝐛∗\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathbf{M}\Phi\mathbf{b}^{*} is possible, provided that 𝐌\mathbf{M} and Φ\Phi are chosen to ensure low coherence in the modular structure. However, recovery algorithms are more complex due to the finite nature of the field and may involve different mathematical tools (e.g., algebraic techniques from coding theory) instead of standard optimization methods.

Matrix Factorization

We can see 𝐀∗∈𝔽pn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} as representing a binary operation over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, and the aim is to learn this operation from a proportion of sample333For example, 𝐀∗=𝐮𝐮⊤\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top} with 𝐮=[0,…,p−1]\mathbf{u}=\left[0,\dots,p-1\right] for the multiplication operation.. This is the vanilla setup where grokking was first observed (Power et al., 2022). Large-scale initialization can not explain the grokking phenomenon in such a setup since it is often observed with standard initialization. Many works also use mechanistic interpretability to find the algorithm deep neural networks use to generalize in such a setup and propose a progression measure for generalization (Nanda et al., 2023; Gromov, 2023). Still, none explain what makes such data particular. Liu et al. (2023b) propose the representation learning hypothesis but uses a loss function that encourages such representation to emerge for standard deep neural networks (MLP and Transformer). Mohamadi et al. (2024) explain grokking in modular addition as a transition from a kernel regime, where generalization fails, to a rich regime that captures the task’s global algebraic structure—making grokking especially pronounced in modular arithmetic. Investigating how our work can effectively answer why grokking is naturally observed in such a setup is a future direction for this work.

Appendix C Proofs

C.1 Proof of Theorem 2.1

Let g:ℝp→[0,∞)g:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to[0,\infty) be a differentiable function, h:ℝp→[0,∞)h:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to[0,\infty) be a subdifferentiable (often convex) function and β>0\beta>0. We want to minimize f:=g+β​hf:=g+\beta h using gradient descent with a learning rate α>0\alpha>0. The subgradient update rule for this problem is given by

𝐱(t+1)=𝐱(t)−α​F​(𝐱(t))=𝐱(t)−α​(G​(𝐱(t))+β​H​(𝐱(t)))​∀t≥0\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)}=\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\alpha F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})=\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\alpha\left(G(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\right)\ \forall t\geq 0 (3)

where F​(𝐱)∈∂f​(𝐱)=G​(𝐱)+β​∂h​(𝐱)F(\mathbf{x})\in\partial f(\mathbf{x})=G(\mathbf{x})+\beta\partial h(\mathbf{x}), with G​(𝐱)=∇g​(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x})=\nabla g(\mathbf{x}) the gradient of gg at 𝐱\mathbf{x} and H​(𝐱)∈∂h​(𝐱)H(\mathbf{x})\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}) any subgradient of h​(𝐱)h(\mathbf{x}) at 𝐱\mathbf{x}. We want to show that, under certain conditions on α\alpha and β\beta, this procedure will first converge to a solution 𝐱^\hat{\mathbf{x}} that minimize gg after t1<∞t_{1}<\infty training steps, then take additional Δ​t=Θ​(1α​β)\Delta t=\Theta(\frac{1}{\alpha\beta}) training steps to converge to a solution 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} that minimizes both hh and ff. Subdifferentiability, convexity, and smoothness are defined below for completeness.

Definition C.1 (Subdifferentiability).

A function φ:ℝp→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} is said to be subdifferentiable at 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} if and only if there exists 𝐳∈ℝp\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, φ​(𝐲)≥φ​(𝐱)+(𝐲−𝐱)⊤​𝐳∀𝐲∈ℝp\varphi(\mathbf{y})\geq\varphi(\mathbf{x})+(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})^{\top}\mathbf{z}\quad\forall\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}. The set of all such 𝐳\mathbf{z} at is called the subdifferential of φ\varphi at 𝐱\mathbf{x} and is denoted ∂φ​(𝐱)\partial\varphi(\mathbf{x}). When ∂φ​(𝐱)\partial\varphi(\mathbf{x}) is the singleton set, we say that φ\varphi is differentiable at 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

Definition C.2 (Convexity).

A subdifferentiable function φ:ℝp→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} is said to be convex if and only if φ​(𝐲)≥φ​(𝐱)+(𝐲−𝐱)⊤​𝐳∀𝐱,𝐲∈ℝp,∀𝐳∈∂φ​(𝐱)\varphi(\mathbf{y})\geq\varphi(\mathbf{x})+(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})^{\top}\mathbf{z}\quad\forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p},\quad\forall\mathbf{z}\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{x}).

Definition C.3 (Smoothness).

Let g:ℝp→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} be a differentiable function and L>0L>0. We say that gg is LL-smooth if and only if ‖∇g​(𝐲)−∇g​(𝐱)‖2≤L​‖𝐲−𝐱‖2​∀𝐱,𝐲∈ℝp\|\nabla g(\mathbf{y})-\nabla g(\mathbf{x})\|_{2}\leq L\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}\ \forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}. This is equivalent to saying that the the first derivative of gg is LL-Lipschitz continuous, g​(𝐲)≤g​(𝐱)+(𝐲−𝐱)⊤​∇g​(𝐱)+L2​‖𝐲−𝐱‖22​∀𝐱,𝐲∈ℝpg(\mathbf{y})\leq g(\mathbf{x})+(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})^{\top}\nabla g(\mathbf{x})+\frac{L}{2}\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\ \forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}. For a twice-differentiable function, this means λmax​(∇2g​(𝐱))≤L∀𝐱∈ℝp\lambda_{\max}\left(\nabla^{2}g(\mathbf{x})\right)\leq L\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}. For convex gg, this is equivalent to saying ∇g\nabla g is 1/L1/L-cocoercive (Baillon–Haddad inequality (Bauschke & Combettes, 2009)): (∇g​(𝐲)−∇g​(𝐱))⊤​(𝐱−𝐲)≥1L​‖∇g​(𝐲)−∇g​(𝐱)‖22​∀𝐱,𝐲∈ℝp\left(\nabla g(\mathbf{y})-\nabla g(\mathbf{x})\right)^{\top}\left(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\right)\geq\frac{1}{L}\|\nabla g(\mathbf{y})-\nabla g(\mathbf{x})\|_{2}^{2}\ \forall\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}.

Lemma C.4.

Let g:ℝp⟶[0,∞)g:\mathbb{R}^{p}\longrightarrow[0,\infty) be differentiable LL-smooth function, L>0L>0. We have ‖∇g​(𝐱)‖22≤2​L​g​(𝐱)​∀𝐱∈ℝp\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x})\|_{2}^{2}\leq 2Lg(\mathbf{x})\ \forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}.

Proof.

Fix any 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and set 𝐲:=𝐱−1L​∇g​(𝐱)\mathbf{y}:=\mathbf{x}-\frac{1}{L}\,\nabla g(\mathbf{x}) to have 0≤g​(𝐲)≤g​(𝐱)+(𝐲−𝐱)⊤​∇g​(𝐱)+L2​‖𝐲−𝐱‖22=g​(𝐱)−12​L​‖∇g​(𝐱)‖220\leq g(\mathbf{y})\leq g(\mathbf{x})+(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})^{\top}\nabla g(\mathbf{x})+\frac{L}{2}\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}=g(\mathbf{x})-\frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x})\|_{2}^{2}. ∎

We use the following notations :

    For a non empty set Θ⊂ℝp\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{p} and a vector 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, we let dist⁡(𝐱,Θ):=inf𝐲∈Θ‖𝐱−𝐲‖2\operatorname{dist}(\mathbf{x},\Theta):=\inf_{\mathbf{y}\in\Theta}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}.

  • •

    hg∗:=inf𝐱∈Θgh​(𝐱)h_{g}^{*}:=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{g}}h(\mathbf{x}), i.e. hg∗=inf𝐱∈ℝph​(𝐱)​ s.t. ​𝐱∈Θgh_{g}^{*}=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}h(\mathbf{x})\text{ s.t. }\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{g}, and Θhg:=arg​min𝐱∈Θg⁡h​(𝐱)\Theta_{h}^{g}:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{g}}h(\mathbf{x}).

In general, f∗≠g∗+β​h∗f^{*}\neq g^{*}+\beta h^{*}. In fact, we have f∗≥g∗+β​h∗f^{*}\geq g^{*}+\beta h^{*}. This implies

f∗≥g∗+β​h∗⟺−f∗≤−g∗−β​h∗⟹0≤f​(𝐱)−f∗≤f​(𝐱)−g∗−β​h∗=g​(𝐱)−g∗+β​(h​(𝐱)−h∗)⟹|f​(𝐱)−f∗|≤|g​(𝐱)−g∗+β​(h​(𝐱)−h∗)|≤|g​(𝐱)−g∗|+β​|h​(𝐱)−h∗|\begin{split}f^{*}\geq g^{*}+\beta h^{*}&\Longleftrightarrow-f^{*}\leq-g^{*}-\beta h^{*}\\ &\Longrightarrow 0\leq f(\mathbf{x})-f^{*}\leq f(\mathbf{x})-g^{*}-\beta h^{*}=g(\mathbf{x})-g^{*}+\beta(h(\mathbf{x})-h^{*})\\ &\Longrightarrow|f(\mathbf{x})-f^{*}|\leq|g(\mathbf{x})-g^{*}+\beta(h(\mathbf{x})-h^{*})|\leq|g(\mathbf{x})-g^{*}|+\beta|h(\mathbf{x})-h^{*}|\end{split} (4)

So g​(𝐱)→g∗g(\mathbf{x})\rightarrow g^{*} and h​(𝐱)→h∗h(\mathbf{x})\rightarrow h^{*} implies f​(𝐱)→f∗f(\mathbf{x})\rightarrow f^{*}. But in general, it will not be possible to jointly have g​(𝐱(t))→g∗g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\rightarrow g^{*} and h​(𝐱(t))→h∗h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\rightarrow h^{*} by gradient descent. We will show that we first have g​(𝐱(t))→g∗g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\rightarrow g^{*}, then h​(𝐱(t))→hg∗h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\rightarrow h_{g}^{*}.

Assumption C.5.

Θf∩Θg≠∅\Theta_{f}\cap\Theta_{g}\neq\emptyset.

This assumption assumes too little noise compared to the signal. Even if initially g​(𝐱(t))→g∗g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\rightarrow g^{*} (i.e., memorization of training data with associated noise), as soon as generalization occurs, |g​(𝐱(t))−g∗||g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-g^{*}| becomes proportional to the noise. But under this assumption, when memorization is achieved, we can not have f​(𝐱(t))→f∗f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\rightarrow f^{*} without having h​(𝐱(t))→hg∗h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\rightarrow h_{g}^{*}.

Lemma C.6.

If assumption C.5 holds, then f∗=g∗+β​hg∗f^{*}=g^{*}+\beta h_{g}^{*}; and hence β​(h​(𝐱)−hg∗)≤g​(𝐱)−g∗+β​(h​(𝐱)−hg∗)≤f​(𝐱)−f∗∀𝐱∈ℝp\beta(h(\mathbf{x})-h_{g}^{*})\leq g(\mathbf{x})-g^{*}+\beta(h(\mathbf{x})-h_{g}^{*})\leq f(\mathbf{x})-f^{*}\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}.

Proof.

Assume Θf∩Θg≠∅\Theta_{f}\cap\Theta_{g}\neq\emptyset. Then there exists 𝐱f∗∈Θf\mathbf{x}_{f}^{*}\in\Theta_{f} such that g​(𝐱f∗)=g∗g(\mathbf{x}_{f}^{*})=g^{*}. This implies 𝐱f∗∈Θg\mathbf{x}_{f}^{*}\in\Theta_{g}. Under this assumption, f∗=g​(𝐱f∗)+β​h​(𝐱f∗)=g∗+β​h​(𝐱f∗)f^{*}=g(\mathbf{x}_{f}^{*})+\beta h(\mathbf{x}_{f}^{*})=g^{*}+\beta h(\mathbf{x}_{f}^{*}). Since 𝐱f∗∈Θg\mathbf{x}_{f}^{*}\in\Theta_{g}, h​(𝐱f∗)≥hg∗h(\mathbf{x}_{f}^{*})\geq h_{g}^{*}, so f∗≥g∗+β​hg∗f^{*}\geq g^{*}+\beta h_{g}^{*}. Conversely, we have g∗+β​hg∗=g​(𝐱)+β​h​(𝐱)=f​(𝐱)≥f∗g^{*}+\beta h_{g}^{*}=g(\mathbf{x})+\beta h(\mathbf{x})=f(\mathbf{x})\geq f^{*} for any 𝐱∈Θhg⊂Θg\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{h}^{g}\subset\Theta_{g}. Therefore, f∗=g∗+β​hg∗f^{*}=g^{*}+\beta h_{g}^{*}. This implies f​(𝐱)−f∗=g​(𝐱)−g∗+β​(h​(𝐱)−hg∗)≥β​(h​(𝐱)−hg∗)f(\mathbf{x})-f^{*}=g(\mathbf{x})-g^{*}+\beta(h(\mathbf{x})-h_{g}^{*})\geq\beta(h(\mathbf{x})-h_{g}^{*}) since g​(𝐱)−g∗≥0g(\mathbf{x})-g^{*}\geq 0. ∎

Assumption C.7.

Since Θg=arg​min𝐱∈ℝp⁡(g​(𝐱)−g∗)\Theta_{g}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}(g(\mathbf{x})-g^{*}), we assume without loss of generality g∗=0g^{*}=0.

If gg is the loss function of an overparameterized neural network, then for β=0\beta=0, f=gf=g converges to a solution 𝐱∗\mathbf{x}^{*} close to the initialization 𝐱(0)\mathbf{x}^{(0)} such that g​(𝐱∗)=0g(\mathbf{x}^{*})=0, under certain conditions on α\alpha and 𝐱(0)\mathbf{x}^{(0)} (see, for example, Theorems C.25 and C.15). We will extend this result to the case β>0\beta>0.

χ​(φ,𝐱,r,ϕ):={∞if ​ϕ​(𝐲)=0​∀𝐲∈B​(𝐱,r)inf𝐲∈B​(𝐱,r)ϕ​(𝐲)≠0inf𝐳∈∂φ​(𝐲)‖𝐳‖22φ​(𝐲)otherwise.={∞if ​ϕ​(𝐲)=0​∀𝐲∈B​(𝐱,r)inf𝐲∈B​(𝐱,r)ϕ​(𝐲)≠0‖∇φ​(𝐲)‖22φ​(𝐲)otherwise.​ if φ is differentiable\begin{split}\chi(\varphi,\mathbf{x},r,\phi)&:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\infty&\mbox{if }\phi(\mathbf{y})=0\ \forall\mathbf{y}\in B(\mathbf{x},r)\\ \inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{y}\in B(\mathbf{x},r)\\ \phi(\mathbf{y})\neq 0\end{subarray}}\frac{\inf_{\mathbf{z}\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{y})}\|\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}}{\varphi(\mathbf{y})}&\mbox{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.\\ &=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\infty&\mbox{if }\phi(\mathbf{y})=0\ \forall\mathbf{y}\in B(\mathbf{x},r)\\ \inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{y}\in B(\mathbf{x},r)\\ \phi(\mathbf{y})\neq 0\end{subarray}}\frac{\|\nabla\varphi(\mathbf{y})\|_{2}^{2}}{\varphi(\mathbf{y})}&\mbox{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.\text{ if $\varphi$ is differentiable}\end{split} (5)
