β​mint1≤t≤t2⁡(h​(𝐱(t))−hg∗)≤mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐱(t))−f∗)≤dist2⁡(𝐱(t1),Θf)+(t2−t1)​α2​maxt1≤t≤t2⁡‖F​(𝐱(t))‖222​(t2−t1)​α\begin{split}\beta\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-h_{g}^{*}\right)\leq\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-f^{*}\right)\leq\frac{\operatorname{dist}^{2}(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})},\Theta_{f})+(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha^{2}\max_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}}{2(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha}\end{split} (15)
Proof.

By the definition of the subgradient F​(𝐱(t2))F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}) of ff at 𝐱(t2)\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}, we have (𝐱−𝐱(t2))⊤​F​(𝐱(t2))≤f​(𝐱)−f​(𝐱(t2))∀𝐱⟺−(𝐱(t2)−𝐱)⊤​F​(𝐱(t2))≤−(f​(𝐱(t2))−f​(𝐱))∀𝐱\left(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}\right)^{\top}F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\leq f(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\Longleftrightarrow-\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\right)^{\top}F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\leq-(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-f(\mathbf{x}))\quad\forall\mathbf{x}. So, for all 𝐱\mathbf{x}, we have

‖𝐱(t2+1)−𝐱‖22=‖𝐱(t2)−α​F​(𝐱(t2))−𝐱‖22=‖𝐱(t2)−𝐱‖22−2​α​(𝐱(t2)−𝐱)⊤​F​(𝐱(t2))+α2​‖F​(𝐱(t2))‖22≤‖𝐱(t2)−𝐱‖22−2​α​(f​(𝐱(t2))−f​(𝐱))+α2​‖F​(𝐱(t2))‖22≤‖𝐱(t1)−𝐱‖22−2​α​∑t=t1t2(f​(𝐱(t))−f​(𝐱))+α2​∑t=t1t2‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22\begin{split}\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2}+1)}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}&=\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\alpha F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\\ &=\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\right)^{\top}F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})+\alpha^{2}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\leq\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-f(\mathbf{x})\right)+\alpha^{2}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\leq\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{x})\right)+\alpha^{2}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}\end{split} (16)

This implies

0≤inf𝐱∈Θf‖𝐱(t2+1)−𝐱‖22≤inf𝐱∈Θf‖𝐱(t1)−𝐱‖22−2​α​sup𝐱∈Θf∑t=t1t2(f​(𝐱(t))−f​(𝐱))+α2​∑t=t1t2‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22⟹2​α​sup𝐱∈Θf∑t=t1t2(f​(𝐱(t))−f​(𝐱))≤dist2⁡(𝐱(t1),Θf)+α2​∑t=t1t2‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22⟹2​α​(t2−t1)​sup𝐱∈Θfmint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐱(t))−f​(𝐱))≤dist2⁡(𝐱(t1),Θf)+(t2−t1)​α2​maxt1≤t≤t2⁡‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22⟺mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐱(t))−inf𝐱∈Θff​(𝐱))≤dist2⁡(𝐱(t1),Θf)+(t2−t1)​α2​maxt1≤t≤t2⁡‖F​(𝐱(t))‖222​(t2−t1)​α\begin{split}&0\leq\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{f}}\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2}+1)}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{f}}\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{f}}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{x})\right)+\alpha^{2}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\Longrightarrow 2\alpha\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{f}}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{x})\right)\leq\operatorname{dist}^{2}(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})},\Theta_{f})+\alpha^{2}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\Longrightarrow 2\alpha(t_{2}-t_{1})\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{f}}\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{x})\right)\leq\operatorname{dist}^{2}(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})},\Theta_{f})+(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha^{2}\max_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\Longleftrightarrow\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{f}}f(\mathbf{x})\right)\leq\frac{\operatorname{dist}^{2}(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})},\Theta_{f})+(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha^{2}\max_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}}{2(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha}\end{split} (17)

This proves the first inequality. We also have, for all 𝐱\mathbf{x}, −(𝐱(t2)−𝐱)⊤​H​(𝐱(t2))≤−(h​(𝐱(t2))−h​(𝐱))-\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\right)^{\top}H(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\leq-(h(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-h(\mathbf{x})) and −(𝐱(t2)−𝐱)⊤​G​(𝐱(t2))≤−(g​(𝐱(t2))−g​(𝐱))-\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\right)^{\top}G(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\leq-(g(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-g(\mathbf{x})), and so

‖𝐱(t2+1)−𝐱‖22=‖𝐱(t2)−α​F​(𝐱(t2))−𝐱‖22=‖𝐱(t2)−𝐱‖22−2​α​(𝐱(t2)−𝐱)⊤​F​(𝐱(t2))+α2​‖F​(𝐱(t2))‖22=‖𝐱(t2)−𝐱‖22−2​α​(𝐱(t2)−𝐱)⊤​G​(𝐱(t2))−2​α​β​(𝐱(t2)−𝐱)⊤​H​(𝐱(t2))+α2​‖F​(𝐱(t2))‖22≤‖𝐱(t2)−𝐱‖22−2​α​(g​(𝐱(t2))−g​(𝐱))−2​α​β​(h​(𝐱(t2))−h​(𝐱))+α2​‖F​(𝐱(t2))‖22≤‖𝐱(t1)−𝐱‖22−2​α​∑t=t1t2(g​(𝐱(t))−g​(𝐱))−2​α​β​∑t=t1t2(h​(𝐱(t))−h​(𝐱))+α2​∑t=t1t2‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22\begin{split}\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2}+1)}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}&=\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\alpha F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}\\ &=\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\right)^{\top}F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})+\alpha^{2}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &=\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\right)^{\top}G(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-2\alpha\beta\left(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\right)^{\top}H(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})+\alpha^{2}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\leq\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-g(\mathbf{x})\right)-2\alpha\beta\left(h(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})-h(\mathbf{x})\right)+\alpha^{2}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{2})})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\leq\|\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}-2\alpha\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-g(\mathbf{x})\right)-2\alpha\beta\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-h(\mathbf{x})\right)+\alpha^{2}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}\end{split} (18)

2​α​[sup𝐱∈Θg∑t=t1t2(g​(𝐱(t))−g​(𝐱))+β​sup𝐱∈Θg∑t=t1t2(h​(𝐱(t))−h​(𝐱))]≤dist2⁡(𝐱(t1),Θg)+α2​∑t=t1t2‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22⟺mint1≤t≤t2⁡[(g​(𝐱(t))−g∗)+β​(h​(𝐱(t))−hg∗)]≤dist2⁡(𝐱(t1),Θg)+(t2−t1)​α2​maxt1≤t≤t2⁡‖F​(𝐱(t))‖222​(t2−t1)​α\begin{split}&2\alpha\left[\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{g}}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-g(\mathbf{x})\right)+\beta\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{g}}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-h(\mathbf{x})\right)\right]\leq\operatorname{dist}^{2}(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})},\Theta_{g})+\alpha^{2}\sum_{t=t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\Longleftrightarrow\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left[\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-g^{*}\right)+\beta\left(h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-h_{g}^{*}\right)\right]\leq\frac{\operatorname{dist}^{2}(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})},\Theta_{g})+(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha^{2}\max_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}}{2(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha}\end{split} (19)

If Θf∩Θg\Theta_{f}\cap\Theta_{g}, then f​(𝐱)−f∗≥β​(h​(𝐱)−hg∗)f(\mathbf{x})-f^{*}\geq\beta(h(\mathbf{x})-h_{g}^{*}) (Lemma C.6), and so

β​mint1≤t≤t2⁡(h​(𝐱(t))−hg∗)≤mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐱(t))−f∗)=mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐱(t))−inf𝐱∈Θff​(𝐱))\beta\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-h_{g}^{*}\right)\leq\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-f^{*}\right)=\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta_{f}}f(\mathbf{x})\right) (20)

Theorem C.13.

Let t1>0t_{1}>0. Define R:=dist⁡(𝐱(t1),Θf)R:=\operatorname{dist}(\mathbf{x}^{(t_{1})},\Theta_{f}) and L:=maxt1≤t⁡‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22L:=\max_{t_{1}\leq t}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}. Moreover, if Assumptions C.5 holds, then mint1≤t≤t2⁡(h​(𝐱(t))−hg∗)≤η+C​α​β2\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(h(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-h_{g}^{*}\right)\leq\frac{\eta+C\alpha\beta}{2} if and only if t2≥t1+R2α​β​ηt_{2}\geq t_{1}+\frac{R^{2}}{\alpha\beta\eta}.

We have L=maxt1≤t⁡‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22≥maxt1≤t≤t2⁡‖F​(𝐱(t))‖22L=\max_{t_{1}\leq t}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}\geq\max_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}. From Lemma C.12, we derive the following :

mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐱(t))−f∗)≤R2+C​(t2−t1)​α2​β22​(t2−t1)​α≤(η+C​α​β)​β2⟺R22​α​(t2−t1)≤η​β2⟺t2−t1≥R2α​β​η\begin{split}&\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-f^{*}\right)\leq\frac{R^{2}+C(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha^{2}\beta^{2}}{2(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha}\leq\frac{\left(\eta+C\alpha\beta\right)\beta}{2}\Longleftrightarrow\frac{R^{2}}{2\alpha(t_{2}-t_{1})}\leq\frac{\eta\beta}{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}-t_{1}\geq\frac{R^{2}}{\alpha\beta\eta}\end{split} (21)

and

γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2≥β​Lhτk−j​ and ​β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2∀ 0≤j≤k\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}\geq\frac{\beta L_{h}}{\tau^{k-j}}\text{ and }\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}\quad\forall\ 0\leq j\leq k (24)

and

‖G​(𝐱(k+1))‖2≥τ​β​Lh​ with ​τ​β​Lh<β​Lh\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)})\|_{2}\geq\tau\beta L_{h}\text{ with }\tau\beta L_{h}<\beta L_{h} (25)

As a consequence,

‖G​(𝐱(1))−G​(𝐱(0))‖2≤L​‖𝐱(1)−𝐱(0)‖2≤α​L​‖G​(𝐱(0))+β​H​(𝐱(0))‖2≤α​L​(‖G​(𝐱(0))‖2+β​‖H​(𝐱(0))‖2)≤(1+γ)​α​L​‖G​(𝐱(0))‖2\begin{split}\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(1)})-G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}&\leq L\|\mathbf{x}^{(1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\|_{2}\\ &\leq\alpha L\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}\\ &\leq\alpha L\left(\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}+\beta\|H(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}\right)\\ &\leq(1+\gamma)\alpha L\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}\end{split} (26)

So

‖G​(𝐱(1))‖2≥‖G​(𝐱(0))‖2−‖G​(𝐱(1))−G​(𝐱(0))‖2≥‖G​(𝐱(0))‖2−(1+γ)​α​L​‖G​(𝐱(0))‖2=τ​‖G​(𝐱(0))‖2≥β​Lhγ​τk−1\begin{split}\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(1)})\|_{2}&\geq\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}-\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(1)})-G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}\\ &\geq\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}-(1+\gamma)\alpha L\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}\\ &=\tau\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}\\ &\geq\frac{\beta L_{h}}{\gamma\tau^{k-1}}\end{split} (27)

We thus have γ​‖G​(𝐱(1))‖2≥β​Lh≥β​H​(𝐱(1))\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(1)})\|_{2}\geq\beta L_{h}\geq\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}). So 𝐱(2)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(2)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) (Lemma C.17), and hence supH∈∂h​(𝐱(2))‖H‖2≤Lh\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(2)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq L_{h}. And so on, we prove that ‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2≥β​Lhγ​τk−j\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}\geq\frac{\beta L_{h}}{\gamma\tau^{k-j}} and β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2∀ 0≤j≤k\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}\quad\forall\ 0\leq j\leq k. We have ‖G​(𝐱(k+1))‖2≥τ​β​Lh​ with ​τ​β​Lh<β​Lh\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)})\|_{2}\geq\tau\beta L_{h}\text{ with }\tau\beta L_{h}<\beta L_{h}. So either ‖G​(𝐱(k+1))‖2≥β​Lh\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)})\|_{2}\geq\beta L_{h} (and we can proceed to the next iteration), or β​Lh≥‖G​(𝐱(k+1))‖2≥τ​β​Lh\beta L_{h}\geq\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)})\|_{2}\geq\tau\beta L_{h} (we do not have control after kk). The last part of the Theorem follows from Theorem C.16. ∎

The following Theorem is an extension of the result obtained by Chatterjee (2022), where we add an additional bound on the gradient. We extend it below to handle the case β≠0\beta\neq 0 in Theorem C.16.

Choose any step size α>0\alpha>0 such that α<min⁡{rL1​p,2​ϵL2​p}\alpha<\min\left\{\frac{r}{L_{1}\sqrt{p}},\frac{2\epsilon}{L_{2}p}\right\} and iteratively define 𝐱(k+1)=𝐱(k)−α​∇g​(𝐱(k))\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)}=\mathbf{x}^{(k)}-\alpha\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}) for each k≥0k\geq 0. Then,

    𝐱(k)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) for all kk, and as k→∞k\rightarrow\infty, 𝐱(k)\mathbf{x}^{(k)} converges to a point 𝐱∗∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{*}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) where g​(𝐱∗)=0g(\mathbf{x}^{*})=0 and ‖∇g​(𝐱∗)‖2=0\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{*})\|_{2}=0.

This is a special case of Theorem C.16. The proof sketch is the following. Since ‖𝐱(k)−𝐱(j)‖2≤∑l=jk−1‖𝐱(l+1)−𝐱(l)‖2=∑l=jk−1α​‖∇g​(𝐱(l))‖2\|\mathbf{x}^{(k)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\|_{2}\leq\sum_{l=j}^{k-1}\|\mathbf{x}^{(l+1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(l)}\|_{2}=\sum_{l=j}^{k-1}\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(l)})\|_{2}, Lemma C.17 use the fact that, if for some k≥1k\geq 1, 𝐱(1),…,𝐱(k−1)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{(k-1)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) (this is need to prove Lemma C.17 by induction), then ∑l=jk−1α​‖∇g​(𝐱(l))‖2≤(1−δ)j/2​4​g​(𝐱(0))χ​(g,𝐱(0),r)⋅(1−ϵ)2\sum_{l=j}^{k-1}\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(l)})\|_{2}\leq(1-\delta)^{j/2}\sqrt{\frac{4g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})}{\chi(g,\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r)\cdot(1-\epsilon)^{2}}} for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1 (Lemma C.22); so that ‖𝐱(k)−𝐱(0)‖2<r\|\mathbf{x}^{(k)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\|_{2}<r since 4​g​(𝐱(0))<(1−ϵ)2​r2⋅χ​(g,𝐱(0),r)4g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})<(1-\epsilon)^{2}r^{2}\cdot\chi(g,\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r), i.e 𝐱(k)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r).     L1:=sup𝐱∈B​(𝐱(0),r)‖∇g​(𝐱)‖∞<∞L_{1}:=\sup_{\mathbf{x}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r)}\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x})\|_{\infty}<\infty be a uniform upper bound on the magnitudes of the first-order derivatives of gg in B​(𝐱(0),r)B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r)

(31)

with

then we have ‖𝐱(k)−𝐱(j)‖≤ε\|\mathbf{x}^{(k)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\|\leq\varepsilon for all j,k>K​(ε)j,k>K(\varepsilon). So the sequence {𝐱(j)}0≤j<k\{\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\}_{0\leq j<k} is Cauchy.

Lemma C.17 (Iterates stay inside the ball).

For all k≥0k\geq 0 such that ∀ 0≤j​<k,β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))∥​H∥2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2\forall\ 0\leq j<k,\ \beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}, we have 𝐱(1),…,𝐱(k)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r).

Proof.

We prove that 𝐱(k)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) for all k≥0k\geq 0 such that β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2∀ 0≤j<k\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}\quad\forall\ 0\leq j<k by induction on kk. The base case k=0k=0 is obvious since β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(0))‖H‖2≤βmax​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(0))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(0))‖2\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\beta_{\max}\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\|_{2}. Let k≥1k\geq 1. Assume 𝐱(j)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) and β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2} for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1. Then 𝐱(k)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) since

‖𝐱(k)−𝐱(0)‖2≤∑l=0k−1α​‖G​(𝐱(l))+β​H​(𝐱(l))‖2≤{4​(1+γ)2​g​(𝐱(0))χ​(1−ϵ)2if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​p4​(1+γ)2​g​(𝐱(0))χ​(1−(ϵ+γ))2if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p​ (Lemma C.22 with j=0)<{rif ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​p​ since ​4​g​(𝐱(0))<(1−ϵ1+γ)2​r2​χ​ (Equation (29))rif ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p​ since ​4​g​(𝐱(0))<(1−(ϵ+γ)1+γ)2​r2​χ​ (Equation (30))\begin{split}\|\mathbf{x}^{(k)}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\|_{2}&\leq\sum_{l=0}^{k-1}\alpha\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(l)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(l)})\|_{2}\\ &\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\sqrt{\frac{4(1+\gamma)^{2}g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})}{\chi(1-\epsilon)^{2}}}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ \sqrt{\frac{4(1+\gamma)^{2}g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})}{\chi\left(1-(\epsilon+\gamma)\right)^{2}}}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.\text{ (Lemma~\ref{lemma:bounding_cumulative_step_lengths_beta_non_zero} with $j=0$)}\\ &<\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}r&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\text{ since }4g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})<\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{1+\gamma}\right)^{2}r^{2}\chi\text{ (Equation~\eqref{eq:choice_epsilon_theo2_case_1})}\\ r&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\text{ since }4g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})<\left(\frac{1-(\epsilon+\gamma)}{1+\gamma}\right)^{2}r^{2}\chi\text{ (Equation~\eqref{eq:choice_epsilon_theo2_case_2})}\end{array}\right.\end{split} (36)

∎

Lemma C.18 (Second-order Taylor formula with integral remainder).

Let g:ℝp→ℝg:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} be a C2C^{2} function. For every base point 𝐱\mathbf{x}∈ℝp\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and step 𝐡\mathbf{h}∈ℝp\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, g​(𝐱+𝐡)=g​(𝐱)+∇g​(𝐱)⊤​𝐡+∫01(1−t)​𝐡⊤​∇2g​(𝐱+t​𝐡)​𝐡​𝑑tg(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})=g(\mathbf{x})+\nabla g(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\mathbf{h}+\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\mathbf{h}^{\top}\nabla^{2}g(\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{h})\mathbf{h}dt.

Lemma C.19 (Second-order remainder control).

For each j≥0j\geq 0 set Rj:=g​(𝐱(j+1))−g​(𝐱(j))+α​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22R_{j}:=g(\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)})-g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})+\alpha\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}. Suppose that 𝐱(j)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) and β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2} for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1, for some k≥1k\geq 1. Then for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1,

|Rj|≤{ϵ​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​p(ϵ+γ)​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p|R_{j}|\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\epsilon\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ (\epsilon+\gamma)\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right. (37)
Proof.

Let Sj:=g​(𝐱(j+1))−g​(𝐱(j))+α​G​(𝐱(j))⊤​(G​(𝐱(j))+β​H​(𝐱(j)))=Rj+α​β​G​(𝐱(j))⊤​H​(𝐱(j))S_{j}:=g(\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)})-g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})+\alpha G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{\top}(G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}))=R_{j}+\alpha\beta G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{\top}H(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}). Fix j≤k−1j\leq k-1 and let 𝐱​(t):=𝐱(j)−t​α​(G​(𝐱(j))+β​H​(𝐱(j)))\mathbf{x}(t):=\mathbf{x}^{(j)}-t\alpha\left(G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\right) with t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. Apply the second-order Taylor formula with integral remainder (Lemma C.18):

g​(𝐱(j+1))=g​(𝐱(j)−α​(G​(𝐱(j))+β​H​(𝐱(j))))=g​(𝐱(j))−α​G​(𝐱(j))⊤​(G​(𝐱(j))+β​H​(𝐱(j)))+α2​∫01∇g​(𝐱(j))⊤​∇2g​(𝐱​(t))​∇g​(𝐱(j))​(1−t)​𝑑t\begin{split}g(\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)})&=g\left(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}-\alpha(G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}))\right)\\ &=g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-\alpha G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{\top}(G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}))+\alpha^{2}\int_{0}^{1}\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{\top}\nabla^{2}g\left(\mathbf{x}(t)\right)\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})(1-t)dt\end{split} (38)

Hence

Sj=α2​∫01∇g​(𝐱(j))⊤​∇2g​(𝐱​(t))​∇g​(𝐱(j))​(1−t)​𝑑tS_{j}=\alpha^{2}\int_{0}^{1}\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{\top}\nabla^{2}g(\mathbf{x}(t))\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})(1-t)dt (39)

Along the segment 𝐱​(t)\mathbf{x}(t) with t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] we have 𝐱​(0)=𝐱(j)\mathbf{x}(0)=\mathbf{x}^{(j)}, 𝐱​(1)=𝐱(j+1)\mathbf{x}(1)=\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)}. So all points 𝐱​(t)\mathbf{x}(t) lie in the line segment joining 𝐱(j)\mathbf{x}^{(j)} and 𝐱(j+1)\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)}. Because ‖𝐱(j+1)−𝐱(j)‖2≤p​‖𝐱(j+1)−𝐱(j)‖∞=α​p​‖G​(𝐱(j))+β​H​(𝐱(j))‖∞=α​p​(L1+β​Lh)≤r\|\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{p}\|\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\|_{\infty}=\alpha\sqrt{p}\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{\infty}=\alpha\sqrt{p}(L_{1}+\beta L_{h})\leq r, that segment stays inside B​(𝐱(0),2​r)B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},2r); thus every entry of ∇2g​(𝐱​(t))\nabla^{2}g(\mathbf{x}(t)) is bounded by L2L_{2}. Therefore, for every tt,

|∇g​(𝐱(j))⊤​∇2g​(𝐱​(t))​∇g​(𝐱(j))|=|∑i=1p∑i′=1p[∇g​(𝐱(j))]i​[∇2g​(𝐱​(t))​∇g​(𝐱(j))]i,i′​[∇g​(𝐱(j))]i′|≤L2∑i=1p∑i′=1p|[∇g(𝐱(j))]i||g(𝐱(j))]i′|=L2∥∇g(𝐱(j))∥12≤L2p∥∇g(𝐱(j))∥22\begin{split}\left|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{\top}\nabla^{2}g(\mathbf{x}(t))\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\right|&=\left|\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{p}[\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})]_{i}[\nabla^{2}g(\mathbf{x}(t))\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})]_{i,i^{\prime}}[\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})]_{i^{\prime}}\right|\\ &\leq L_{2}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{i^{\prime}=1}^{p}\left|[\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})]_{i}\right|\left|g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})]_{i^{\prime}}\right|=L_{2}\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{1}^{2}\leq L_{2}p\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}\end{split} (40)

So

|Sj|≤α2​∫01|∇g​(𝐱(j))⊤​∇2g​(𝐱​(t))​∇g​(𝐱(j))|​|1−t|​𝑑t≤α2​L2​p​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22​∫01(1−t)​𝑑t=α22​L2​p​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22≤{(ϵ−γ)​α​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​pϵ​α​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p\begin{split}|S_{j}|&\leq\alpha^{2}\int_{0}^{1}\left|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{\top}\nabla^{2}g(\mathbf{x}(t))\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\right|\left|1-t\right|dt\\ &\leq\alpha^{2}L_{2}p\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)dt\\ &=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}L_{2}p\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(\epsilon-\gamma)\alpha\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ \epsilon\alpha\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.\end{split} (41)

This implies

|Rj|=|Sj−α​β​G​(𝐱(j))⊤​H​(𝐱(j))|≤|Sj|+α​β​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2​‖H​(𝐱(j))‖2≤|Sj|+α​γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22≤{(ϵ−γ)​α​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22+α​γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​pϵ​α​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22+α​γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p\begin{split}|R_{j}|&=|S_{j}-\alpha\beta G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{\top}H(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})|\leq|S_{j}|+\alpha\beta\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}\|H(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}\\ &\leq|S_{j}|+\alpha\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(\epsilon-\gamma)\alpha\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}+\alpha\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ \epsilon\alpha\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}+\alpha\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.\end{split} (42)

Lemma C.20 (Geometric decay of the objective).

Let

δ:={(1−ϵ)​χ​αif ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​p(1−(ϵ+γ))​χ​αif ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p\delta:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(1-\epsilon)\chi\alpha&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ \left(1-(\epsilon+\gamma)\right)\chi\alpha&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right. (43)

If 𝐱(j)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) and β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2} for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1, for some k≥1k\geq 1; then g​(𝐱(j))≤(1−δ)j​g​(𝐱(0))​ for all ​0≤j≤kg(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\leq(1-\delta)^{j}g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\text{ for all }0\leq j\leq k with δ≤1\delta\leq 1.

Proof.

By the definition of χ:=χ​(g,𝐱(0),r)\chi:=\chi(g,\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r), we have χ​g​(𝐱)≤‖∇g​(𝐱)‖22\chi g(\mathbf{x})\leq\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x})\|_{2}^{2} for all 𝐱∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r). Since 𝐱(j)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1, ‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22≥χ​g​(𝐱(j))\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}\geq\chi g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}) for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1. So, for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1,

g​(𝐱(j+1))=g​(𝐱(j))−α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22+Rj​ by the definition of ​Rj≤{g​(𝐱(j))−α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22+ϵ​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​pg​(𝐱(j))−α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22+(ϵ+γ)​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p​ (Lemma C.19)={g​(𝐱(j))−(1−ϵ)​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​pg​(𝐱(j))−(1−(ϵ+γ))​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p≤{g​(𝐱(j))−(1−ϵ)​α​χ​g​(𝐱(j))if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​pg​(𝐱(j))−(1−(ϵ+γ))​α​χ​g​(𝐱(j))if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p=(1−δ)​g​(𝐱(j))\begin{split}g(\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)})&=g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}+R_{j}\text{ by the definition of }R_{j}\\ &\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}+\epsilon\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}+(\epsilon+\gamma)\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.\text{ (Lemma~\ref{lemma:remainder_bound_beta_non_zero})}\\ &=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-(1-\epsilon)\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-\left(1-(\epsilon+\gamma)\right)\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.\\ &\leq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-(1-\epsilon)\alpha\chi g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-\left(1-(\epsilon+\gamma)\right)\alpha\chi g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.\\ &=\left(1-\delta\right)g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\end{split} (44)

Moreover, taking j=0j=0 gives g​(𝐱(1))≤(1−δ)​g​(𝐱(0))⟹1−δ≥g​(𝐱(1))/g​(𝐱(0))≥0⟹δ≤1g(\mathbf{x}^{(1)})\leq\left(1-\delta\right)g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\Longrightarrow 1-\delta\geq g(\mathbf{x}^{(1)})/g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})\geq 0\Longrightarrow\delta\leq 1. ∎

Lemma C.21 (One-step descent bound).

Suppose that 𝐱(j)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) and β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2} for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1, for some k≥1k\geq 1. Then for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1,

g​(𝐱(j))−g​(𝐱(j+1))≥{(1−ϵ)​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​p(1−(ϵ+γ))​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p=δχ​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22\begin{split}g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-g(\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)})&\geq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(1-\epsilon)\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ \left(1-(\epsilon+\gamma)\right)\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.=\frac{\delta}{\chi}\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}\end{split} (45)
Proof.

For all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1,

g​(𝐱(j))−g​(𝐱(j+1))=α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22−Rj​ by the definition of ​Rj≥{α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22−ϵ​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​pα​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22−(ϵ+γ)​α​‖∇g​(𝐱(j))‖22if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p​ (Lemma C.19)\begin{split}g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})-g(\mathbf{x}^{(j+1)})&=\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}-R_{j}\text{ by the definition of }R_{j}\\ &\geq\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}-\epsilon\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ \alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}-(\epsilon+\gamma)\alpha\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2}^{2}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.\text{ (Lemma~\ref{lemma:remainder_bound_beta_non_zero})}\end{split} (46)

Lemma C.22 (Bounding cumulative step lengths).

Suppose that 𝐱(j)∈B​(𝐱(0),r)\mathbf{x}^{(j)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},r) and β​supH∈∂h​(𝐱(j))‖H‖2≤γ​‖G​(𝐱(j))‖2\beta\sup_{H\in\partial h(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})}\|H\|_{2}\leq\gamma\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})\|_{2} for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1, for some k≥1k\geq 1. Then for all 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1,

∑l=jk−1α​‖G​(𝐱(l))+β​H​(𝐱(l))‖2={(1−δ)j/2​4​(1+γ)2​g​(𝐱(0))χ​(1−ϵ)2if ​α≤2​(ϵ−γ)/L2​p(1−δ)j/2​4​(1+γ)2​g​(𝐱(0))χ​(1−(ϵ+γ))2if ​α≤2​ϵ/L2​p\begin{split}\sum_{l=j}^{k-1}\alpha\|G(\mathbf{x}^{(l)})+\beta H(\mathbf{x}^{(l)})\|_{2}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}(1-\delta)^{j/2}\sqrt{\frac{4(1+\gamma)^{2}g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})}{\chi(1-\epsilon)^{2}}}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2(\epsilon-\gamma)/L_{2}p\\ (1-\delta)^{j/2}\sqrt{\frac{4(1+\gamma)^{2}g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})}{\chi\left(1-(\epsilon+\gamma)\right)^{2}}}&\mbox{if }\alpha\leq 2\epsilon/L_{2}p\end{array}\right.\end{split} (47)

C.2 Main Theorem under Polyak-Łojasiewicz Inequality

In this section, we recall a convergence guaranteed for gg under the classical Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality. This is a standard result that can be found in the literature (e.g., Karimi et al. (2020)). The CL inequality can be seen as strengthening the PL inequality (Theorem C.24) and is related to the classical Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz inequality (Karimi et al., 2020; Chatterjee, 2022).

Definition C.23 (Generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality).

Let φ:ℝp→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} be a sub-differentiable function such that Θφ:=arg​min𝐱∈ℝp⁡φ​(𝐱)≠∅\Theta_{\varphi}:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\neq\emptyset. Let φ∗:=min𝐱∈ℝp⁡φ​(𝐱)\varphi^{*}:=\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\varphi(\mathbf{x}), and μ>0\mu>0. The function φ\varphi is said to satisfy the μ\mu-PL (Polyak-Łojasiewicz) inequality if and only if

φ​(𝐱)−φ∗≤12​μ​inf𝐳∈∂φ​(𝐱)‖𝐳‖22∀𝐱∈ℝp\varphi(\mathbf{x})-\varphi^{*}\leq\frac{1}{2\mu}\inf_{\mathbf{z}\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{x})}\|\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} (49)

The PL inequality is typically stated for differentiable functions. This version allows φ\varphi to be merely subdifferentiable, which is a generalization, and thus is not always equivalent to properties known for the smooth case. Still, some of them hold under this generalized definition (e.g., strong convexity implies PL).

Theorem C.24.

Let φ:ℝp→[0,∞)\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to[0,\infty) be a subdifferentiable function such that arg​min𝐱∈ℝp⁡φ​(𝐱)≠∅\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\neq\emptyset. Assume φ∗:=min𝐱∈ℝp⁡φ​(𝐱)=0\varphi^{*}:=\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})=0 (without loss of generality). If φ\varphi is μ\mu-PL for some μ>0\mu>0, then for all 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, φ\varphi is rr-CL at 𝐱\mathbf{x} whatever r2≥2​φ​(𝐱)/μr^{2}\geq 2\varphi(\mathbf{x})/\mu.

Proof.

Assume φ\varphi is μ\mu-PL. Then

φ​(𝐲)−φ∗≤12​μ​inf𝐳∈∂φ​(𝐲)‖𝐳‖22∀𝐲∈ℝp⟹2​μ​(1−φ∗φ​(𝐲))≤inf𝐳∈∂φ​(𝐲)‖𝐳‖22φ​(𝐲)∀𝐲∈ℝp,φ​(𝐲)≠0⟹4​φ​(𝐱)r2≤inf𝐳∈∂φ​(𝐲)‖𝐳‖22φ​(𝐲)∀𝐲∈ℝp,φ​(𝐲)≠0⟺4​φ​(𝐱)≤r2​inf𝐲∈B​(𝐱,r),φ​(𝐲)≠0inf𝐳∈∂φ​(𝐲)‖𝐳‖22φ​(𝐲)=r2​α​(φ,𝐱,r)\begin{split}\varphi(\mathbf{y})-\varphi^{*}\leq\frac{1}{2\mu}\inf_{\mathbf{z}\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{y})}\|\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\forall\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}&\Longrightarrow 2\mu\left(1-\frac{\varphi^{*}}{\varphi(\mathbf{y})}\right)\leq\frac{\inf_{\mathbf{z}\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{y})}\|\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}}{\varphi(\mathbf{y})}\quad\forall\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p},\ \varphi(\mathbf{y})\neq 0\\ &\Longrightarrow\frac{4\varphi(\mathbf{x})}{r^{2}}\leq\frac{\inf_{\mathbf{z}\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{y})}\|\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}}{\varphi(\mathbf{y})}\quad\forall\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p},\ \varphi(\mathbf{y})\neq 0\\ &\Longleftrightarrow 4\varphi(\mathbf{x})\leq r^{2}\inf_{\mathbf{y}\in B(\mathbf{x},r),\ \varphi(\mathbf{y})\neq 0}\frac{\inf_{\mathbf{z}\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{y})}\|\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}}{\varphi(\mathbf{y})}=r^{2}\alpha(\varphi,\mathbf{x},r)\end{split} (50)

∎

Theorem C.25 (Convergence of fixed-step gradient descent under PL condition).

Let g:ℝp→[0,∞)g:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to[0,\infty) be a nonnegative C2C^{2} function such that Θg:=arg​min𝐱∈ℝp⁡g​(𝐱)≠∅\Theta_{g}:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}g(\mathbf{x})\neq\emptyset, and let g∗:=min𝐱∈ℝp⁡g​(𝐱)g^{*}:=\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}g(\mathbf{x}). Assume gg is LL-smooth and μ\mu-PL for some L,μ>0L,\mu>0. Take any 𝐱(0)∈ℝp\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, choose any step size α>0\alpha>0 such that α<2/L\alpha<2/L, and iteratively define 𝐱(t+1)=𝐱(t)−α​∇g​(𝐱(t))\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)}=\mathbf{x}^{(t)}-\alpha\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}) for each t≥0t\geq 0. Then

g​(𝐱(t))−g∗≤(1−μ​α​(2−α​L))t​(g​(𝐱(0))−g∗)=(μL)t​(g​(𝐱(0))−g∗)​ for ​α=1/L\begin{split}g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-g^{*}&\leq\left(1-\mu\alpha\left(2-\alpha L\right)\right)^{t}\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})-g^{*}\right)=\left(\frac{\mu}{L}\right)^{t}\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})-g^{*}\right)\text{ for }\alpha=1/L\end{split} (51)
Proof.

Since gg has an LL-Lipschitz continuous gradient,

g​(𝐱(t+1))−g∗≤g​(𝐱(t))+(𝐱(t+1)−𝐱(t))⊤​∇g​(𝐱(t))+L2​‖𝐱(t+1)−𝐱(t)‖22−g∗=g​(𝐱(t))−α​∇g​(𝐱(t))⊤​∇g​(𝐱(t))+L2​‖α​∇g​(𝐱(t))‖22−g∗=g​(𝐱(t))−α​(1−α​L2)​‖∇g​(𝐱(t))‖22−g∗=g​(𝐱(t))−α2​(2−α​L)​‖∇g​(𝐱(t))‖22−g∗≤g​(𝐱(t))−μ​α​(2−α​L)​(g​(𝐱(t))−g∗)−g∗​ since g is μ-PL and 2−α​L>0 =(1−μ​α​(2−α​L))​(g​(𝐱(t))−g∗)≤(1−μ​α​(2−α​L))t+1​(g​(𝐱(0))−g∗)\begin{split}g(\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)})-g^{*}&\leq g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})+(\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(t)})^{\top}\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})+\frac{L}{2}\|\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)}-\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\|_{2}^{2}-g^{*}\\ &=g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-\alpha\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})^{\top}\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})+\frac{L}{2}\|\alpha\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}-g^{*}\\ &=g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-\alpha\left(1-\frac{\alpha L}{2}\right)\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}-g^{*}\\ &=g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-\frac{\alpha}{2}\left(2-\alpha L\right)\|\nabla g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}-g^{*}\\ &\leq g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-\mu\alpha\left(2-\alpha L\right)\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-g^{*}\right)-g^{*}\text{ since $g$ is $\mu$-PL and $2-\alpha L>0$ }\\ &=\left(1-\mu\alpha\left(2-\alpha L\right)\right)\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(t)})-g^{*}\right)\\ &\leq\left(1-\mu\alpha\left(2-\alpha L\right)\right)^{t+1}\left(g(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})-g^{*}\right)\end{split} (52)

C.3 Preservation of the Chatterjee–Łojasiewicz Inequality under Perturbation

In Section C.1, we study how gg behaves when a regularization hh is added to the optimization objective f=g+β​hf=g+\beta h. We also study the behavior of ff and the regularization term hh when gg and its gradient are already small. We establish below that, under some assumptions on hh and gg, if gg is rr-CL at 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, then for all ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there exists βmax=βmax​(ε,𝐱,r)>0\beta_{\max}=\beta_{\max}(\varepsilon,\mathbf{x},r)>0 such that for all β<βmax\beta<\beta_{\max}, the function f=g+β​hf=g+\beta h is also ε​r\varepsilon r-CL at 𝐱\mathbf{x}. This means that Theorem C.15 also applies to f−f∗f-f^{*}. In other words, we also have (undefined terms are those of Theorem C.15):

  • •

    𝐱(k)∈B​(𝐱(0),ε​r)\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},\varepsilon r) for all kk, and as k→∞k\rightarrow\infty, 𝐱(k)\mathbf{x}^{(k)} converges to a point 𝐱∗∈B​(𝐱(0),ε​r)\mathbf{x}^{*}\in B(\mathbf{x}^{(0)},\varepsilon r) where f​(𝐱∗)=f∗f(\mathbf{x}^{*})=f^{*}.

  • •

    For each k≥0k\geq 0, ‖𝐱(k)−𝐱∗‖22≤(1−δ)k​ε2​r2\|\mathbf{x}^{(k)}-\mathbf{x}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}\leq(1-\delta)^{k}\varepsilon^{2}r^{2}, (f​(𝐱(k))−f∗)≤(1−δ)k​(f​(𝐱(0))−f∗)\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(k)})-f^{*}\right)\leq(1-\delta)^{k}\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(0)})-f^{*}\right) with δ:=min⁡{1,(1−ϵ)⋅χ​(f,𝐱(0),ε​r)⋅α}\delta:=\min\{1,(1-\epsilon)\cdot\chi(f,\mathbf{x}^{(0)},\varepsilon r)\cdot\alpha\}.

We start by introducing a property less restrictive than convexity, which we call the Zero-Stationary Property (ZSP).

Definition C.26 (Zero-Stationary Property).

A subdifferentiable function φ:ℝp→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} is said to satisfy the zero-stationary property (ZSP) or to be ZSP on U⊂ℝpU\subset\mathbb{R}^{p} if and only if for all 𝐱∈U\mathbf{x}\in U, 0∈∂φ​(𝐱)⟹φ​(𝐱)=00\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{x})\Longrightarrow\varphi(\mathbf{x})=0.

For a ZSP function, if a point is stationary (in the sense that 0 is a subgradient), its value must be zero. In the context of non-negative functions, this implies that only points with the optimal value (zero) can be stationary. This is linked to Fermat’s or interior extremum theorem (which identifies stationary points via derivatives), but adds a zero constraint on the function’s value. The ℓp\ell_{p} norm (p>0p>0) and nuclear norm ℓ∗\ell_{*} are ZSP on ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}. Convex functions are not ZSP in general. Take for example φ​(𝐱)=1\varphi(\mathbf{x})=1 or φ​(𝐱)=(𝐱−1)2−1\varphi(\mathbf{x})=(\mathbf{x}-1)^{2}-1. But if φ\varphi is convex and φ∗:=inf𝐱∈ℝpφ​(𝐱)\varphi^{*}:=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\varphi(\mathbf{x}) is in the image Im​(φ)\text{Im}(\varphi) of φ\varphi, then φ\varphi is ZSP (Lemma C.27). The ZSP property does not imply convexity. The ZSP is local because it only constrains the function’s value at points where the subgradient contains zero. It does not constrain the function’s curvature or behavior away from these stationary points. Therefore, for a ZSP function to be convex, it must satisfy one of the standard conditions that define or characterize convexity (first or second-order condition, Jensen’s inequality, convexity of the Epigraph, etc).

Lemma C.27.

Let φ:ℝp→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R} be a subdifferentiable function such that −∞<φ∗:=inf𝐱∈ℝpφ​(𝐱)∈Im​(φ)-\infty<\varphi^{*}:=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\in\text{Im}(\varphi). If φ\varphi is convex, then φ−φ∗\varphi-\varphi^{*} is ZSP. The converse is false.

Proof.

Let φ\varphi be convex and assume −∞<φ∗=inf𝐱∈ℝpφ​(𝐱)∈Im​(φ)-\infty<\varphi^{*}=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\in\text{Im}(\varphi). Define φ~​(𝐱):=φ​(𝐱)−φ∗\tilde{\varphi}(\mathbf{x}):=\varphi(\mathbf{x})-\varphi^{*}. Let 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} such that 0∈∂φ~​(𝐱)=∂φ​(𝐱)0\in\partial\tilde{\varphi}(\mathbf{x})=\partial\varphi(\mathbf{x}). By the definition of convexity, we know that φ​(𝐲)≥φ​(𝐱)+(𝐲−𝐱)⊤​𝐳\varphi(\mathbf{y})\geq\varphi(\mathbf{x})+(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})^{\top}\mathbf{z} for all 𝐲\mathbf{y} and all 𝐳∈∂φ​(𝐱)\mathbf{z}\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{x}). Since 0∈∂φ​(𝐱)0\in\partial\varphi(\mathbf{x}), we choose 𝐳=0\mathbf{z}=0, and get φ​(𝐲)≥φ​(𝐱)\varphi(\mathbf{y})\geq\varphi(\mathbf{x}) for all 𝐲\mathbf{y}. This means that 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a global minimum of φ\varphi. Since φ∗∈Im​(φ)\varphi^{*}\in\text{Im}(\varphi), we conclude φ​(𝐱)=φ∗\varphi(\mathbf{x})=\varphi^{*}, i.e. φ~​(𝐱)=0\tilde{\varphi}(\mathbf{x})=0. This proves that φ~\tilde{\varphi} is ZSP.

Take φ​(x)=x21+x2\varphi(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{1+x^{2}} for x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}, with φ∗=0\varphi^{*}=0. Since φ′​(x)=2​x(1+x2)2\varphi^{\prime}(x)=\frac{2x}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}, we have 0∈∂φ​(x)⟺x=0⟺φ​(x)=00\in\partial\varphi(x)\Longleftrightarrow x=0\Longleftrightarrow\varphi(x)=0. So φ−φ∗\varphi-\varphi^{*} is ZSP. But φ\varphi is neither globally convex nor globally concave on ℝ\mathbb{R} because φ′′​(x)=2​(1−3​x2)(1+x2)3\varphi^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{2(1-3x^{2})}{(1+x^{2})^{3}} changes sign. ∎

Theorem C.28 (Chatterjee–Łojasiewicz stability under ZSP Perturbation).

Let g:ℝp→[0,∞)g:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to[0,\infty) be a differentiable function, and let h:ℝp→[0,∞)h:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to[0,\infty) be a subdifferentiable function. For all 𝐱∈ℝp\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and r>0r>0, if gg satisfies the rr-CL inequality at 𝐱\mathbf{x}, i.e 4​g​(𝐱)<r2⋅χ​(g,𝐱,r)4g(\mathbf{x})<r^{2}\cdot\chi(g,\mathbf{x},r), then:

Moreover, if g​(𝐲)=0⟹f​(𝐲)=0g(\mathbf{y})=0\Longrightarrow f(\mathbf{y})=0, then f=g+β​hf=g+\beta h satisfies the r′r^{\prime}-CL inequality at 𝐱\mathbf{x} provided that β\beta satisfies this constraint, i.e., 4​f​(𝐱)<r′⁣2⋅χ​(f,𝐱,r′)4f(\mathbf{x})<r^{\prime 2}\cdot\chi(f,\mathbf{x},r^{\prime}).

‖F​(𝐚(t))‖2=‖G​(𝐚(t))+β​H​(𝐚(t))‖2≤‖G​(𝐚(t))‖2+β​‖H​(𝐚(t))‖2∝2​α​β​n1−ρ2​‖𝐗⊤​𝐗‖2→2+β​n=n​(2​σmax​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)+1)​β\begin{split}\|F(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})\|_{2}&=\|G(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})+\beta H(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})\|_{2}\\ &\leq\|G(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})\|_{2}+\beta\|H(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})\|_{2}\\ &\propto\frac{2\alpha\beta\sqrt{n}}{1-\rho_{2}}\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\|_{2\to 2}+\beta\sqrt{n}\\ &=\sqrt{n}\left(2\sigma_{\max}\left(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\right)+1\right)\beta\end{split} (83)

Also, since 𝐗​(𝐚(t)−^​𝐚)∈Col⁡(𝐗)=Col⁡(𝐔)\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{a})\in\operatorname{Col}(\mathbf{X})=\operatorname{Col}(\mathbf{U}) and 𝐗𝐚^−𝐲∗=(𝕀N−𝐔𝐔⊤)𝝃∈Col(𝐔)⟂\mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{a}}-\mathbf{y}^{*}=(\mathbb{I}_{N}-\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\top})\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\operatorname{Col}(\mathbf{U})^{\perp}, we have for t≥t1t\geq t_{1},

g​(𝐚(t))−g​(𝐚^)=12​‖𝐗𝐚(t)−𝐲∗‖22−12​‖𝐗​^​𝐚−𝐲∗‖22=12​‖𝐗​(𝐚(t)−^​𝐚)+(𝐗​^​𝐚−𝐲∗)‖22−12​‖𝐗​^​𝐚−𝐲∗‖22=12​‖𝐗​(𝐚(t)−^​𝐚)‖22+12​‖𝐗​^​𝐚−𝐲∗‖22−12​‖𝐗​^​𝐚−𝐲∗‖22=12​‖𝐗​(𝐚(t)−^​𝐚)‖22\begin{split}g(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-g(\hat{\mathbf{a}})&=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\hat{}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{a})+\left(\mathbf{X}\hat{}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\right)\|_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\hat{}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{a})\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\hat{}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\hat{}\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{a})\|_{2}^{2}\end{split} (84)

So

g​(𝐚(t))−g​(𝐚^)≤12​‖𝐗‖2→22​‖𝐚(t)−^​𝐚‖22≤2​n​α2​β2​σmax2​(𝐗)(1−ρ2)2∝2​n​β2​σmax​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)\begin{split}g(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-g(\hat{\mathbf{a}})&\leq\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\|_{2\to 2}^{2}\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{a}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{2n\alpha^{2}\beta^{2}\sigma_{\max}^{2}(\mathbf{X})}{(1-\rho_{2})^{2}}\propto 2n\beta^{2}\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})\end{split} (85)

All this shows that after t1t_{1}, the iterate 𝐚(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)}, its error g​(𝐚(t))g(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}), and the associated gradient G​(𝐚(t))G(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}) behave respectively like 𝐚^\hat{\mathbf{a}}, g​(𝐚^)g(\hat{\mathbf{a}}), and G​(𝐚^)=0G(\hat{\mathbf{a}})=0 up to an error of order 𝒪​(β)\mathcal{O}(\beta). Note that we assume 0<β​n≪σmax​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)0<\beta\sqrt{n}\ll\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}). So, the gradient of gg can be made much smaller than the subgradient term after t1t_{1} by choosing β\beta sufficiently small. After time t1t_{1}, the contribution of the gradient GG to the update of 𝐚i(t)\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t)} is dominated by the ℓ1\ell_{1}–regularization term up to an error of order 𝒪​(β)\mathcal{O}(\beta). Specifically for all t≫t1t\gg t_{1}, the update rule approximates 𝐚i(t+1)≈𝐚i(t)−α​β​H​(𝐚i(t))\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t+1)}\approx\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t)}-\alpha\beta H(\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t)}). If |𝐚i(t1)|>|𝐚i∗||\mathbf{a}^{(t_{1})}_{i}|>|\mathbf{a}_{i}^{*}|, then H​(𝐚i(t))=H​(𝐚i(t)−𝐚i∗)H(\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t)})=H(\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}_{i}) (Lemma C.32), and so 𝐚i(t+1)−𝐚i∗=𝐚i(t)−𝐚i∗−α​β​H​(𝐚i(t)−𝐚i∗)\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t+1)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}_{i}=\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}_{i}-\alpha\beta H(\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}_{i}) for all t≥t1t\geq t_{1}. By Lemma C.31, this lead to |𝐚i(t)−𝐚i∗|≤α​β|\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}_{i}|\leq\alpha\beta for (and only for) t≥t1+⌊|𝐚i(t1)−𝐚i∗|α​β⌋t\geq t_{1}+\left\lfloor\frac{|\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{a}^{*}_{i}|}{\alpha\beta}\right\rfloor. This suggest that we may have ‖𝐚(t)−𝐚∗‖∞=𝒪​(α​β)\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{\infty}=\mathcal{O}(\alpha\beta) for (and only for) t≥t1+⌊‖𝐚(t1)−𝐚∗‖∞α​β⌋t\geq t_{1}+\left\lfloor\frac{\|\mathbf{a}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{\infty}}{\alpha\beta}\right\rfloor. In fact, considering the canonical subgradient H​(𝐚)=sign⁡(𝐚)H(\mathbf{a})=\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{a}), we have 𝐚t+1−𝐚∗=𝐚(t)−𝐚∗−α​G​(𝐚(t))−α​β​sign⁡(𝐚(t))=Cα​β​(𝐚(t)−𝐚∗−α​G​(𝐚(t)))\mathbf{a}^{t+1}-\mathbf{a}^{*}=\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}-\alpha G(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-\alpha\beta\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})=C_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*}-\alpha G(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})) with

Cγ​(z)={z−γif ​z>γz+γif ​z<γ∈[z−γ,z+γ]if −γ≤z≤γ∈z±γC_{\gamma}(z)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}z-\gamma&\mbox{if }z>\gamma\\ z+\gamma&\mbox{if }z<\gamma\\ \in[z-\gamma,z+\gamma]&\mbox{if }-\gamma\leq z\leq\gamma\end{array}\right.\in z\pm\gamma

a coordinate shrink operator, since

|Cγ​(z)|={|z|−γif ​|z|>γ∈[0,γ]if ​|z|≤γ≤max⁡(|z|−γ,γ)|C_{\gamma}(z)|=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}|z|-\gamma&\mbox{if }|z|>\gamma\\ \in[0,\gamma]&\mbox{if }|z|\leq\gamma\end{array}\right.\leq\max(|z|-\gamma,\gamma)

So the goal of H​(𝐚)H(\mathbf{a}) is to reduce the components of 𝐚(t)−𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*} at each iteration until they are all in [−α​β,α​β][-\alpha\beta,\alpha\beta]. We now prove this intuition below using Lemma C.12, which proves the second part of the theorem.

We have g​(𝐚(t))=12​‖𝐗𝐚(t)−𝐲∗‖22g(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}, h​(𝐚(t))=‖𝐚(t)‖1h(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})=\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}, f​(𝐚(t))=g​(𝐚(t))+β​h​(𝐚(t))f(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})=g(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})+\beta h(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}) and f​(𝐚∗)=β​‖𝐚∗‖1+12​‖𝝃‖22f(\mathbf{a}^{*})=\beta\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}. We also have Θf={𝐚∗}\Theta_{f}=\{\mathbf{a}^{*}\} and Θg={𝐚∣𝐗​(𝐚−𝐚∗)=𝝃}\Theta_{g}=\{\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*})=\boldsymbol{\xi}\}. Applying Lemma C.12, we get

mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐚(t))−f​(𝐚∗))≤‖𝐚(t1)−𝐚∗‖22+(t2−t1)​α2​maxt1≤t≤t2⁡‖F​(𝐚(t))‖222​α​(t2−t1)∀t2≥t1\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{a}^{*})\right)\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{a}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}+(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha^{2}\max_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|F(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})\|_{2}^{2}}{2\alpha(t_{2}-t_{1})}\quad\forall t_{2}\geq t_{1} (86)

Using ‖F​(𝐚(t))‖2=𝒪​(β)​∀t≥t1\|F(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})\|_{2}=\mathcal{O}\left(\beta\right)\ \forall t\geq t_{1} (Equation (83)) we get from Theorem C.13 that there exists C′>0C^{\prime}>0,

mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐚(t))−f​(𝐚∗))≤(η+C′​α​β)​β2⟺t2≥t1+‖𝐚(t1)−𝐚∗‖22α​β​η\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{a}^{*})\right)\leq\frac{\left(\eta+C^{\prime}\alpha\beta\right)\beta}{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\frac{\|\mathbf{a}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}}{\alpha\beta\eta} (87)

And it Θf∩Θg≠∅\Theta_{f}\cap\Theta_{g}\neq\emptyset, i.e. 𝝃=0\boldsymbol{\xi}=0,

mint1≤t≤t2⁡(‖𝐚(t)‖1−‖𝐚∗‖1)≤η+C′​α​β2⟺t2≥t1+‖𝐚(t1)−𝐚∗‖22α​β​η\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\right)\leq\frac{\eta+C^{\prime}\alpha\beta}{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\frac{\|\mathbf{a}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}}{\alpha\beta\eta} (88)

We now prove this result in a general case 𝝃≠0\boldsymbol{\xi}\neq 0. Let R​(𝐚):=(𝐚−𝐚∗)⊤​G​(𝐚)R(\mathbf{a}):=\left(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\right)^{\top}G(\mathbf{a}). We have from Lemma C.12,

mint1≤t≤t2⁡[R​(𝐚(t))+β​(‖𝐚(t)‖1−‖𝐚∗‖1)]≤mint1≤t≤t2⁡[(g​(𝐚(t))−g​(𝐚∗))+β​(‖𝐚(t)‖1−‖𝐚∗‖1)]≤mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐚(t))−f​(𝐚∗))∀t2≥t1\begin{split}\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left[R(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})+\beta\left(\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\right)\right]&\leq\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left[\left(g(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-g(\mathbf{a}^{*})\right)+\beta\left(\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\right)\right]\\ &\leq\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{a}^{*})\right)\quad\forall t_{2}\geq t_{1}\end{split} (89)

So

β​mint1≤t≤t2⁡(‖𝐚(t)‖1−‖𝐚∗‖1)≤mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐚(t))−f​(𝐚∗))−(mint1≤t≤t2⁡g​(𝐚(t))−12​‖𝝃‖22)∀t2≥t1\begin{split}\beta\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\right)&\leq\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{a}^{*})\right)-\left(\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}g(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}\right)\quad\forall t_{2}\geq t_{1}\end{split} (90)

Since

g​(𝐚(t))−12​‖𝝃‖22=g​(𝐚^)+12​‖𝐗​(𝐚(t)−^​𝐚)‖22−12​‖𝝃‖22=12​‖𝐗​(𝐚(t)−^​𝐚)‖22−12​‖𝐔⊤​𝝃‖22≥−12​‖𝐔⊤​𝝃‖22\begin{split}g(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}&=g(\hat{\mathbf{a}})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{a})\|_{2}^{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{a})\|_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}\geq-\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}\end{split} (91)

We obtain

β​mint1≤t≤t2⁡(‖𝐚(t)‖1−‖𝐚∗‖1)≤mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐚(t))−f​(𝐚∗))+12​‖𝐗⊤​𝝃‖22∀t2≥t1≤(η+C′​α​β)​β2+C​α​β22⟺t2≥t1+Δ​t​(η,t1)​ since ​‖𝐗⊤​𝝃‖2≤C​α​β=(η+(C+C′)​α​β)​β2⟺t2≥t1+Δ​t​(η,t1)\begin{split}\beta\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\right)&\leq\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{a}^{*})\right)+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\forall t_{2}\geq t_{1}\\ &\leq\frac{\left(\eta+C^{\prime}\alpha\beta\right)\beta}{2}+\frac{C\alpha\beta^{2}}{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\Delta t(\eta,t_{1})\text{ since }\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{C\alpha}\beta\\ &=\frac{\left(\eta+(C+C^{\prime})\alpha\beta\right)\beta}{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\Delta t(\eta,t_{1})\end{split} (92)

Lemma C.30.

Given α>0\alpha>0 and a(1)∈ℝa^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}, let a(t+1)=a(t)−α​H​(a(t))a^{(t+1)}=a^{(t)}-\alpha H(a^{(t)}) for all t≥1t\geq 1, where H​(a)∈∂|a|H(a)\in\partial|a|.

  1. 1.

    A point aa is stationary for this dynamical system if and only if |a|≤α|a|\leq\alpha.

  2. 2.

    We have |a(t)|≤α|a^{(t)}|\leq\alpha if and only if t>⌊|a(1)|α⌋t>\lfloor\frac{|a^{(1)}|}{\alpha}\rfloor.

  3. 3.

    In particular, for h​(a)=sign⁡(a)​∀a∈ℝh(a)=\operatorname{sign}(a)\ \forall a\in\mathbb{R}, if a(1)/α∈ℤa^{(1)}/\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}, then a(t)=0a^{(t)}=0 for all t>⌊|a(1)|α⌋t>\lfloor\frac{|a^{(1)}|}{\alpha}\rfloor.

Proof.

Let first consider the simple case H​(a)=sign⁡(a)H(a)=\operatorname{sign}(a), so that a(t+1)=a(t)−α​sign⁡(a(t))a^{(t+1)}=a^{(t)}-\alpha\operatorname{sign}(a^{(t)}).

  • •

    If a(t)∈{0,α,−α}a^{(t)}\in\{0,\alpha,-\alpha\}, then a(t+Δ)=0a^{(t+\Delta)}=0 for all Δ>0\Delta>0.

  • •

    If a(t)∈(0,α)a^{(t)}\in(0,\alpha), then a(t+1)=a(t)−α∈(−α,0)a^{(t+1)}=a^{(t)}-\alpha\in(-\alpha,0), and a(t+2)=a(t+1)+α=a(t)∈(0,α)a^{(t+2)}=a^{(t+1)}+\alpha=a^{(t)}\in(0,\alpha), and so on.

  • •

    If a(t)∈(−α,0)a^{(t)}\in(-\alpha,0), then a(t+1)=a(t)+α∈(0,α)a^{(t+1)}=a^{(t)}+\alpha\in(0,\alpha), and a(t+2)=a(t+1)−α=a(t)∈(−α,0)a^{(t+2)}=a^{(t+1)}-\alpha=a^{(t)}\in(-\alpha,0), and so on.

  • •

    If a(t)>αa^{(t)}>\alpha (resp. a(t)<−αa^{(t)}<-\alpha), it will be decreased (resp. increase) by α\alpha until a(t)∈(0,α]a^{(t)}\in(0,\alpha] (resp. a(t)∈[−α,0)a^{(t)}\in[-\alpha,0)), and we get back to the previous cases. In that case, |a(t+1)|=|a(t)|−α=|a(1)|−t​α≤α⟹t+1≥|a(1)|α|a^{(t+1)}|=|a^{(t)}|-\alpha=|a^{(1)}|-t\alpha\leq\alpha\Longrightarrow t+1\geq\frac{|a^{(1)}|}{\alpha}.

Now consider the general dynamic a(t+1)=a(t)−α​H​(a(t))a^{(t+1)}=a^{(t)}-\alpha H(a^{(t)}). If a(1)≠0a^{(1)}\neq 0 (the case a(1)=0a^{(1)}=0 is trivial), then the dynamic is a(t+1)=a(t)−α​sign⁡(a(t))a^{(t+1)}=a^{(t)}-\alpha\operatorname{sign}(a^{(t)}) as long as |a(t)|≥α|a^{(t)}|\geq\alpha, after which it will just oscillate in the ball {a,|a|≤α}\{a,|a|\leq\alpha\} indefinitely. In fact, a fixed point aa must satisfy a=a−α​H​(a)a=a-\alpha H(a); i.e. H​(a)=0H(a)=0. The only case where 0∈∂|a|0\in\partial|a| is a=0a=0 or when it lies in the interval where the subgradient can be 0. However, for any aa such that |a|≤α|a|\leq\alpha, it is possible to choose H​(a)H(a) (for instance, H​(a)=a/αH(a)=a/\alpha) such that a=a−α​H​(a)a=a-\alpha H(a), making aa a fixed point. Conversely, if |a|>α|a|>\alpha, then |H​(a)|=1|H(a)|=1 and |a−α​H​(a)|=||a|−α|>0|a-\alpha H(a)|=||a|-\alpha|>0, so aa is not a fixed point. ∎

Lemma C.31.

Given α>0\alpha>0 and 𝐚(1)∈ℝn\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, let 𝐚(t+1)=𝐚(t)−α​H​(𝐚(t))\mathbf{a}^{(t+1)}=\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\alpha H(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}) for all t≥1t\geq 1, where H​(𝐚)∈∂‖𝐚‖1H(\mathbf{a})\in\partial\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1}.

  1. 1.

    A point 𝐚\mathbf{a} is stationary for this dynamical system if and only if ‖𝐚‖∞≤α\|\mathbf{a}\|_{\infty}\leq\alpha.

  2. 2.

    We have ‖𝐚(t)‖∞≤α\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{\infty}\leq\alpha if and only if t>⌊‖𝐚(1)‖∞α⌋t>\lfloor\frac{\|\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\|_{\infty}}{\alpha}\rfloor.

  3. 3.

    In particular, for h​(𝐚)=sign⁡(𝐚)​∀𝐚∈ℝnh(\mathbf{a})=\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{a})\ \forall\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we have ‖𝐚(t)‖0=|{i|𝐚i(1)/α∈ℤ}|\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}\|_{0}=\left|\left\{i\ |\ \mathbf{a}^{(1)}_{i}/\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}\right\}\right| for all t>⌊‖𝐚(1)‖∞α⌋t>\lfloor\frac{\|\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\|_{\infty}}{\alpha}\rfloor.

Proof.

The proof is immediate by applying the Lemma C.30 coordinate-wise. In practice, we work with the subgradient H​(𝐚)=sign⁡(𝐚)H(\mathbf{a})=\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{a}), the one provided by automatic differentiation in many optimization libraries, like Pytorch. ∎

Lemma C.32.

Let a,a∗∈ℝa,a^{*}\in\mathbb{R} with a≠0a\neq 0. If |a|>|a∗||a|>|a^{*}|, then sign⁡(a−a∗)=sign⁡(a)\operatorname{sign}(a-a^{*})=\operatorname{sign}(a).

Proof.

We have |a∗|<|a|⟺−|a|<a∗<|a|⟺−|a|−a∗<0<|a|−a∗|a^{*}|<|a|\Longleftrightarrow-|a|<a^{*}<|a|\Longleftrightarrow-|a|-a^{*}<0<|a|-a^{*}. This implies a−a∗<0a-a^{*}<0 for a<0a<0 and 0<a−a∗0<a-a^{*} for 0<a0<a. ∎

Lemma C.33.

Let f​(θ)=g​(θ)+β​h​(θ)f(\theta)=g(\theta)+\beta h(\theta) be a function from ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} to ℝ\mathbb{R}, where gg is a differentiable function and hh is a sub-differentiable function. Consider the subgradient descent update θ(t+1)=θ(t)−α​(∇g​(θ(t))+β​H​(θ(t)))\theta^{(t+1)}=\theta^{(t)}-\alpha\left(\nabla g(\theta^{(t)})+\beta H(\theta^{(t)})\right) with a fixed small step size α>0\alpha>0, where H​(θ(t))∈∂h​(θ)H(\theta^{(t)})\in\partial h(\theta). If β​‖H​(θ(1))‖2≫‖∇g​(θ(1))‖2\beta\|H(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2}\gg\|\nabla g(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2} then the regularization term dominates the updates, causing the sequence {θ(t)}t>1\{\theta^{(t)}\}_{t>1} to exhibit oscillatory behavior without convergence to a minimizer of ff. The condition β​‖H​(θ(1))‖2≫‖∇g​(θ(1))‖2\beta\|H(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2}\gg\|\nabla g(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2} writes β​n≫‖∇g​(θ(1))‖2\beta\sqrt{n}\gg\|\nabla g(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2} for ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization, h​(θ)=‖θ‖1​∀θ∈ℝnh(\theta)=\|\theta\|_{1}\ \forall\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}; and β​min⁡(n1,n2)≫‖∇g​(θ(1))‖2\beta\sqrt{\min(n_{1},n_{2})}\gg\|\nabla g(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2} for ℓ∗\ell_{*} regularization, h​(θ)=‖θ‖∗​∀θ∈ℝn1×n2h(\theta)=\|\theta\|_{*}\ \forall\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}.

Proof Sketch.

Given that ‖∇g​(θ(t))‖2≈‖∇g​(θ(1))‖2\|\nabla g(\theta^{(t)})\|_{2}\approx\|\nabla g(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2} and H​(θ(t))≈H​(θ(1))H(\theta^{(t)})\approx H(\theta^{(1)}) at the beginning of training, if β​‖H​(θ(1))‖2≫‖∇g​(θ(1))‖2\beta\|H(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2}\gg\|\nabla g(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2}, then β​‖H​(θ(t))‖2≫‖∇g​(θ(t))‖2\beta\|H(\theta^{(t)})\|_{2}\gg\|\nabla g(\theta^{(t)})\|_{2}. This inequality implies that the regularization term dominates the update, θ(t+1)≈θ(t)−α​β​H​(θ(t))\theta^{(t+1)}\approx\theta^{(t)}-\alpha\beta H(\theta^{(t)}), with the influence of ∇g​(θ(t))\nabla g(\theta^{(t)}) becoming negligible. Consequently, the iterates do not converge to a stable minimizer of ff, and the training and test error metrics oscillate, remaining above some suboptimal value.

For ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization, h​(θ)=‖θ‖1​∀θ∈ℝnh(\theta)=\|\theta\|_{1}\ \forall\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, given that ‖h​(θ(t))‖2≈n\|h(\theta^{(t)})\|_{2}\approx\sqrt{n} at the beginning of training, if β​n≫‖∇g​(θ(1))‖2\beta\sqrt{n}\gg\|\nabla g(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2}, then that the update becomes dominated by the ℓ1\ell_{1}-term. Because H​(θ(t))H(\theta^{(t)}) reflects the sign of θ(t)\theta^{(t)}, the update effectively pushes the iterates in a direction that primarily depends on sign changes rather than the curvature of gg (Lemma C.31). This leads to overshooting and sign flipping in each coordinate, resulting in oscillations. Consequently, the iterates do not converge to a stable minimizer of ff, and the error metrics oscillate, remaining above some suboptimal value.

For ℓ∗\ell_{*} regularization, h​(θ)=‖θ‖∗​∀θ∈ℝn1×n2h(\theta)=\|\theta\|_{*}\ \forall\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}, the subgradient H​(θ(t))H(\theta^{(t)}) of ‖θ(t)‖∗\|\theta^{(t)}\|_{*} satisfy ‖H​(θ(t))‖∗≈min⁡(n1,n2)\|H(\theta^{(t)})\|_{*}\approx\sqrt{\min(n_{1},n_{2})} at the beginning of training (full rank matrix), so ‖H​(θ(t))‖F≥‖H​(θ(t))‖∗/rank(H​(θ(t)))≈min⁡(n1,n2)/min⁡(n1,n2)=min⁡(n1,n2)\|H(\theta^{(t)})\|_{\text{F}}\geq\|H(\theta^{(t)})\|_{*}/\operatorname*{rank}(H(\theta^{(t)}))\approx\sqrt{\min(n_{1},n_{2})}/\min(n_{1},n_{2})=\sqrt{\min(n_{1},n_{2})}. If β​min⁡(n1,n2)≫‖∇g​(θ(1))‖2\beta\sqrt{\min(n_{1},n_{2})}\gg\|\nabla g(\theta^{(1)})\|_{2}, then the update is dominated by the ℓ∗\ell_{*}-term, making the iterates swing sharply depending on the current singular-vector configuration (Lemma C.42). ∎

C.5 Proof of Theorem 3.3

For a vector 𝐮∈ℝn\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and a set S⊂[n]S\subset[n], we let 𝐮S=[𝐮i]i∈S∈ℝ|S|\mathbf{u}_{S}=[\mathbf{u}_{i}]_{i\in S}\in\mathbb{R}^{|S|}; and S¯=[n]\S\bar{S}=[n]\backslash S.

Definition C.34 (Null Space Property).

A matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is said to satisfy the null space property relative to a set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] if ‖𝐮S‖1<‖𝐮S¯‖1\|\mathbf{u}_{S}\|_{1}<\|\mathbf{u}_{\bar{S}}\|_{1} for all non zero vector 𝐮∈ℝn\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} in ker⁡𝐀\ker\mathbf{A}. It is said to satisfy the null space property of order s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N} if it satisfies the null space property relative to any set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] with |S|≤s|S|\leq s.

If we add ‖𝐮S‖1\|\mathbf{u}_{S}\|_{1} on both side of ‖𝐮S‖1<‖𝐮S¯‖1\|\mathbf{u}_{S}\|_{1}<\|\mathbf{u}_{\bar{S}}\|_{1} we obtain the equivalent formulation 2​‖𝐮S‖1<‖𝐮‖12\|\mathbf{u}_{S}\|_{1}<\|\mathbf{u}\|_{1}. On the other hand, by choosing SS as an index set of ss largest (in absolute value) entries of 𝐮\mathbf{u} and this time by adding ‖𝐮S¯‖1\|\mathbf{u}_{\bar{S}}\|_{1} to both sides of the inequality, the null space property of order ss reads ‖𝐮‖1<2​σ1​(𝐮)\|\mathbf{u}\|_{1}<2\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{u}), where σp​(𝐮)=inf‖𝐯‖0≤s‖𝐮−𝐯‖p\sigma_{p}(\mathbf{u})=\inf_{\|\mathbf{v}\|_{0}\leq s}\|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}\|_{p}. In fact, σp​(𝐮)\sigma_{p}(\mathbf{u}) is achieve (but not only) at 𝐯=Hs​(𝐮)\mathbf{v}=H_{s}(\mathbf{u}), with HsH_{s} the hard thresholding operator (it keeps the ss largest entries of 𝐮\mathbf{u} in absolute value, and set the remaining to 0). We have ‖𝐮−Hs​(𝐮)‖p=‖𝐮S¯‖p\|\mathbf{u}-H_{s}(\mathbf{u})\|_{p}=\|\mathbf{u}_{\bar{S}}\|_{p} with SS the support of Hs​(𝐮)H_{s}(\mathbf{u}).

In theory, sparse recovery methods are designed to recover exactly sparse vectors. However, in more realistic scenarios, the vectors we aim to recover are not exactly sparse but can be well-approximated by sparse vectors. In other words, while the true signal may not have strictly zero entries outside a small support, most of its energy or information content is concentrated on a small number of components. This motivates the need for recovery guarantees that extend beyond exact sparsity. In such settings, we no longer expect perfect recovery of the original vector. Instead, we aim to reconstruct a vector 𝐚\mathbf{a} such that the error between 𝐚\mathbf{a} and the true signal 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} is controlled by how well the true signal can be approximated by an ss-sparse vector. In other words, the reconstruction error should scale with the sparsity defect σs​(𝐚∗)\sigma_{s}(\mathbf{a}^{*}), which is typically measured by the distance from the signal to the set of exactly ss-sparse vectors. A reconstruction scheme that provides such guarantees is said to be stable with respect to the sparsity defect (Foucart & Rauhut, 2013).

Definition C.35 (Stable Null Space Property).

A matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is said to satisfy the stable null space property with constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) relative to a set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] if ‖𝐮S‖1​<ρ∥​𝐮S¯∥1\|\mathbf{u}_{S}\|_{1}<\rho\|\mathbf{u}_{\bar{S}}\|_{1} for all 𝐮∈ker⁡𝐀\mathbf{u}\in\ker\mathbf{A}. It is said to satisfy the robust null space property of order s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N} with constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) if it satisfies the robust null space property with constant ρ\rho relative to any set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] with |S|≤s|S|\leq s.

Theorem C.36 (Theorem 4.14 (Foucart & Rauhut, 2013)).

The matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} satisfies the stable null space property with constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) relative to a set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] if and only if ‖𝐯−𝐮‖1≤1+ρ1−ρ​(‖𝐯‖1−‖𝐮‖1+2​‖𝐮S¯‖1)\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}\|_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}(\|\mathbf{v}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{u}\|_{1}+2\|\mathbf{u}_{\bar{S}}\|_{1}) for all vector 𝐮,𝐯∈ℝn\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with 𝐀𝐮=𝐀𝐯\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}.

If we apply this to the noiseless version of problem (P1)(P_{1}), with 𝐚\mathbf{a} the solution return by, say basis pursuit, and SS the support of Hs​(𝐚)H_{s}(\mathbf{a}), the we get ‖𝐚−𝐚∗‖1≤2​(1+ρ)1−ρ​σs​(𝐚)\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\leq\frac{2(1+\rho)}{1-\rho}\sigma_{s}(\mathbf{a}) since ‖𝐚∗‖1≤‖𝐚‖1\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{1}\leq\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1} and ‖𝐚S¯‖1=σs​(𝐚)\|\mathbf{a}_{\bar{S}}\|_{1}=\sigma_{s}(\mathbf{a}).

In practical applications, it is fundamentally unrealistic to assume that we can observe or measure a signal 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} with perfect, infinite precision. All real-world measurements are subject to various sources of error, such as sensor inaccuracies, quantization effects, environmental noise, or other imperfections in the acquisition process. As a result, the measurement vector 𝐲∗\mathbf{y}^{*} that we actually obtain is not exactly equal to the ideal linear measurement 𝐗𝐚∗\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}^{*}, but only an approximation of it. This deviation is typically modeled as an additive noise term so that we only know that the measurement error is bounded, ‖𝐲∗−𝐗𝐚∗‖2=‖𝝃‖2≤ϵ\|\mathbf{y}^{*}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}=\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon for some known or estimated noise level ϵ>0\epsilon>0. In this noisy setting, an effective reconstruction scheme should not aim to recover 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} exactly since doing so is impossible, but instead produce an estimate 𝐚\mathbf{a} that is close to the true signal 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}, with an error that is controlled by the magnitude of the measurement error ϵ\epsilon. That is, small changes or perturbations in the observed measurements should only lead to small changes in the reconstructed signal. This desirable behavior is known as the robustness of the reconstruction scheme with respect to measurement error.

Definition C.37 (Robust Null Space Property).

A matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is said to satisfy the robust null space property (with respect to ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|) with constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and τ>0\tau>0 relative to a set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] if ‖𝐮S‖1​<ρ∥​𝐮S¯∥1+τ​‖𝐀𝐮‖\|\mathbf{u}_{S}\|_{1}<\rho\|\mathbf{u}_{\bar{S}}\|_{1}+\tau\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}\| for all 𝐮∈ℝn\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. It is said to satisfy the robust null space property of order s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N} with constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and τ>0\tau>0 if it satisfies the robust null space property with constant ρ\rho and τ\tau relative to any set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] with |S|≤s|S|\leq s.

Theorem C.38 (Theorem 4.20  (Foucart & Rauhut, 2013)).

The matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} satisfies the robust null space property with constant ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and τ>0\tau>0 relative to a set S⊂[n]S\subset[n] if and only if ‖𝐯−𝐮‖1≤1+ρ1−ρ​(‖𝐯‖1−‖𝐮‖1+2​‖𝐮S¯‖1)+2​τ1−ρ​‖𝐀​(𝐯−𝐮)‖\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}\|_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}(\|\mathbf{v}\|_{1}-\|\mathbf{u}\|_{1}+2\|\mathbf{u}_{\bar{S}}\|_{1})+\frac{2\tau}{1-\rho}\|\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u})\| for all vector 𝐮,𝐯∈ℝn\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

First, we observe that if β\beta is too high, the subgradient term H​(𝐀)H(\mathbf{A}) dominates early, and there is no convergence, i.e., no memorization nor generalization. Specifically for all t≫t1t\gg t_{1}, the update rule approximates 𝐀(t+1)≈𝐀(t)−α​β​H​(𝐀i(t))=𝐀(t)−α​β​H​(𝐀(t)−𝐀∗)\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}\approx\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\alpha\beta H(\mathbf{A}_{i}^{(t)})=\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\alpha\beta H(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\mathbf{A}^{*}) up to an error 𝐄∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} of order ‖𝐄‖F=𝒪​(α​β​rank(𝐀(t1))σmin​(𝐀(t1))/σmax​(𝐀∗)−1)\|\mathbf{E}\|_{\text{F}}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\alpha\beta\sqrt{\operatorname*{rank}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t_{1})}\right)}}{\sigma_{\min}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t_{1})}\right)/\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^{*})-1}\right) (Lemma C.45). We have g​(𝐀(t))=12​‖𝐗​vec⁡𝐀(t)−𝐲∗‖22g(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\operatorname{vec}\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}, h​(𝐀(t))=‖𝐀(t)‖∗h(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})=\|\mathbf{A}^{(t)}\|_{*}, f​(𝐀(t))=g​(𝐀(t))+β​h​(𝐀(t))f(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})=g(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})+\beta h(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}) and f​(𝐀∗)=β​‖𝐀∗‖∗+12​‖𝝃‖22f(\mathbf{A}^{*})=\beta\|\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{*}+\frac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}, Θf={𝐀∗}\Theta_{f}=\{\mathbf{A}^{*}\} and Θg={𝐀∣𝐗​vec⁡(𝐀−𝐀∗)=𝝃}\Theta_{g}=\{\mathbf{A}\mid\mathbf{X}\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*})=\boldsymbol{\xi}\}. Applying Lemma C.12, we get

mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐀(t))−f​(𝐀∗))≤‖vec⁡(𝐀(t1)−𝐀∗)‖22+(t2−t1)​α2​maxt1≤t≤t2⁡‖vec⁡(F​(𝐀(t)))‖222​α​(t2−t1)∀t2≥t1\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{A}^{*})\right)\leq\frac{\|\operatorname{vec}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t_{1})}-\mathbf{A}^{*}\right)\|_{2}^{2}+(t_{2}-t_{1})\alpha^{2}\max_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\|\operatorname{vec}\left(F(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})\right)\|_{2}^{2}}{2\alpha(t_{2}-t_{1})}\quad\forall t_{2}\geq t_{1} (99)

and

β​mint1≤t≤t2⁡(‖𝐀(t)‖∗−‖𝐀∗‖∗)≤mint1≤t≤t2⁡(f​(𝐀(t))−f​(𝐀∗))−(mint1≤t≤t2⁡g​(𝐀(t))−12​‖𝝃‖22)∀t2≥t1≤(η+C′​α​β)​β2+12​‖𝐗⊤​𝝃‖22⟺t2≥t1+Δ​t​(η,t1)≤(η+(C+C′)​α​β)​β2⟺t2≥t1+Δ​t​(η,t1)​ since ​‖𝐗⊤​𝝃‖2≤C​α​β\begin{split}\beta\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(\|\mathbf{A}^{(t)}\|_{*}-\|\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{*}\right)&\leq\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}\left(f(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})-f(\mathbf{A}^{*})\right)-\left(\min_{t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}}g(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}\right)\quad\forall t_{2}\geq t_{1}\\ &\leq\frac{\left(\eta+C^{\prime}\alpha\beta\right)\beta}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\Delta t(\eta,t_{1})\\ &\leq\frac{\left(\eta+(C+C^{\prime})\alpha\beta\right)\beta}{2}\Longleftrightarrow t_{2}\geq t_{1}+\Delta t(\eta,t_{1})\text{ since }\|\mathbf{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{C\alpha}\beta\end{split} (101)

since g​(𝐀(t))−12​‖𝝃‖22=12​‖𝐗​vec⁡(𝐀(t)−^​𝐀)‖22−12​‖𝐔⊤​𝝃‖22≥−12​‖𝐔⊤​𝝃‖22g(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\hat{}\mathbf{A})\|_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}\geq-\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}^{2}. ∎

Lemma C.41.

Let 𝐀∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}. We have ‖vec⁡(𝐇)‖p≤(n1​n2)1/p\|\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{H})\|_{p}\leq(n_{1}n_{2})^{1/p} for all 𝐇∈∂‖𝐀‖∗\mathbf{H}\in\partial\|\mathbf{A}\|_{*} and p>0p>0.

Proof.

Let 𝐇∈∂‖𝐀‖∗\mathbf{H}\in\partial\|\mathbf{A}\|_{*}. Then ‖𝐇‖2→2≤1\|\mathbf{H}\|_{2\to 2}\leq 1. So by the definition of the spectral (operator) norm, we have ‖𝐇‖2→2=sup𝐱≠0‖𝐇𝐱‖2‖𝐱‖2=σmax​(𝐇)≤1\|\mathbf{H}\|_{2\to 2}=\sup_{\mathbf{x}\neq 0}\frac{\|\mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}}=\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{H})\leq 1. Taking 𝐱=𝐞j(n2)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{e}^{(n_{2})}_{j}, the jj-th standard basis vector in ℝn2\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}, we obtain ‖𝐇:,j‖2=‖𝐇𝐞j(n2)‖2≤1\|\mathbf{H}_{:,j}\|_{2}=\|\mathbf{H}\mathbf{e}^{(n_{2})}_{j}\|_{2}\leq 1; which implied 𝐇i​j≤‖𝐇:,j‖2≤1\mathbf{H}_{ij}\leq\|\mathbf{H}_{:,j}\|_{2}\leq 1. So ‖vec⁡(𝐇)‖p=(∑i=1n1∑j=1n2|𝐇i​j|p)1/p≤(n1​n2)1/p\|\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{H})\|_{p}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{2}}|\mathbf{H}_{ij}|^{p}\right)^{1/p}\leq\left(n_{1}n_{2}\right)^{1/p}. ∎

Lemma C.42.

Given α>0\alpha>0 and 𝐀(1)∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}, let 𝐀(t+1)=𝐀(t)−α​H​(𝐀(t))\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}=\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\alpha H(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}) for all t≥1t\geq 1, where H​(𝐀)∈∂‖𝐀‖∗H(\mathbf{A})\in\partial\|\mathbf{A}\|_{*}.

  1. 1.

    A point 𝐀\mathbf{A} is stationary for this dynamical system if and only if ‖𝐀‖2→2=σmax​(𝐀)<α\|\mathbf{A}\|_{2\rightarrow 2}=\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A})<\alpha.

  2. 2.

    ‖𝐀(t)‖2→2<α\|\mathbf{A}^{(t)}\|_{2\rightarrow 2}<\alpha if and only if t>⌊‖𝐀(1)‖2→2α⌋t>\lfloor\frac{\|\mathbf{A}^{(1)}\|_{2\rightarrow 2}}{\alpha}\rfloor.

  3. 3.

    For all t>⌊‖𝐀(1)‖2→2α⌋t>\lfloor\frac{\|\mathbf{A}^{(1)}\|_{2\rightarrow 2}}{\alpha}\rfloor, rt:=rank(𝐀(t))=|{i|σi(1)/α∈ℤ}|r_{t}:=\operatorname*{rank}(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})=\left|\{i\quad|\quad\sigma^{(1)}_{i}/\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}\}\right|, with σ1(1),…,σr1(1)\sigma^{(1)}_{1},\dots,\sigma^{(1)}_{r_{1}} the singular values of 𝐀(1)\mathbf{A}^{(1)}.

Proof.

We start with the subgradient H​(𝐀)=𝐔𝐕⊤H(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top} for 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top}, so that the update rule becomes

𝐀(t+1)=𝐀(t)−α​𝐔(t)​𝐕(t)⊤=𝐔(t)​(Σ(t)−α​𝕀rt)​𝐕(t)⊤​for all ​t≥1\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}=\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\alpha\mathbf{U}^{(t)}\mathbf{V}^{(t)\top}=\mathbf{U}^{(t)}\left(\Sigma^{(t)}-\alpha\mathbb{I}_{r_{t}}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(t)\top}\text{for all }t\geq 1 (102)

This equation also writes

𝐀(t+1)=𝐔(t+1)​Σ(t+1)​𝐕(t+1)⊤=∑i=1rt+1σi(t+1)​𝐔:,i(t+1)​𝐕:,i(t+1)⊤=∑i=1rt(σi(t)−α)​𝐔:,i(t)​𝐕:,i(t)⊤=∑i=1rt|σi(t)−α|⋅sign⁡(σi(t)−α)​𝐔:,i(t)​𝐕:,i(t)⊤\begin{split}\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}&=\mathbf{U}^{(t+1)}\Sigma^{(t+1)}\mathbf{V}^{(t+1)\top}=\sum_{i=1}^{r_{t+1}}\sigma^{(t+1)}_{i}\mathbf{U}^{(t+1)}_{:,i}\mathbf{V}^{(t+1)\top}_{:,i}\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{r_{t}}(\sigma^{(t)}_{i}-\alpha)\mathbf{U}^{(t)}_{:,i}\mathbf{V}^{(t)\top}_{:,i}=\sum_{i=1}^{r_{t}}|\sigma^{(t)}_{i}-\alpha|\cdot\operatorname{sign}(\sigma^{(t)}_{i}-\alpha)\mathbf{U}^{(t)}_{:,i}\mathbf{V}^{(t)\top}_{:,i}\end{split} (103)

This implies σi(t+1)=|σi(t)−α|∀i∈[r1]\sigma^{(t+1)}_{i}=|\sigma^{(t)}_{i}-\alpha|\quad\forall i\in[r_{1}]. So starting at σi(1)\sigma^{(1)}_{i}, each σi\sigma_{i} decay at each step by α\alpha until σi(t)=:σi∗∈[0,α)\sigma^{(t)}_{i}=:\sigma_{i}^{*}\in[0,\alpha), and start oscillating between σi∗\sigma^{*}_{i} and α−σi∗\alpha-\sigma^{*}_{i}. It starts doing so when t>ti:=⌊σi(1)α⌋t>t_{i}:=\lfloor\frac{\sigma^{(1)}_{i}}{\alpha}\rfloor. We take t=maxi⁡tit=\max_{i}t_{i}.

In general, we have H​(𝐀)=𝐔𝐕⊤+𝐖,‖𝐖‖2→2≤1,𝐔⊤​𝐖=0,𝐖𝐕=0H(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}+\mathbf{W},\|\mathbf{W}\|_{2\to 2}\leq 1,\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{W}=0,\mathbf{W}\mathbf{V}=0. The dynamics becomes 𝐀(t+1)=𝐔(t)​(Σ(t)−α​𝕀rt)​𝐕(t)⊤−α​𝐖(t)\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}=\mathbf{U}^{(t)}\left(\Sigma^{(t)}-\alpha\mathbb{I}_{r_{t}}\right)\mathbf{V}^{(t)\top}-\alpha\mathbf{W}^{(t)} with 𝐔(t)⊤​𝐖(t)=0,𝐖(t)​𝐕(t)=0\mathbf{U}^{(t)\top}\mathbf{W}^{(t)}=0,\mathbf{W}^{(t)}\mathbf{V}^{(t)}=0. So 𝐔(t)⊤​𝐀(t+1)​𝐕(t)=Σ(t)−α​𝕀rt\mathbf{U}^{(t)\top}\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}\mathbf{V}^{(t)}=\Sigma^{(t)}-\alpha\mathbb{I}_{r_{t}}, leading again to σi(t+1)=|σi(t)−α|∀i∈[r1]\sigma^{(t+1)}_{i}=|\sigma^{(t)}_{i}-\alpha|\quad\forall i\in[r_{1}]. ∎

We show in Lemma C.32 that for a,a∗∈ℝa,a^{*}\in\mathbb{R}, |a|>|a∗|⟹sign⁡(a−a∗)=sign⁡(a)|a|>|a^{*}|\Longrightarrow\operatorname{sign}(a-a^{*})=\operatorname{sign}(a), with sign⁡(a)∈∂|a|\operatorname{sign}(a)\in\partial|a|. Now, considering the canonical nuclear–norm subgradient H​(𝐀)=𝐔𝐕⊤∈∂‖𝐀‖∗H(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\partial\|\mathbf{A}\|_{*} for 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}, we ask if σmin​(𝐀)>σmax​(𝐀∗)⟹H​(𝐀−𝐀∗)=H​(𝐀)\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{A})>\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^{*})\Longrightarrow H(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*})=H(\mathbf{A}), and if not, how does H​(𝐀−𝐀∗)H(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*}) deviate from H​(𝐀)H(\mathbf{A}). Throughout, let 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} of rank r≥1r\geq 1, and 𝐀−𝐀∗=~​𝐔​Σ~​~​𝐕⊤∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*}=\widetilde{}\mathbf{U}\widetilde{\Sigma}\widetilde{}\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}.

There exist matrices with σmin​(𝐀)>σmax​(𝐀∗)\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{A})>\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^{*}) for which H​(𝐀−𝐀∗)≠H​(𝐀)H(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*})\neq H(\mathbf{A}). For example, 𝐀=[2000]\mathbf{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix} and 𝐀∗=[0100]\mathbf{A}^{*}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix}. But if σmin​(𝐀)>σmax​(𝐀∗)\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{A})>\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{A}^{*}) and 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} have the same singular directions, then H​(𝐀−𝐀∗)=H​(𝐀)H(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*})=H(\mathbf{A}).

Lemma C.43.

Let 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}. If 𝐀∗=𝐔𝐁𝐕⊤\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{V}^{\top} with σmax​(𝐁)<σmin​(𝐀)\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{B})<\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf{A}), then H​(𝐀−𝐀∗)=H​(𝐀)H(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*})=H(\mathbf{A}).

Proof.

We have 𝐀−𝐀∗=𝐔​(Σ−𝐁)​𝐕⊤\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{U}(\Sigma-\mathbf{B})\mathbf{V}^{\top} under SVD, hence H​(𝐀−𝐀∗)=𝐔𝐕⊤=H​(𝐀)H(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*})=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}=H(\mathbf{A}). ∎

Now we focus on bounding ‖H​(𝐀−𝐀∗)−H​(𝐀)‖\|H(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*})-H(\mathbf{A})\|. We introduce some notations, then Wedin’s sin⁡Θ\sin\Theta bound (Wedin, 1972), and our result. Write H​(𝐀)=𝐔𝐕⊤H(\mathbf{A})=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top} and H​(𝐀−𝐀∗)=~​𝐔​~​𝐕⊤H(\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*})=\widetilde{}\mathbf{U}\widetilde{}\mathbf{V}^{\top}, with 𝐔,~​𝐔∈ℝn1×r\mathbf{U},\widetilde{}\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times r} and 𝐕,~​𝐕∈ℝn2×r\mathbf{V},\widetilde{}\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}\times r} having orthonormal columns. Let SL=span⁡(𝐔)⊂ℝn1S_{L}=\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{U})\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} and S~L=span⁡(~​𝐔)⊂ℝn1\widetilde{S}_{L}=\operatorname{span}(\widetilde{}\mathbf{U})\subset\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}. The principal angles 0≤θ1≤⋯≤θr≤π/20\leq\theta_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{r}\leq\pi/2 between SLS_{L} and S~L\widetilde{S}_{L} are defined by cos⁡θi=σi​(𝐔⊤​~​𝐔)∀i∈[r]\cos\theta_{i}=\sigma_{i}\left(\mathbf{U}^{\top}\widetilde{}\mathbf{U}\right)\quad\forall i\in[r], where σ1≥⋯≥σr\sigma_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{r} are the singular values. It is customary to collect the angles into a diagonal matrix ΘL:=diag⁡(θ1,…,θr)\Theta_{L}:=\operatorname{diag}(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{r}). Applying sin⁡(⋅)\sin(\cdot) entry-wise gives sin⁡ΘL:=diag⁡(sin⁡θ1,…,sin⁡θr)\sin\Theta_{L}:=\operatorname{diag}\left(\sin\theta_{1},\dots,\sin\theta_{r}\right). One never needs to compute the angles explicitly because ‖sin⁡ΘL‖2→2=‖𝐔⊤​~​𝐔⟂‖2→2=sin⁡θmax\left\|\sin\Theta_{L}\right\|_{2\to 2}=\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\widetilde{}\mathbf{U}^{\perp}\|_{2\to 2}=\sin\theta_{\max} where θmax=θr\theta_{\max}=\theta_{r} is the largest principal angle, and ~​𝐔⟂\widetilde{}\mathbf{U}^{\perp} is an orthonormal basis of S~L⟂\widetilde{S}_{L}^{\perp}. Thus ‖sin⁡ΘL‖2→2\|\sin\Theta_{L}\|_{2\to 2} measures the worst-case misalignment between the two subspaces; it equals the operator norm of the difference of their orthogonal projections. In the following, we use sin⁡ΘL\sin\Theta_{L} in place of ‖sin⁡ΘL‖2→2\|\sin\Theta_{L}\|_{2\to 2} by abuse of notation.

Lemma C.44 (Wedin’s sin⁡Θ\sin\Theta bound).

Let 𝐄∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} and set ~​𝐀:=𝐀+𝐄\widetilde{}\mathbf{A}:=\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{E}. An analogous bound on sin⁡ΘR:=‖𝐕r⊤​~​𝐕r⟂‖2→2\sin\Theta_{R}:=\|\mathbf{V}_{r}^{\top}\widetilde{}\mathbf{V}_{r}^{\perp}\|_{2\to 2} holds on the right singular side.

Appendix D Other Iterative Method for ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ∗\ell_{*} Minimization

D.1 Sparse Recovery

For the experiments of this section, we use (n,ζ,α,β)=(102,10−6,10−1,10−5)(n,\zeta,\alpha,\beta)=(10^{2},10^{-6},10^{-1},10^{-5}). We solve the sparse recovery problem using the projected subgradient (Figure 12) and the soft-thresholding algorithm (Figure 13). We observe a grokking-like pattern similar to the subgradient case. One training step is enough for the projected subgradient to get zero training error. This further shows that generalization is driven by α\alpha and, more importantly, β\beta.

Projected subgradient

To ensure memorization, we can use the projected subgradient for problem of minimizing ‖𝐚‖1\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1} subject to the constraint 𝐗𝐚=𝐲∗\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{y}^{*}, where at each step the update (using now just β​H​(𝐚)\beta H(\mathbf{a}) as gradient, not the whole F​(𝐚)F(\mathbf{a})) is projected onto the constraint set. We can show that the ℓ1\ell_{1} optimal gap of this method enjoys the same bound given above for the non-projected case. For the experiments of this section we use (n1,n2,r,N,ζ,α,β)=(10,10,2,70,10−6,10−1,10−4)(n_{1},n_{2},r,N,\zeta,\alpha,\beta)=(10,10,2,70,10^{-6},10^{-1},10^{-4}) for a matrix sensing. Figure 14 shows the results for the projected subgradient and Figure 15 shows the results for the proximal gradient method.

Projected subgradient

At each step, the update (using now just β​H​(𝐀)\beta H(\mathbf{A}) as gradient) is projected onto the constraint set. Proximal Gradient Descent
