The final form of the update is then 𝐀(t+1)=Sα​β​(𝐀(t)−α​G​(𝐀(t)))∀t>1.\mathbf{A}^{(t+1)}=S_{\alpha\beta}\left(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}-\alpha G(\mathbf{A}^{(t)})\right)\quad\forall t>1.

Appendix E Grokking Without Understanding

Consider the sparse recovery problem (the explanation below also holds for matrix factorization). We start the optimization at 𝐚(1)​∼i​i​d​ζ​𝒩​(0,1/n)\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\overset{iid}{\sim}\zeta\mathcal{N}(0,1/n) with ζ≥0\zeta\geq 0 the initialization scale. With a small initialization, ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization is sufficient for generalization to happen, provided NN is large enough and ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization is not very large. If the scale at initialization is large, then adding ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization is necessary to generalize, but is it sufficient? That is, can we generalize to the problem studied here with only ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization?

As shown in Section C.8, the answer to this question is no. But what we want to illustrate here is a phenomenon that contradicts previous art (Liu et al., 2023a; Lyu et al., 2023), namely that in the over-parametrized regime (N<nN<n in our case), large initialization and non-zero weight decay do not always lead to grokking. What happens is that, because of the large initialization, a more or less abrupt transition is observed in the generalization error during training, corresponding to a transition in the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the model parameters. But this can not be called grokking because the model only converges to a sub-optimal solution. What is more, this transition appears even if the problem posed admits no solution, e.g., sparse recovery or matrix completion with a number NN of examples far below the theoretical limit required for the solution to the problem posed to be the optimal solution (by any method whatsoever). This transition appears abrupt just because the training error is large at the beginning of training, since the model’s outputs are large. When its ℓ2\ell_{2} norm becomes small, its outputs also become small, leading to a transition in error. In Figure 16, without visualization of the error on a logarithmic scale, it looks like grokking has occurred, whereas this is not the case. For this figure we use (n,s,N,α)=(100,5,30,10−1)(n,s,N,\alpha)=(100,5,30,10^{-1}).

We call this phenomenon “grokking without understanding” like Levi et al. (2024) who illustrated it in the case of linear classification. They show that the sharp increase in generalization accuracy may often not imply a transition from “memorization” to “understanding” but can be an artifact of the accuracy measure. But in our case, we are not using any significant scale at initialization (we focus on 0≤ζ≤10−50\leq\zeta\leq 10^{-5}) and are not dealing with the generalization measure problem since our test error is directly the recovery error in the function space, not the accuracy.

We hypothesize that the interplay between large initialization and small non-zero weight decay that leads to grokking as predicted (provably) by Lyu et al. (2023) does not hold in our setting because our model violates they Assumption 3.2. Let y𝐚​(𝐱)=𝐚⊤​𝐱y_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{x} denote our model.

  • •

    Assumption 3.1 (Lyu et al., 2023): For all 𝐱∈ℝn\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the function 𝐚→y𝐚​(𝐗)\mathbf{a}\to y_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{X}) is 11-homogeneous since yc​𝐚​(𝐱)=c1​y𝐚​(𝐱)y_{c\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x})=c^{1}y_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x}) for all c>0c>0.

  • •

    Assumption 3.2 (Lyu et al., 2023): for ζ=0\zeta=0, y𝐚(1)​(𝐱)=0y_{\mathbf{a}^{(1)}}(\mathbf{x})=0 for all 𝐱\mathbf{x} (there is generalization in this case with ℓ1\ell_{1}), but if ζ>0\zeta>0 (for instance ζ\zeta large), this is (almost surely) no longer true. So, this assumption is violated (with high probability).

  • •

    Assumption 3.8 (Lyu et al., 2023): The NTK (Neural Tangent Kernel) features of training samples {∇𝐚y𝐚​(𝐗i)}i∈[N]\{\nabla_{\mathbf{a}}y_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{X}_{i})\}_{i\in[N]} are linearly independent (almost surely) at initialisation 𝐚=𝐚(1)\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{a}^{(1)}. In fact, ∇𝐚y𝐚​(𝐱)=𝐱​∀𝐱\nabla_{\mathbf{a}}y_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}\ \forall\mathbf{x}. In the over-parametrized regime N<nN<n, If 𝐌∈ℝN×n\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n} has entries iid from a normal distribution, then the NTK features {𝐗i}i∈[N]\{\mathbf{X}_{i}\}_{i\in[N]} are linearly independent with high probability (because the rank of 𝐗\mathbf{X} is NN with high probability), so this assumption is verified.

Appendix F Implicit Bias of the Depth

F.1 Deep Sparse Recovery

For sparse recovery, let now use the parameterization 𝐚=⊙k=1L𝐀k∈ℝn\mathbf{a}=\odot_{k=1}^{L}\mathbf{A}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, with 𝐀∈ℝL×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times n}. This corresponds to a linear network with LL layers, where each hidden layer has the parameter diag⁡(𝐀k)∈ℝn×n\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{A}_{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}—with this, increasing LL leads to overparameterization without altering the expressiveness of the function class 𝐚→ℱ𝐚​(𝐱)=𝐱⊤​𝐚\mathbf{a}\to\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\mathbf{a}, since the model remains linear with respect to the input 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Unlike the shallow case (L=1L=1), there is no need for ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization to generalize when L≥2L\geq 2 (and the initialization scale is small), as the experiments of this section suggest. With depth, the update for the whole iteration (which is now replaced by a product of matrices and a vector) is similar to the shallow case, but with a preconditioner in front of the gradient. This preconditioner makes it possible to recover the sparse signal without any regularization.

The update rule for each 𝐀i\mathbf{A}_{i} is

The depth adds the preconditioning 𝐏(t)=(1−α​β)​diag⁡(𝐜(t))\mathbf{P}^{(t)}=(1-\alpha\beta)\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{c}^{(t)}) in front of the update for 𝐚\mathbf{a}. This preconditioning mechanism seems to implicitly favor sparsity and, thus, a perfect recovery after memorization. In fact, when 𝐜i(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}_{i} goes to zero (which is the case when 𝐚i(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)}_{i} is also small), the update becomes 𝐚i(t+1)≈(1−2​α​β)​𝐚i(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t+1)}_{i}\approx(1-2\alpha\beta)\mathbf{a}^{(t)}_{i}, and thus push 𝐚i(t+1)\mathbf{a}^{(t+1)}_{i} to 0 at a geometric rate of 𝒪​(1−2​α​β)\mathcal{O}(1-2\alpha\beta). Otherwise, 𝐜i(t)\mathbf{c}^{(t)}_{i} (large) will amplify the gradient so that 𝐜i(t)​G​(𝐚(t))i\mathbf{c}^{(t)}_{i}G(\mathbf{a}^{(t)})_{i} dominates the update, which pushes 𝐚(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)} towards 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} (as the gradient G​(𝐚(t))G(\mathbf{a}^{(t)}) points towards a small error 𝐚(t)−𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{(t)}-\mathbf{a}^{*} direction, particularly for full rank 𝐗\mathbf{X} and high signal to ratio regime).

With the deep parametrization above, we solve the sparse recovery problem using the subgradient descent method with (n,s,α,β)=(102,5,10−1,0)(n,s,\alpha,\beta)=(10^{2},5,10^{-1},0), for different values of NN and L∈{1,2,3,4}L\in\{1,2,3,4\} (Figure 17 and 18). We use a small initialization scale ζ=10−6\zeta=10^{-6} for L=1L=1 and ζ=10−2\zeta=10^{-2} for L>1L>1. Here, initializing 𝐀\mathbf{A} too close to the origin (initialization scale ζ→0\zeta\rightarrow 0) leads 𝐚\mathbf{a} to not change during training. The model is able to recover the true signal 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}, and the generalization delay becomes extremely small (compared to the shallow case with non-zero ℓ1\ell_{1} coefficient) for L=2L=2 and disappears (ungrokking) for L>2L>2. As LL becomes larger, the phase transition to generalization becomes extremely abrupt. The loss decreases in a staircase fashion, with more or less long plateaus of suboptimal generalization error during training. This type of behavior is generally observed in the optimization of Soft Committee Machines (Biehl & Schwarze, 1995; Saad & Solla, 1995b, a, 1996; Engel & Broeck, 2001; Aubin et al., 2018; Goldt et al., 2020), which are two-layer linear or non-linear teacher-student systems, with the output layer of the student fixed to that of the teacher during training.

Additionally, for a fixed number NN of measures, the test error decreases with LL, indicating that depth aids in finding the signal with a smaller number of measures, albeit at the expense of a longer training time. So, the depth seems to have the same effect on generalization as ℓ1\ell_{1}. This is in accord with the result of Arora et al. (2018) in the context of matrix factorization. They show that introducing depth effectively turns gradient descent into a shallow (single-layer) training process equipped with a built-in preconditioning mechanism. This mechanism biases updates toward directions already explored by the optimization, serving as an acceleration technique that fuses momentum with adaptive step sizes. Furthermore, they demonstrate that depth-based overparameterization can substantially speed up training, even in straightforward convex tasks like linear regression with ℓp\ell_{p} loss, p>2p>2.

Note that for L≥2L\geq 2, using a large-scale initialization and a small but non-zero ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization β\beta results in grokking, unlike the case of L=1L=1 that gives the “grokking without understanding” phenomenon. In this regime, when LL increases, the number of steps required for the model to move from memorization to generalization is reduced (grokking acceleration), and the generalization error at the end of training is considerably lower. Lyu et al. (2023) used a similar setup to show that an interplay between large initialization and small nonzero weights decay gives rise to grokking with the diagonal linear network y​(𝐱)=(𝐮⊙L−𝐯⊙L)⊤​𝐱y(\mathbf{x})=\left(\mathbf{u}^{\odot L}-\mathbf{v}^{\odot L}\right)^{\top}\mathbf{x} in the context of binary classification, but there did not study the impact of LL on the generalization delay, and instead focus on characterizing how sharp is the transition from memorization to generalization as a function of the initialization scale and the weight decay coefficient, and how long it takes for this transition to occurs. This diagonal linear network is also often used for sparse recovery problems (Vaškevičius et al., 2019), but the focus is generally on its ability to recover the optimal solution, not grokking.

F.2 Deep Matrix Factorization

For matrix factorization, let use the parameterization 𝐀=∏k=1L𝒜k\mathbf{A}=\prod_{k=1}^{L}\mathcal{A}_{k}, with 𝒜1∈ℝn1×d\mathcal{A}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times d}, 𝒜L∈ℝd×n2\mathcal{A}_{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n_{2}}, and 𝒜i∈ℝd×d\mathcal{A}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} for all i∈(1,L)i\in(1,L). This corresponds to a linear network with LL layers, where each hidden layer has the parameter 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k}—with this, increasing LL leads to overparameterization without altering the expressiveness of the function class 𝐀→ℱ𝐀​(𝐱)=𝐱⊤​vec⁡𝐀\mathbf{A}\to\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{A}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\operatorname{vec}\mathbf{A}, since the model remains linear with respect to the input 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Like in compressed sensing, there is no need for ℓ∗\ell_{*} (or any other form of regularization) to generalize when L≥2L\geq 2 (and the initialization scale is small), unlike the shallow case (L=1L=1). This is an observation already made and proven in previous art (Gunasekar et al., 2017; Arora et al., 2019; Gidel et al., 2019; Gissin et al., 2019; Razin & Cohen, 2020; Li et al., 2020). Gunasekar et al. (2017); Arora et al. (2019) show that increasing LL implicitly biases 𝐀\mathbf{A} toward a low-rank solution, which oftentimes leads to more accurate recovery for sufficiently large NN. In fact, with depth, the update for the whole iterate is similar to the shallow case but with a preconditioner in front of the gradient (like in section F.1). This preconditioner makes it possible to recover the low-rank matrix without any regularization and with fewer samples than in the shallow case (Arora et al., 2018, 2019). It is also shown specifically for this problem that initializing the model very far from the origin and using a small (but non-zero) weight decay leads to grokking (Lyu et al., 2023), i.e., the model first memorizes the observed entries, then after a long training period, converges to the sought matrices provided the number of such observe entries is large enough.

We say that ℱ\mathcal{F} satisfies rr-RIP if ℱ\mathcal{F} satisfies (r,δr)(r,\delta_{r})-RIP with some δr∈(0,1)\delta_{r}\in(0,1), and the rr-RIC of ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined as the infimum δr​(ℱ)\delta_{r}(\mathcal{F}) of all possible δr\delta_{r} such that ℱ\mathcal{F} satisfy the (r,δr)(r,\delta_{r})-RIP.

Definition G.2 (Coherence).

The coherence between two matrices 𝐀∈ℝq×m\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times m} and 𝐁∈ℝq×n\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times n} is μ​(𝐀,𝐁)=maxi∈[m],j∈[n]⁡|⟨𝐀:,i,𝐁:,j⟩|‖𝐀:,i‖​‖𝐁:,j‖=maxi∈[m],j∈[n]⁡|[𝐀⊤​𝐁]i,j|‖𝐀:,i‖​‖𝐁:,j‖\mu(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})=\max_{i\in[m],j\in[n]}\frac{|\langle\mathbf{A}_{:,i},\mathbf{B}_{:,j}\rangle|}{\|\mathbf{A}_{:,i}\|\|\mathbf{B}_{:,j}\|}=\max_{i\in[m],j\in[n]}\frac{|[\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{B}]_{i,j}|}{\|\mathbf{A}_{:,i}\|\|\mathbf{B}_{:,j}\|}. Coherence measures how similar or aligned two matrices or vectors are. Specifically, it measures how much overlap there is between the columns of 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B}. High coherence means they are similar or aligned, and low coherence (or incoherence) means they are very different. Incoherence is essentially the opposite of coherence. It refers to a low overlap or low similarity between the columns of 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B}.

The mutual coherence of a matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is μ​(𝐀)=max(i,j)∈[m]×[n],i≠j⁡|⟨𝐀:,i,𝐀:,j⟩|‖𝐀:,i‖​‖𝐀:,j‖=max(i,j)∈[m]×[n],i≠j⁡[𝐀⊤​𝐀]i,j‖𝐀:,i‖​‖𝐀:,j‖\mu(\mathbf{A})=\max_{(i,j)\in[m]\times[n],i\neq j}\frac{|\langle\mathbf{A}_{:,i},\mathbf{A}_{:,j}\rangle|}{\|\mathbf{A}_{:,i}\|\|\mathbf{A}_{:,j}\|}=\max_{(i,j)\in[m]\times[n],i\neq j}\frac{[\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{A}]_{i,j}}{\|\mathbf{A}_{:,i}\|\|\mathbf{A}_{:,j}\|}. If the coherence is small, then the columns of 𝐀\mathbf{A} are almost mutually orthogonal. A small coherence is desired in order to have good sparse recovery properties. We also have the 1-coherence μ1​(𝐀,s)=maxi∈[n]⁡maxJ⊆[n]\i,|J|≤s​∑j∈J|⟨𝐀:,i,𝐀:,j⟩|‖𝐀:,i‖​‖𝐀:,j‖≤s​μ​(𝐀)\mu_{1}(\mathbf{A},s)=\max_{i\in[n]}\max_{J\subseteq[n]\backslash i,|J|\leq s}\sum_{j\in J}\frac{|\langle\mathbf{A}_{:,i},\mathbf{A}_{:,j}\rangle|}{\|\mathbf{A}_{:,i}\|\|\mathbf{A}_{:,j}\|}\leq s\mu(\mathbf{A}).

For a matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with unit norm columns, μ​(𝐀)≥n−mm​(n−1)\mu(\mathbf{A})\geq\sqrt{\frac{n-m}{m(n-1)}} and μ1​(𝐀,s)≥s​n−mm​(n−1)\mu_{1}(\mathbf{A},s)\geq s\sqrt{\frac{n-m}{m(n-1)}} whenever s≤n−1s\leq\sqrt{n-1} (Rauhut, 2010). In high dimensional space (large nn), μ​(𝐀)≥n−mm​(n−1)\mu(\mathbf{A})\geq\sqrt{\frac{n-m}{m(n-1)}} becomes μ​(𝐀)≳1m\mu(\mathbf{A})\gtrsim\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}} : this lower bound is achieve when 𝐀\mathbf{A} is an equiangular tight frame.

Proposition G.3 (Relation between μ\mu and δ\delta).

For a matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with unit norm columns, μ​(𝐀)=δ2​(𝐀)\mu(\mathbf{A})=\delta_{2}(\mathbf{A}), μ1​(𝐀,s)=maxJ∈[n],|J|≤s+1⁡‖𝐀:,J⊤​𝐀:,J−𝕀‖1→1\mu_{1}(\mathbf{A},s)=\max_{J\in[n],|J|\leq s+1}\|\mathbf{A}_{:,J}^{\top}\mathbf{A}_{:,J}-\mathbb{I}\|_{1\rightarrow 1}, and δs​(𝐀)≤μ1​(𝐀,s−1)≤(s−1)​μ​(𝐀)\delta_{s}(\mathbf{A})\leq\mu_{1}(\mathbf{A},s-1)\leq(s-1)\mu(\mathbf{A}) (Rauhut, 2010).

G.1.1 The Problem

Given the sparse basis (or dictionary) Φ∈ℝn×n\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, the measurement matrix 𝐌∈ℝN×n\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n}, and the measures 𝐲∗=ℱ𝐛∗​(𝐌)+𝝃=𝐌𝐛∗+𝝃∈ℝN\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{b}^{*}}(\mathbf{M})+\boldsymbol{\xi}=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{b}^{*}+\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}; we aim to solve (P0)​ Minimize ​‖𝐚‖0​ s.t. ​‖ℱ𝐚​(𝐌​Φ)−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ(P_{0})\text{ Minimize }\|\mathbf{a}\|_{0}\text{ s.t. }\|\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{M}\Phi)-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon, and more precisely, its convex relaxation (P1)​ Minimize ​‖𝐚‖1​ s.t. ​‖ℱ𝐚​(𝐌​Φ)−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ(P_{1})\text{ Minimize }\|\mathbf{a}\|_{1}\text{ s.t. }\|\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{M}\Phi)-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon. This problem has been well studied in the signal processing literature under the name Basis Pursuit. It is well known that under certain conditions on the measurement matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M} (e.g., coherence with respect to Φ\Phi) and the sparsity of 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*} in Φ\Phi, sufficiently sparse solutions of (P1)(P_{1}) are also solutions of (P0)(P_{0}) (Donoho & Elad, 2003; Candes et al., 2006). Many lower bounds on the number of measures NN guaranteeing ‖𝐚−𝐚∗‖2≤ϵ\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon with high probability have also been derived. Such lower bounds generally have the form N=Ω​(δ−C1​(s​logC2⁡(n/s)+log⁡1/η))N=\Omega\left(\delta^{-C_{1}}\left(s\log^{C_{2}}\left(n/s\right)+\log 1/\eta\right)\right) (Rauhut, 2010), where δ\delta capture the Restricted Isometry Property (Definition G.1) of 𝐗=𝐌​Φ\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{M}\Phi (δ2​s​(𝐗)≤δ\delta_{2s}(\mathbf{X})\leq\delta) and is also related to the coherence (Definition G.2) of 𝐌\mathbf{M} with respect to Φ\Phi (Proposition G.3), η\eta is the percentage of error (i.e. NN guaranteed a recovery with probability at least 1−η1-\eta), 𝐂1>0\mathbf{C}_{1}>0 and C2>0C_{2}>0 are constants. Observe that in the noiseless setting, we want 𝐚\mathbf{a} such that 𝐗𝐚=𝐗𝐚∗\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}^{*}, that is 𝐚∈𝐚∗+Null​(𝐗)\mathbf{a}\in\mathbf{a}^{*}+\text{Null}(\mathbf{X}). Donoho (2006b, a) show that the nullspace {𝐚,𝐗𝐚=0}\left\{\mathbf{a},\mathbf{X}\mathbf{a}=0\right\} has a very special structure for certain 𝐗\mathbf{X} (e.g. incoherent with any orthonormal basis): when 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} is sparse, the only element in the affine subspace 𝐚∗+Null​(𝐗)\mathbf{a}^{*}+\text{Null}(\mathbf{X}) that can have a small ℓ1\ell_{1} norm is 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} itself.

We will assume for simplicity that Φ\Phi is an orthonormal matrix, Φ⊤​Φ=𝕀n\Phi^{\top}\Phi=\mathbb{I}_{n}. It is common in sparse coding theory to consider Φ∈ℝn×m\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} as a dictionary with mm columns referred to as atoms (square, n=mn=m; undercomplete, n>mn>m; or overcomplete, n<mn<m); and saying 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*} is sparse means it can be written as a linear combination of a few of such atoms. But here, we assume for simplicity that we have 𝐛∗=Φ​𝐚∗\mathbf{b}^{*}=\Phi\mathbf{a}^{*} with 𝐚∗∈ℝm\mathbf{a}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and Φ∈ℝn×m\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} a set of m≤nm\leq n linearly independent vectors (its column). Let Φ⟂∈ℝn×(n−m)\Phi^{\perp}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)} be the orthogonal complement of Φ\Phi in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, Ψ:=[ΦΦ⟂]∈ℝn×n\Psi:=\left[\Phi\quad\Phi^{\perp}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, Φ~:=Ψ​(Ψ⊤​Ψ)−1/2∈ℝn×n\tilde{\Phi}:=\Psi\left(\Psi^{\top}\Psi\right)^{-1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} the orthonormal version of Ψ\Psi, and 𝐚~∗:=(Ψ⊤​Ψ)1/2​[𝐚∗0]\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{*}:=\left(\Psi^{\top}\Psi\right)^{1/2}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{a}^{*}\\ 0\end{bmatrix}. We still have 𝐛∗=Φ~​𝐚~∗\mathbf{b}^{*}=\tilde{\Phi}\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{*}, with ‖𝐚~∗‖0=‖𝐚∗‖0\|\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{*}\|_{0}=\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{0} since Ψ⊤​Ψ\Psi^{\top}\Psi is diagonal. So, assuming Φ\Phi orthonormal is without loss of generality.

Example G.1.

For the Fourier basis n​Φj​i=𝐞−2​π​i​j​in\sqrt{n}\Phi_{ji}=\mathbf{e}^{-2\pi\textbf{i}\frac{ji}{n}}, we have μ1​(Φ,s)=s​μ​(Φ)=s/n\mu_{1}(\Phi,s)=s\mu(\Phi)=s/\sqrt{n} (Rauhut, 2010). Each column in this basis vector corresponds to a specific frequency. For a signal 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*}, if only a few frequency components contribute significantly to 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*}, then 𝐚∗=Φ−1​𝐛∗\mathbf{a}^{*}=\Phi^{-1}\mathbf{b}^{*}, the Fourier transform of 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*}, will be sparse.

G.1.2 The controls parameters

The incoherence between the measurement vectors (line of 𝐌\mathbf{M}) and the sparse basis (column of Φ\Phi) is crucial for successfully recovering 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*} (or equivalently 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}, the sparse representation). If 𝐌\mathbf{M} is incoherent with Φ\Phi, each measurement captures a distinct “view” of 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*}, reducing redundancy. This diversity of information allows for the successful reconstruction of 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} even with fewer measurements (e.g., below the Nyquist rate for signals). Achieving low coherence (high incoherence) can be done by designing 𝐌\mathbf{M} to be a random matrix (e.g., Sub-Gaussian like Gaussian or Bernoulli matrices). Such random matrices are, with high probability, incoherent with any fixed orthonormal basis, as Theorems G.4 and G.5 show.

Theorem G.4.

Le m≤nm\leq n and Φ∈ℝn×m\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} with Φ⊤​Φ=𝕀m\Phi^{\top}\Phi=\mathbb{I}_{m}. For any N≥1N\geq 1, C1>0C_{1}>0 and C2≥1C_{2}\geq 1; the matrix 𝐌∈ℝN×n\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n} with nC1​𝐌​∼i​i​d​𝒩​(0,1)n^{C_{1}}\mathbf{M}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal{N}\left(0,1\right) satisfies μ​(𝐌⊤,Φ)≤2​C2​ln⁡(n​N)nC1\mu(\mathbf{M}^{\top},\Phi)\leq 2C_{2}\frac{\sqrt{\ln(nN)}}{n^{C_{1}}} with probability at least 1−1/(n​N)2​C22−11-1/(nN)^{2C_{2}^{2}-1}.

Proof.

Let σ=n−C1\sigma=n^{-C_{1}}, C1>0C_{1}>0. We have 𝐌​∼i​i​d​𝒩​(0,σ2)\mathbf{M}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), so [𝐌​Φ]i​j​∼i​i​d​𝒩​(0,σ2)\left[\mathbf{M}\Phi\right]_{ij}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) since Φ\Phi has normal columns. This implies ℙ​[|[𝐌​Φ]i​j|≥t]≤exp⁡(−t22​σ2)\mathbb{P}\left[\left|\left[\mathbf{M}\Phi\right]_{ij}\right|\geq t\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right), which in turn implies ℙ​[maxi,j⁡|[𝐌​Φ]i​j|≥t]≤∑i,jℙ​[|[𝐌​Φ]i​j|≥t]≤n​N​exp⁡(−t22​σ2)\mathbb{P}\left[\max_{i,j}\left|\left[\mathbf{M}\Phi\right]_{ij}\right|\geq t\right]\leq\sum_{i,j}\mathbb{P}\left[\left|\left[\mathbf{M}\Phi\right]_{ij}\right|\geq t\right]\leq nN\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right). Using t=2​C2​ln⁡(n​N)nC1t=2C_{2}\frac{\sqrt{\ln(nN)}}{n^{C_{1}}} with C2≥1C_{2}\geq 1, we have t2=2​(1nC1)2​ln⁡(n​Nη)t^{2}=2\left(\frac{1}{n^{C_{1}}}\right)^{2}\ln\left(\frac{nN}{\eta}\right) with η=(n​N)1−2​C22\eta=(nN)^{1-2C_{2}^{2}}, so n​N​exp⁡(−t22​σ2)=ηnN\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)=\eta. ∎

We also have the following theorem from Rauhut (2010) about the RIP of such a matrix.

Theorem G.5.

Let 𝐌∈ℝN×n\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n} be a Gaussian or Bernoulli random matrix. Let η,δ∈(0,1)\eta,\delta\in(0,1) and assume N≥C​δ−2​(s​ln⁡(n/s)+ln⁡(1/η))N\geq C\delta^{-2}\left(s\ln\left(n/s\right)+\ln\left(1/\eta\right)\right) for a universal constant C>0C>0. Then, δs​(𝐌)≤δ\delta_{s}(\mathbf{M})\leq\delta with probability at least 1−η1-\eta .

G.1.3 Impact of Coherence on Grokking

Convex Optimization

We fix n=102n=10^{2} and solve for different (N,s,τ)(N,s,\tau) the problem (P1)(P_{1}) using the cvxpy library. As ss and/or τ\tau increases, Nmin​(s,τ)N_{\text{min}}(s,\tau), the number of samples needs for perfect recovery increases (Figures 19 and 20). When τ\tau converges to 11, Nmin​(s,τ)→nN_{\text{min}}(s,\tau)\rightarrow n for all ss. The error in those figures is the relative recovery error ‖𝐚−𝐚∗‖2/‖𝐚∗‖2\|\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}/\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}. This error is usually of the order of 10−610^{-6}, giving us a basis for comparison with other methods.

Gradient Descent

Here, we also observe that the generalization time and the generalization delay increase with τ\tau while the generalization error decreases with it (Figures 21 and 22). For N<nN<n, when τ→1\tau\rightarrow 1, the generalization time t2→∞t_{2}\rightarrow\infty. This is because each measurement captures a single view (component) of 𝐛∗=Φ​𝐚∗\mathbf{b}^{*}=\Phi\mathbf{a}^{*}, and this makes it impossible to find the optimal 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} by solving the equation 𝐌​Φ​𝐚=𝐲∗\mathbf{M}\Phi\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{y}^{*} for N<nN<n (by any method whatsoever). On the other hand, as τ→0\tau\rightarrow 0, 𝐌\mathbf{M} becomes completely random, and every measurement captures a distinct “view” of 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*}, giving the best possible generalization time for the data size considered. The error ‖𝐚(t2)−𝐚∗‖2/‖𝐚∗‖2\|\mathbf{a}^{(t_{2})}-\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2}/\|\mathbf{a}^{*}\|_{2} at generalization (t2t_{2}) as a function of NN and τ\tau has the same shape as in the convex programming. We use (n,s,α,β,ζ)=(102,5,10−1,10−5,10−6)(n,s,\alpha,\beta,\zeta)=(10^{2},5,10^{-1},10^{-5},10^{-6}) in the experiments.

G.2 Matrix Factorization

G.2.1 The Problem

Given a low rank rr matrix 𝐀∗∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}, a measurement matrix 𝐗∈ℝN×n1​n2\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n_{1}n_{2}}; we aim to solve the following problem for 𝐀∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}; (P3)​ Minimize ​rank(𝐀)⁡ subject to ​‖ℱvec⁡(𝐀)​(𝐗)−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ(P_{3})\text{ Minimize }\operatorname*{rank}(\mathbf{A})\text{ subject to }\|\mathcal{F}_{\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A})}\left(\mathbf{X}\right)-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon; and more precisely, its convex relaxation (P4)​ Minimize ​‖𝐀‖∗=∑iσi​(𝐀)​ subject to ​‖ℱvec⁡(𝐀)​(𝐗)−𝐲∗‖2≤ϵ(P_{4})\text{ Minimize }\|\mathbf{A}\|_{*}=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}(\mathbf{A})\text{ subject to }\|\mathcal{F}_{\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A})}\left(\mathbf{X}\right)-\mathbf{y}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon; where 𝐲∗=ℱvec⁡(𝐀∗)​(𝐗)+𝝃\mathbf{y}^{*}=\mathcal{F}_{\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})}\left(\mathbf{X}\right)+\boldsymbol{\xi} are the measures and ϵ\epsilon an upper bound on the size of the error term 𝝃∈ℝN\boldsymbol{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, ‖𝝃‖2≤ϵ\|\boldsymbol{\xi}\|_{2}\leq\epsilon.

Matrix Sensing

Matrix sensing seeks to recover a low rank matrix 𝐀∗∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} from NN measurement matrices {𝐗i∈ℝn1×n2}i∈[N]\{\mathbf{X}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}\}_{i\in[N]} and measures 𝐲∗=(tr⁡(𝐗i⊤​𝐀∗))i∈[N]\mathbf{y}^{*}=\left(\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{X}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{*})\right)_{i\in[N]}. We have 𝐲i∗=tr(𝐗i⊤𝐀∗)=vec(𝐗i)⊤vec(𝐀∗)=ℱvec⁡(𝐀∗)(vec(𝐗i))\mathbf{y}^{*}_{i}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{X}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{A}^{*})=\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X}_{i})^{\top}\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})=\mathcal{F}_{\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})}(\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X}_{i})). This gives us a compressed sensing problem, with the signal vector vec⁡(𝐀∗)∈ℝn1​n2\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}n_{2}} and the measurement matrix 𝐗=[vec⁡(𝐗i)]i∈[N]∈ℝN×n1​n2\mathbf{X}=[\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X}_{i})]_{i\in[N]}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n_{1}n_{2}}. In fact, under full SVD 𝐀∗=𝐔∗​Σ∗​𝐕∗⊤\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{U}^{*}\Sigma^{*}\mathbf{V}^{*\top}, we have 𝐚∗=vec⁡(𝐀∗)=Φ​vec⁡(Σ∗)\mathbf{a}^{*}=\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})=\Phi\operatorname{vec}(\Sigma^{*}); where vec⁡(Σ∗)∈ℝn1​n2\operatorname{vec}(\Sigma^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}n_{2}}, is sparse since ‖vec⁡(Σ∗)‖0=rank(𝐀∗)≤min⁡(n1,n2)≪n1​n2\|\operatorname{vec}(\Sigma^{*})\|_{0}=\operatorname*{rank}(\mathbf{A}^{*})\leq\min(n_{1},n_{2})\ll n_{1}n_{2}; and Φ=𝐕∗⊗𝐔∗∈ℝn1​n2×n1​n2\Phi=\mathbf{V}^{*}\otimes\mathbf{U}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}n_{2}\times n_{1}n_{2}} has orthonormal column since Φ⊤​Φ=(𝐕∗⊤​𝐕∗)⊗(𝐔∗⊤​𝐔∗)=𝕀n1​n2\Phi^{\top}\Phi=\left(\mathbf{V}^{*\top}\mathbf{V}^{*}\right)\otimes\left(\mathbf{U}^{*\top}\mathbf{U}^{*}\right)=\mathbb{I}_{n_{1}n_{2}}.

Matrix Completion

For a matrix completion problem with matrix 𝐀∗∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}, we have NN measurement vectors (𝐗i(1),𝐗i(2))∈ℝn1×ℝn2\left(\mathbf{X}^{(1)}_{i},\mathbf{X}^{(2)}_{i}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}\times\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}} and measures 𝐲i∗=𝐗i(1)⊤​𝐀∗​𝐗i(2)=(𝐗i(2)⊗𝐗i(1))⊤​vec⁡(𝐀∗)=ℱvec⁡(𝐀∗)​(𝐗i(2)⊗𝐗i(1))\mathbf{y}_{i}^{*}=\mathbf{X}^{(1)\top}_{i}\mathbf{A}^{*}\mathbf{X}^{(2)}_{i}=\left(\mathbf{X}^{(2)}_{i}\otimes\mathbf{X}^{(1)}_{i}\right)^{\top}\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})=\mathcal{F}_{\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(2)}_{i}\otimes\mathbf{X}^{(1)}_{i}\right), i.e. 𝐲∗=(𝐗(2)∙𝐗(1))​vec⁡(𝐀∗)=ℱvec⁡(𝐀∗)​(𝐗(2)∙𝐗(1))\mathbf{y}^{*}=\left(\mathbf{X}^{(2)}\bullet\mathbf{X}^{(1)}\right)\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})=\mathcal{F}_{\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})}\left(\mathbf{X}^{(2)}\bullet\mathbf{X}^{(1)}\right). This gives us a compressed sensing problem, with the signal vector vec⁡(𝐀∗)∈ℝn1​n2\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}n_{2}} and the measurement matrix 𝐗=𝐗(2)∙𝐗(1)∈ℝN×n1​n2\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}^{(2)}\bullet\mathbf{X}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n_{1}n_{2}}. Standard matrix completion is usually defined as recovering missing elements of a matrix from its incomplete observation. This is equivalent to requiring 𝐗i(k)\mathbf{X}^{(k)}_{i} to be selection vectors for all k∈[K]k\in[K] (with K=2K=2), i.e. 𝐗i(k)\mathbf{X}^{(k)}_{i} is the s​(i,k)ths(i,k)^{\text{th}} vector of the canonical basis of ℝnk\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}} for a certain s​(i,k)∈[nk]s(i,k)\in[n_{k}]. This make each 𝐗i=𝐗i(2)⊗𝐗i(1)\mathbf{X}_{i}=\mathbf{X}_{i}^{(2)}\otimes\mathbf{X}_{i}^{(1)} a selection vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and 𝐗=𝐗(2)∙𝐗(1)\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}^{(2)}\bullet\mathbf{X}^{(1)} a selection matrix in ℝN×n\mathbb{R}^{N\times n}, so that 𝐲i∗=𝐀s​(i,1),s​(i,2)∗​∀i∈[N]\mathbf{y}^{*}_{i}=\mathbf{A}^{*}_{s(i,1),s(i,2)}\forall i\in[N]. So, in this formulation, each 𝐗i(k)\mathbf{X}^{(k)}_{i} is a sample from the columns of 𝕀nk\mathbb{I}_{n_{k}}. Note that under a change of basis 𝐗~i(k)=𝐏(k)​𝐗i(k)\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{i}^{(k)}=\mathbf{P}^{(k)}\mathbf{X}_{i}^{(k)}, we have 𝐲~i∗=(⊗k=1K𝐏(k))𝐲i∗\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{*}=\left(\otimes_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{P}^{(k)}\right)\mathbf{y}^{*}_{i}, that is 𝐲~∗=𝐲∗(⊗k=1K𝐏(k))⊤\tilde{\mathbf{y}}^{*}=\mathbf{y}^{*}\left(\otimes_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{P}^{(k)}\right)^{\top}. A less standard formulation of the matrix completion task requires each 𝐗i(k)\mathbf{X}^{(k)}_{i} to be a sample from an orthonormal basis, i.e., 𝐗i(k)\mathbf{X}^{(k)}_{i} is a sample from the columns of 𝐕(k)∈ℝnk×nk\mathbf{V}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times n_{k}} with 𝐕(k)⊤​𝐕(k)=𝕀nk\mathbf{V}^{(k)\top}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}=\mathbb{I}_{n_{k}}. We let 𝐗i(k)\mathbf{X}^{(k)}_{i} be the s​(i,k)ths(i,k)^{\text{th}} column of 𝐕(k)\mathbf{V}^{(k)} for a certain s​(i,k)∈[nk]s(i,k)\in[n_{k}]. Then 𝐲i∗=𝐀∗~s​(i,1),⋯,s​(i,K)\mathbf{y}^{*}_{i}=\tilde{\mathbf{A}^{*}}_{s(i,1),\cdots,s(i,K)} with 𝐀~∗=𝐀∗×1𝐕(1)×2𝐕(2)\tilde{\mathbf{A}}^{*}=\mathbf{A}^{*}\times_{1}\mathbf{V}^{(1)}\times_{2}\mathbf{V}^{(2)}. So, any result state of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} in the standard formulation where the measurement vectors are selection vectors is valid for the matrix 𝐀~∗\tilde{\mathbf{A}}^{*}.

Assume the target matrix 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} has rank rr. Then it has r​(n1+n2−r)r(n_{1}+n_{2}-r) degree of freedom101010 The first rr columns of 𝐔∗\mathbf{U}^{*} form an orthonormal basis for a rr-dimensional subspace of ℝn1\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}} (the columns space of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*}). Specifying this requires r​(n1−r)r(n_{1}-r) parameters. Similarly, the first rr columns of 𝐕∗\mathbf{V}^{*} form an orthonormal basis for a rr-dimensional subspace of ℝn2\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}} (the rows space of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*}), and specifying this requires r​(n2−r)r(n_{2}-r) parameters. The rr non-zero singular values are independent parameters. Thus, specifying them requires rr parameters. , and we need to observe at least r​(n1+n2−r)r(n_{1}+n_{2}-r) entries for perfect recovery. This bound can be improved by considering the structure of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*}. Let 𝐀∗=𝐔∗​Σ∗​𝐕∗⊤\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{U}^{*}\Sigma^{*}\mathbf{V}^{*\top} be the full SVD of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*}. As observed above, we are dealing with a compressed sensing problem with the signal vector 𝐚∗=vec⁡(𝐀∗)=Φ​vec⁡(Σ∗)\mathbf{a}^{*}=\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{A}^{*})=\Phi\operatorname{vec}(\Sigma^{*}); where vec⁡(Σ∗)∈ℝn1​n2\operatorname{vec}(\Sigma^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}n_{2}} is sparse and Φ=𝐕∗⊗𝐔∗∈ℝn1​n2×n1​n2\Phi=\mathbf{V}^{*}\otimes\mathbf{U}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}n_{2}\times n_{1}n_{2}} has orthonormal column.

G.2.2 The control parameters

In this sub-section, we assume standard matrix completion. But the theories outlined here also apply to the general framework. The theory gives the minimal number of observations that guarantee 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} to be a unique solution to problem (P4)(P_{4}) and allow perfect recovery of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with fewer samples  (Candès & Tao, 2010; Candes & Recht, 2012; Chen et al., 2014). Generally, the lower bound on NN has a form N≥Cmax(n1,n2)C2(rC3logC1(max(n1,n2))+log1η)N\geq C\max(n_{1},n_{2})^{C_{2}}\left(r^{C_{3}}\log^{C_{1}}\left(\max(n_{1},n_{2})\right)+\log\frac{1}{\eta}\right) where η\eta is the percentage of error (i.e NN guaranteed perfect recovery with probability at least 1−η1-\eta), C1>0C_{1}>0, C2>0C_{2}>0, C3>0C_{3}>0 are constant, and C>0C>0 a universal constant. For example, in Candes & Recht (2012), (C1,C2,C3)=(1,1.2,1)(C_{1},C_{2},C_{3})=(1,1.2,1) for small rank r≤max(n1,n2)0.2r\leq\max(n_{1},n_{2})^{0.2}, and C2=1.25C_{2}=1.25 for any rank. The term max⁡(n1,n2)​log⁡(max⁡(n1,n2))\max(n_{1},n_{2})\log\left(\max(n_{1},n_{2})\right) is due to the coupon collector effect since to recover an unknown matrix, one needs at least one observation per row and one observation per column (Candes & Recht, 2012).

Definition G.6 (Random orthogonal model (Candes & Recht, 2012)).

For a given rr, we generate two orthonormal matrices 𝐔∗∈ℝn1×r\mathbf{U}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times r} and 𝐕∗∈ℝn2×r\mathbf{V}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}\times r} with columns selected uniformly at random among all families of rr orthonormal vectors; and a diagonal matrix Σ∗\Sigma^{*} with only the first rr diagonal element non-zero (with no assumptions about the singular values111111Unless otherwise specified, we default the nonzero singular values to 1/r1/\sqrt{r}.), then set 𝐀∗=𝐔∗​Σ∗​𝐕∗⊤\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{U}^{*}\Sigma^{*}\mathbf{V}^{*\top}.

We have the following result about the standard formulation for such matrices in the absence of noise.

Theorem G.7 (Theorem 1.1, Candes & Recht (2012)).

Let 𝐀∗∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} be a matrix of rank rr sampled from the random orthogonal model, and put n=max⁡(n1,n2)n=\max(n_{1},n_{2}). Suppose we observe NN entries of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with locations sampled uniformly at random. Then there are numerical constants CC and cc such that if N≥C​n5/4​r​log⁡(n)N\geq Cn^{5/4}r\log\left(n\right), the minimizer to the problem (P4)(P_{4}) is unique and equal to 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with probability at least 1−c/n31-c/n^{3}; that is to say, the semidenite program (P4)(P_{4}) recovers all the entries of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with no error. In addition, if r≤n1/5r\leq n^{1/5}, then the recovery is exact with probability at least 1−c/n31-c/n^{3} provided that N≥C​n6/5​r​log⁡(n)N\geq Cn^{6/5}r\log\left(n\right).

Assume for example 𝐀∗=𝐞k(n1)​𝐞ℓ(n2)\mathbf{A}^{*}=\mathbf{e}_{k}^{(n_{1})}\mathbf{e}_{\ell}^{(n_{2})} for (k,ℓ)∈[n1]×[n2](k,\ell)\in[n_{1}]\times[n_{2}]. Even if this matrix ranks at 11, it has only zeros everywhere except 11 at position (k,ℓ)(k,\ell), so we have very little chance of reconstructing it in a high dimension by observing a portion of its inputs. The only way to guarantee observation of the input at position (k,ℓ)(k,\ell) is to choose measurements coherently with its singular basis 𝐞k(n2)⊗𝐞ℓ(n1)\mathbf{e}_{k}^{(n_{2})}\otimes\mathbf{e}_{\ell}^{(n_{1})}. This idea is formulated more generally below.

Definition G.8.

Let UU be a subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} of dimension rr and 𝐏U\mathbf{P}_{U} be the orthogonal projection onto UU. Then, the coherence of UU vis-a-vis a basis {𝐮i(n)}i∈[n]\{\mathbf{u}^{(n)}_{i}\}_{i\in[n]} is defined by μ​(U)=nr​maxi⁡‖𝐏U​𝐮i(n)‖2\mu(U)=\frac{n}{r}\max_{i}\|\mathbf{P}_{U}\mathbf{u}_{i}^{(n)}\|^{2}. We have 1≤μ​(U)≤n/r1\leq\mu(U)\leq n/r (Candes & Recht, 2012).

For a matrix 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} under the compact SVD, the projection on the left singular value is 𝐱→𝐔𝐔⊤​𝐱\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{x}, and ‖𝐔𝐔⊤​𝐱‖22=‖𝐔⊤​𝐱‖22\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{x}\|^{2}_{2}=\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{x}\|^{2}_{2} for all 𝐱\mathbf{x} (similarly for the right singular value). We have the following definition of coherence, which considers each matrix entry.

Definition G.9 (Local coherence & Leverage score).

Let 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} be the compact SVD of a matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} of rank rr. The local coherences of 𝐀\mathbf{A} are defined by

μi​(𝐀)=n1r​‖𝐔⊤​𝐞i(n1)‖2=n1r​‖𝐔i,:‖2∀i∈[n1]νj​(𝐀)=n2r​‖𝐕⊤​𝐞j(n2)‖2=n2r​‖𝐕j,:‖2∀j∈[n2]\begin{split}&\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A})=\frac{n_{1}}{r}\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(n_{1})}\|^{2}=\frac{n_{1}}{r}\|\mathbf{U}_{i,:}\|^{2}\quad\forall i\in[n_{1}]\\ &\nu_{j}(\mathbf{A})=\frac{n_{2}}{r}\|\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{j}^{(n_{2})}\|^{2}=\frac{n_{2}}{r}\|\mathbf{V}_{j,:}\|^{2}\quad\forall j\in[n_{2}]\end{split} (122)

with μi\mu_{i} for row ii and νj\nu_{j} for row jj. The quantities ‖𝐔⊤​𝐞i(n1)‖2\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(n_{1})}\|^{2} and ‖𝐕⊤​𝐞i(n2)‖2\|\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(n_{2})}\|^{2} are the leverage score of 𝐀\mathbf{A} (Chen et al., 2014), which indicate how “aligned” each row or column of the original data matrix is with the principal components (the columns of 𝐔\mathbf{U} or 𝐕\mathbf{V}). For each row ii, μi​(𝐀)\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A}) measures how much this row vector projects onto the subspace spanned by the first rr left singular vectors in 𝐔\mathbf{U}. Rows with high leverage scores contribute more to the low-rank structure of 𝐀\mathbf{A} and are more “influential” in representing 𝐀\mathbf{A}. Similarly, νj​(𝐀)\nu_{j}(\mathbf{A}) measures the coherence of each column jj in 𝐀\mathbf{A} with respect to the low-rank subspace formed by the right singular vectors in 𝐕\mathbf{V}. High values indicate columns well-aligned with the principal directions of 𝐀\mathbf{A} and play a significant role in capturing its structure. Matrices with uniformly low coherence scores have rows and columns that are evenly influential. In contrast, matrices with high coherence scores for certain rows or columns have a few specific rows or columns that dominate the low-rank structure.

In the general formulation, this definition can be extended to the set from which the measures are chosen. But in general, it leads back to the standard formulation under the change of basis.

Definition G.10 (Generalize local coherence & Leverage score).

We generalize the notion of coherence to any arbitrary set of vectors 𝐔(n1)={𝐮i(n1)}i∈[N1]∈ℝn1×N1\mathbf{U}^{(n_{1})}=\{\mathbf{u}^{(n_{1})}_{i}\}_{i\in[N_{1}]}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times N_{1}} and 𝐕(n2)={𝐯j(n2)}j∈[N2]∈ℝn2×N2\mathbf{V}^{(n_{2})}=\{\mathbf{v}^{(n_{2})}_{j}\}_{j\in[N_{2}]}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}\times N_{2}}, and defined the generalized local coherences as

μi​(𝐀)=n1r​‖𝐔⊤​𝐮i(n1)‖2∀i∈[N1],νj​(𝐀)=n2r​‖𝐕⊤​𝐯j(n2)‖2∀j∈[N2]\begin{split}\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A})=\frac{n_{1}}{r}\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{i}^{(n_{1})}\|^{2}\quad\forall i\in[N_{1}],\qquad\nu_{j}(\mathbf{A})=\frac{n_{2}}{r}\|\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{v}_{j}^{(n_{2})}\|^{2}\quad\forall j\in[N_{2}]\end{split} (123)

Suppose the sets 𝐔(n1)\mathbf{U}^{(n_{1})} and 𝐕(n2)\mathbf{V}^{(n_{2})} are be orthonormal basis (i.e. (N1,N2)=(n1,n2)(N_{1},N_{2})=(n_{1},n_{2}), 𝐮i(n2)⊤​𝐮k(n2)=δi​k{\mathbf{u}^{(n_{2})}_{i}}^{\top}\mathbf{u}^{(n_{2})}_{k}=\delta_{ik} and 𝐯j(n1)⊤​𝐯l(n1)=δj​l{\mathbf{v}^{(n_{1})}_{j}}^{\top}\mathbf{v}^{(n_{1})}_{l}=\delta_{jl}). We can write 𝐮i(n1)=𝐏(1)​𝐞i(n1)\mathbf{u}_{i}^{(n_{1})}=\mathbf{P}^{(1)}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(n_{1})} and 𝐯j(n2)=𝐏(2)​𝐞j(n2)\mathbf{v}_{j}^{(n_{2})}=\mathbf{P}^{(2)}\mathbf{e}_{j}^{(n_{2})} with 𝐏(k)∈ℝnk×nk\mathbf{P}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{k}\times n_{k}} the base change matrix from the canonical basis to 𝐔(n1)\mathbf{U}^{(n_{1})} and 𝐕(n2)\mathbf{V}^{(n_{2})} respectively. So

μi​(𝐀)=n1r​‖𝐔⊤​𝐏(1)​𝐞i(n1)‖2=n1r​‖𝐔~⊤​𝐞i(n1)‖2=μi​(𝐀~)∀i∈[N1]νj​(𝐀)=n2r​‖𝐕⊤​𝐏(2)​𝐞j(n2)‖2=n2r​‖𝐕~⊤​𝐞j(n2)‖2=νi​(𝐀~)∀j∈[N2]\begin{split}&\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A})=\frac{n_{1}}{r}\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{P}^{(1)}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(n_{1})}\|^{2}=\frac{n_{1}}{r}\|\tilde{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(n_{1})}\|^{2}=\mu_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{A}})\quad\forall i\in[N_{1}]\\ &\nu_{j}(\mathbf{A})=\frac{n_{2}}{r}\|\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{P}^{(2)}\mathbf{e}_{j}^{(n_{2})}\|^{2}=\frac{n_{2}}{r}\|\tilde{\mathbf{V}}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{j}^{(n_{2})}\|^{2}=\nu_{i}(\tilde{\mathbf{A}})\quad\forall j\in[N_{2}]\end{split} (124)

with 𝐀~=𝐀×1𝐏(1)×2𝐏(2)=𝐏(1)⊤​𝐀𝐏(2)=𝐏(1)⊤​𝐔​Σ​(𝐏(2)⊤​𝐕)⊤=𝐔~​Σ​𝐕~⊤\tilde{\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{A}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{(1)}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{(2)}=\mathbf{P}^{(1)\top}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}^{(2)}=\mathbf{P}^{(1)\top}\mathbf{U}\Sigma\left(\mathbf{P}^{(2)\top}\mathbf{V}\right)^{\top}=\tilde{\mathbf{U}}\Sigma\tilde{\mathbf{V}}^{\top}. That said, any result stated in the standard formulation for 𝐀\mathbf{A} is valid for 𝐀~\tilde{\mathbf{A}} under the general orthonormal formulation.

Candès & Tao (2010) and Candes & Recht (2012) used mainly an upper bound μ0\mu_{0} on μi\mu_{i} and νi\nu_{i}; μ0≥max⁡(maxi∈[n1]⁡μi​(𝐀∗),maxi∈[n2]⁡νi​(𝐀∗))\mu_{0}\geq\max\left(\max_{i\in[n_{1}]}\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A}^{*}),\max_{i\in[n_{2}]}\nu_{i}(\mathbf{A}^{*})\right), and define a constant μ1\mu_{1} such that the maxi,j[𝐔∗𝐕∗⊤]i​j=maxi,j∑k𝐔i,k∗𝐕j,k∗≤μ1rn1​n2\max_{i,j}[\mathbf{U}^{*}\mathbf{V}^{*\top}]_{ij}=\max_{i,j}\sum_{k}\mathbf{U}^{*}_{i,k}\mathbf{V}^{*}_{j,k}\leq\mu_{1}\sqrt{\frac{r}{n_{1}n_{2}}}. Since |∑k𝐔i,k∗​𝐕j,k∗|≤∑k𝐔i,k∗2​∑k𝐕j,k∗2=‖𝐔i,:∗‖2​‖𝐕j,:∗‖2=rn1​n2​μi​(𝐀∗)​νj​(𝐀∗)≤rn1​n2​μ0\left|\sum_{k}\mathbf{U}^{*}_{i,k}\mathbf{V}^{*}_{j,k}\right|\leq\sqrt{\sum_{k}\mathbf{U}^{*2}_{i,k}}\sqrt{\sum_{k}\mathbf{V}^{*2}_{j,k}}=\|\mathbf{U}^{*}_{i,:}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{V}^{*}_{j,:}\|_{2}=\frac{r}{\sqrt{n_{1}n_{2}}}\sqrt{\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A}^{*})\nu_{j}(\mathbf{A}^{*})}\leq\frac{r}{\sqrt{n_{1}n_{2}}}\mu_{0} for all i,ji,j; we can just take μ1≥μ0​r\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{0}\sqrt{r}. From this, Candes & Recht (2012) show that if the coherence μ0\mu_{0} is low, few samples are required to recover 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*}.

Theorem G.11 (Theorem 1.3, Candes & Recht (2012)).

Let 𝐀∗∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} be a matrix of rank rr sampled from the random orthogonal model, and put n=max⁡(n1,n2)n=\max(n_{1},n_{2}). Suppose we observe NN entries of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with locations sampled uniformly at random. Then there are numerical constants CC and cc such that if N≥C​max⁡(μ12,μ012​μ1,μ0​n14)​n​r​β​log⁡(n)N\geq C\max\left(\mu_{1}^{2},\mu_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mu_{1},\mu_{0}n^{\frac{1}{4}}\right)nr\beta\log\left(n\right) for some β>2\beta>2, the minimizer to the problem (P4)(P_{4}) is unique and equal to 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with probability at least 1−c/n31-c/n^{3}. In addition, if r≤n1/5/μ0r\leq n^{1/5}/\mu_{0}, then the recovery is exact with probability at least 1−c/n31-c/n^{3} provided that N≥C​μ0​n6/5​r​β​log⁡(n)N\geq C\mu_{0}n^{6/5}r\beta\log\left(n\right).

Chen et al. (2014) show that sampling the element at position (i,j)(i,j) with probability pi​j=Ω​(μi+νj)p_{ij}=\Omega(\mu_{i}+\nu_{j}) allows perfect recovery of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with fewer samples, and called such sampling strategies local coherence sampling.

Theorem G.12 (Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3, Chen et al. (2014)).

Let 𝐀∗∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} be a matrix of rank rr with local coherence {μi,νj}i∈[n1],j∈[n2]\{\mu_{i},\nu_{j}\}_{i\in[n_{1}],j\in[n_{2}]}. There are universal constant c0,c1,c2>0c_{0},c_{1},c_{2}>0 such that if each element (i,j)(i,j) is independently observed with probability pi​j≥max⁡{min⁡{c0​(μi+νj)​r​log2⁡(n1+n2)min⁡(n1,n2),1},1min(n1,n2)10}p_{ij}\geq\max\left\{\min\left\{c_{0}\frac{(\mu_{i}+\nu_{j})r\log^{2}(n_{1}+n_{2})}{\min(n_{1},n_{2})},1\right\},\frac{1}{\min(n_{1},n_{2})^{10}}\right\}, then 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} is the unique optimal solution of the nuclear minimization problem (P4)(P_{4}) with probability at least 1−c1/(n1+n2)c21-c_{1}/(n_{1}+n_{2})^{c_{2}}, for a number of sample N∈𝒪​(max⁡(n1,n2)​r​log2⁡(n1+n2))N\in\mathcal{O}\left(\max(n_{1},n_{2})r\log^{2}(n_{1}+n_{2})\right).

Given NN and τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], to control the coherence,

    For matrix factorization, we select the first N1=τ​NN_{1}=\tau N examples with the highest values of μi​(𝐀∗)+νj​(𝐀∗)\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A}^{*})+\nu_{j}(\mathbf{A}^{*}), and select the remaining (1−τ)​N(1-\tau)N examples uniformly among the rest. The positions selected are one-hot encoded in dimensions n1n_{1} (for row positions) and n2n_{2} (for column positions) to have 𝐗(1)\mathbf{X}^{(1)} and 𝐗(2)\mathbf{X}^{(2)}, respectively.

  • •

    For matrix sensing, we generate 𝐗(1)\mathbf{X}^{(1)} (resp. 𝐗(2)\mathbf{X}^{(2)}) by taking the first N1=min⁡(⌊τ​N⌋,n1)N_{1}=\min(\lfloor\tau N\rfloor,n_{1}) (resp. N1=min⁡(⌊τ​N⌋,n2)N_{1}=\min(\lfloor\tau N\rfloor,n_{2})) rows from the first columns of 𝐔∗\mathbf{U}^{*} (resp. 𝐕∗\mathbf{V}^{*}) and the elements of the remaining N2=N−N1N_{2}=N-N_{1} rows iid from the Gaussian distribution 𝒩​(0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) with σ=1/n1\sigma=1/n_{1} (resp. σ=1/n2\sigma=1/n_{2}).

The higher τ\tau (and so N1N_{1}), the less incoherence between the measures (rows of 𝐗=𝐗(2)∙𝐗(1)\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{X}^{(2)}\bullet\mathbf{X}^{(1)}) and Φ=𝐕∗⊗𝐔∗\Phi=\mathbf{V}^{*}\otimes\mathbf{U}^{*}.

G.2.3 Impact of Coherence on Grokking

Linear programming

We fix n1=n2=102n_{1}=n_{2}=10^{2} and 𝝃=0\boldsymbol{\xi}=0 (no noise) and solve for different (N,r,τ)(N,r,\tau) the matrix factorization problem presented above using standard linear programming (we use the cvxpy library). As rr and/or τ\tau increases, the number of samples needed for perfect recovery decreases. The relative recovery error ‖𝐀−𝐀∗‖2/‖𝐀∗‖2\|\mathbf{A}-\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{2}/\|\mathbf{A}^{*}\|_{2} obtained is usually of the order of 10−610^{-6} and gives us a basis for comparison with other methods. We do not include figures to save space.

Gradient Descent

Unlike compressed sensing where large values of τ\tau are detrimental to generalization, here, as τ→1\tau\rightarrow 1, performance improves, and the number of examples required to generalize decreases exponentially, as does the time it takes the models to do so. See Figure 23 for (n1,n2,r,α,β,ζ)=(10,10,2,10−1,10−5,10−6)(n_{1},n_{2},r,\alpha,\beta,\zeta)=(10,10,2,10^{-1},10^{-5},10^{-6}). Note that here, for matrix completion, for a fixed τ\tau, we select the first τ​N\tau N examples with the highest values of μi​(𝐀∗)+νj​(𝐀∗)\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A}^{*})+\nu_{j}(\mathbf{A}^{*}), and select the remaining (1−τ)​N(1-\tau)N examples at random, uniformly.

Appendix H Additional Experiments

H.1 Sparse Recovery

Optimization landscape

We look at the landscape of the solution in the context of sparse recovery. Let I:={i∈[n]∣𝐚i∗≠0}I:=\{i\in[n]\mid\mathbf{a}^{*}_{i}\neq 0\} be the support of the ground truth signal 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}; u​(t)=‖𝐚I(t)‖2u(t)=\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}_{I}\|_{2} and v​(t)=‖𝐚[n]\I(t)‖2v(t)=\|\mathbf{a}^{(t)}_{[n]\backslash I}\|_{2} be the norms of 𝐚(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)} restraint on its indexes in II and outside II, respectively. Figure 24 shows how 𝐚(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)} first converges to the least square solution (memorization), and from the least square solution to 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*} (NN large enough) or a suboptimal solution (NN too small). After memorization, when NN is large enough, v​(t)v(t) converges to zero while u​(t)u(t) converges to the norm of 𝐚∗\mathbf{a}^{*}. This is because the components of 𝐚(t)\mathbf{a}^{(t)} that are not in II are shrunk at each training step until they all reach 0 (Figure 25). This convergence is impossible if the ℓ1\ell_{1} regularization strength is 0 (even if ℓ2\ell_{2} is used). For the experiments of this section we use N∈{20,30,40,50,60,70}N\in\{20,30,40,50,60,70\}, for (n,s)=(100,5)(n,s)=(100,5) and (α,β)=(10−1,10−5)(\alpha,\beta)=(10^{-1},10^{-5}).

Scaling the Learning Rate α\alpha and the Regularization Strength β\beta

We solve the sparse recovery problem using the subgradient descent method with (n,s,N,ζ)=(102,5,30,10−6)(n,s,N,\zeta)=(10^{2},5,30,10^{-6}) for different values of α\alpha and β\beta. As expected, larger α\alpha and/or β\beta lead to fast convergence and do so at a suboptimal value of the test error (Figure 26). However, small values require longer training time to plateau and generally do so at a lower value of recovery error (grokking). These are the experiments used to produce Figure 4.

Scaling the Data Size NN and the Sparsity Parameter ss

We solve the sparse recovery problem using the subgradient descent method with (n,ζ,α,β)=(102,10−6,10−1,10−5)(n,\zeta,\alpha,\beta)=(10^{2},10^{-6},10^{-1},10^{-5}), for s∈{1,5,10,15}s\in\{1,5,10,15\} and N∈{10,20,…​100}N\in\{10,20,\dots 100\}. See Figures 27 and 28 for the results. Smaller ss requires a smaller NN for generalization.

H.2 Matrix Factorization

We optimize the noiseless matrix completion problem using the subgradient descent method with (n1,n2,r,N,ζ)=(10,10,2,70,10−6)(n_{1},n_{2},r,N,\zeta)=(10,10,2,70,10^{-6}) for different values of α\alpha and β\beta. As expected, larger α\alpha and/or β\beta lead to fast convergence and do so at a suboptimal value of the test error (Figure 29). These are the experiments used to produce Figure 6.

H.3 General Setting

In this section we optimize functions of the form f​(θ)=g​(θ)+β​h​(θ)f(\theta)=g(\theta)+\beta h(\theta), where gg is the square loss or cross-entropy loss function of the considered model on the training data, θ\theta the set of model parameters, and hh a regularizer applied to θ\theta. It can be the standard ℓp\ell_{p} norm or quasi-norm of θ\theta, the sum of the nuclear norms of each matrix in θ\theta (i.e. ℓ∗\ell_{*}), etc. By normal initialization for a parameter 𝐀∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}}, we mean 𝐀(1)​∼i​i​d​𝒩​(0,1/n1)\mathbf{A}^{(1)}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,1/n_{1}). For the experiments of this section only, we used Adam as the optimizer, with its default parameters (as specified in PyTorch), except for the learning rate.

We consider addition modulo p=97p=97 as described in Section 2.1 with rtrain=40%r_{\text{train}}=40\%. H.3.3 Domain Specific Regularization

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (Raissi et al., 2019) leverage prior knowledge from differential equations by incorporating their residuals into the loss function, ensuring that solutions remain consistent with physical laws. Sobolev training (Czarnecki et al., 2017) generalizes this idea by incorporating not only input-output pairs but also derivatives of the target function. More precisely, given input-output pairs {(𝐱i,𝐲∗(𝐱i)}i∈[N]\left\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\}_{i\in[N]} along with known derivatives {∂k𝐲∗​(𝐱)∂𝐱k|𝐱=𝐱i}i∈[N]\left\{\frac{\partial^{k}\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{k}}\Big{|}_{\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}_{i}}\right\}_{i\in[N]} for k∈[K]k\in[K], the goal is to train a neural network 𝐲θ​(𝐱)\mathbf{y}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) that approximates both the output and its derivatives. The loss function extends the standard mean squared error (MSE) to include Sobolev penalties:

f​(θ)=1N​∑i=1N‖𝐲θ​(𝐱i)−𝐲∗​(𝐱i)‖2⏟data loss+βN​∑k=1K∑i=1N‖∂k𝐲θ∂𝐱k​(𝐱i)−∂k𝐲∗∂𝐱k​(𝐱i)‖F2⏟Sobolev penaltyf(\theta)=\underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\|\mathbf{y}_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\|^{2}}_{\text{data loss}}+\underbrace{\frac{\beta}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\|\frac{\partial^{k}\mathbf{y}_{\theta}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{k}}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-\frac{\partial^{k}\mathbf{y}^{*}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{k}}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\|_{\text{F}}^{2}}_{\text{Sobolev penalty}} (125)

The hyperparameter β\beta controls the contribution of the derivative alignment term. This penalty ensures that the model not only fits the data but also respects known smoothness constraints or differential structure, which is crucial in physics-based applications (Lu et al., 2021). We consider the two layers feed forward teacher of Section H.3.2, and optimize the parameters θ=(𝐀,𝐁)\theta=(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}) of a student using the sobolev objectify for K=1K=1, ∂𝐲∗​(𝐱)∂𝐱=𝐁∗​diag⁡(ϕ′​(𝐀∗​𝐱))​𝐀∗\frac{\partial\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{B}^{*}\operatorname{diag}\left(\phi^{\prime}(\mathbf{A}^{*}\mathbf{x})\right)\mathbf{A}^{*}. The smaller is α​β\alpha\beta, the longer is the delay between memorization and generalization. See Figure 34 for an experiment with (d,r,c,N)=(100,500,2,102)(d,r,c,N)=(100,500,2,10^{2}).
